en: Through its connection with Bhavabhūti, the speech of this work shines like the very earth of the mountains;
otherwise, why would even a stone weep at his compassion?
— Govardhana.

Although the life story of this poet is not found in its entirety anywhere, nevertheless, since this great poet has provided at least a brief description of his own lineage and other details in the prologues to his three compositions known as the *Mālatīmādhava*, the *Mahāvīracarita*, and the *Uttararāmacarita*, there is no possibility of a lack of interest for those who desire to know. To illustrate: [The text continues with the specific verses from the prologues.]

In the southern region, in Vidarbha, there lived in a city named Padmapura certain Taittirīyas of the Kāśyapa lineage who were preceptors of the Caraṇa school, sanctifiers of the assembly, maintainers of the five sacred fires, performers of Soma sacrifices, and exponents of the Veda known by the surname Udumbara. In that lineage was born a certain Brahmin named Mahākavi, a performer of the Vājapeya sacrifice. The fifth descendant from him was Bhavabhūti, the son of Lakṣmaṇakaṇṭha, whose fame is pure, and the grandson of Bhaṭṭa Gopāla, whose name is auspiciously invoked.
His mother was Jātukarṇī, and his preceptor was named Jñānanidhi, whose name was true to its meaning.

Although he bore the father-given name Śrīkaṇṭha, according to some, he was called Bhavabhūti because: “I bow to the two breasts of Girijā, which have faces made white by Bhava (Śiva), appearing like two smiling faces as if wondering, ‘To what state has this ascetic reached? I praise these breasts, which possess faces whitened by Bhava.

Following the composition of the verse beginning with "iti," according to the opinion of others, after the composition of the verse "Sāmbā punātu bhavabhūtipavitramūrtiḥ," he became renowned in the world by the name Bhavabhūti.

That Bhavabhūti was present in the court of Yaśovarman, the lord of Kānyakubja, as is known from the following verse in the *Rājatarangiṇī*: "Yaśovarman, who had been conquered, went to the state of being praised for his virtues by the poet Vākpatirāja, the illustrious Bhavabhūti, and others."
Yaśovarman lived in the seventh century CE;
furthermore, a certain poet named Vākpatirāja, who was a contemporary of his, respectfully mentioned Bhavabhūti’s name in his own work, and he belonged to the eighth century.
Therefore, it is understood that Bhavabhūti’s period was either the latter half of the seventh century or the beginning of the eighth century.

This poet possesses an exceedingly sharp intellect; though he has studied the Vedas along with their Upaniṣads and has achieved a profound mastery of the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Tarka, Mīmāṃsā, and other sciences, he is nevertheless endowed with such genius that he has grasped every secret of the science of poetics (Sāhitya). Thus, his possession of an all-pervading intellect is manifestly clear.
Apart from this triad of dramas known as the *Mālatīmādhava*, the *Mahāvīracarita*, and the *Uttararāmacarita* composed by this poet, no other work written by him is currently available.

Nevertheless, it is stated in the *Śārṅgadharapaddhati*: "If the verses are faultless, what loss is there to the drama? Would sugarcane become tasteless simply because it has been cast into the hands of beggars?"
Thus says the verse in the *Rasikajīvana* composed by Gadādharabhaṭṭa:
"O Wind, why do you scatter this wave of musk fragrance—followed by swarms of bees and dispelling the fever of the hearts of the connoisseurs—among the vulgar?"
Does the moon awaken the night-lotuses out of a desire for some reciprocal service?
For those of noble mind who are truly virtuous, their very nature is such that their life is dedicated to the passion for helping others.
The two verses beginning with "ra. jī. pra. are found cited under the name Bhavabhūti.

Therefore, it is currently impossible to determine whether another dramatic work or poetic composition was written by this poet, or if these are his *subhāṣitas* (wise sayings), or if there is some other Bhavabhūti who is the author of these verses.

Nevertheless, it can be inferred that some dramatic compositions were composed by this author—given the stage-manager’s statement, "The poet named Bhavabhūti exists among the Bharatas," and the poet’s own remark, "Those who spread contempt for us here"—but having fallen under the power of time, they have perished.

Following this sequence—"Māravīra-karuṇā"—this poet composed *Mālatīmādhava*, which is preeminent in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*); *Mahāvīracarita*, which is preeminent in the heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*); and *Uttararāmacarita*, which is preeminent in the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa-rasa*) and possesses the highest excellence among the three.
Although an abundance of compounds is observed in his works, and particularly in *Mālatīmādhava*, nevertheless, these were written by resorting solely to the Vaidarbha style.
For instance: "Cohesion (*śleṣa*), clarity (*prasāda*), evenness (*samatā*), sweetness (*mādhurya*), delicacy (*sukumāratā*),..."
Lucidity of meaning, nobility, vigor, grace, and concentration—
these ten qualities are traditionally held to be the life-breaths of the Vaidarbha style.
Thus, the qualities mentioned by Daṇḍin appear in their respective forms within his compositions.
Regarding those, the poet himself states the primary ones with the words: "That which is maturity and loftiness of expression, and that which is gravity of meaning," and so forth.

This poet, the author of the *Nāṭaka*, does not merely ascend to the same level as Kālidāsa; rather, it appears that the scholarly consensus—that "Bhavabhūti excels in the *Uttararāmacarita*"—is by no means inconsistent with reason.

Furthermore, the defect of tautology, which is occasionally encountered in the works of Kālidāsa and causes a sense of distaste among sensitive readers, is generally not observed in the compositions of Bhavabhūti. Moreover, such is this poet’s verbal ingenuity and skill in evoking aesthetic flavor (rasa) that his words are truly those of a master of speech.

Thus, regarding this statement of the poet: "O Brahmin, this goddess Speech follows him alone like a submissive servant," what connoisseur would not say: "For that is a declaration of the actual state of affairs; it is no self-praise on the part of the Great-souled One"?
In short, we believe that all the essential qualities of a great poet—inspiration and the rest—are present together in Bhavabhūti.
Regarding what was previously stated— that this poet has composed three dramas—
among them is the *Mālatīmādhava*, a *prakaraṇa*.
Since its definition has already been provided by the commentator, it is not restated here.

In this [drama], the erotic sentiment of union (*saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra*) is the primary element, and that is preceded by the erotic sentiment of separation (*vipralambha*). Other sentiments— such as the heroic (*vīra*), the marvelous (*adbhuta*), the pathetic (*karuṇa*), and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*)— are subordinate to it.

In this regard—here, in the passage beginning with "kimapi," there arises passion (*rāga*) in the hero; and in the verse beginning with "alasavalita-," through the *anubhāvas* (consequent emotions) consisting of side-long glances and spoken words, there is the perception of the state of love (*rati-bhāva*) directed toward Mādhava—which has reached its highest intensity—as well as the perception of the appropriate transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāvas*). Furthermore, through the passage beginning with "mādhavasyāpy apahṛtam," there is the perception of the deep passion residing within Mālatī’s own object of affection, along with its corresponding transitory states and appropriate consequent emotions. Thus, there occurs a simultaneous suggestion (*dhvani*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) based on mutual objects.
For this very reason, the seed (bīja), which consists of mutual affection, is deposited right here. In the same way, other matters should also be inferred in their respective places.
As for the interruption in the middle, the kindling in the middle, the interruption again, and the kindling again—that is solely with regard to the expectation of the nourishment of the limbs (aṅga).
Other matters, such as the sentiments (rasas) of heroism, the marvelous, and the loathsome, should be observed as they have been determined by the commentator in various places.
Furthermore, certain other points not mentioned here may be inferred; however, they are not stated here for fear of prolixity.
Because this is a dramatic work (prakaraṇa), it consists of ten acts (aṅkas).

Since a narrative based on historical events (*itivṛtta*) that is fashioned by the poet’s imagination produces such extraordinary aesthetic delight (*camatkāra*) in the hearts of the sensitive, the poet rightly says: "Does there exist anywhere such a great, wonderful, diverse, beautiful, and radiant *mahāprakaraṇa*?
In this work, the specific features are the absence of a *vidūṣaka* and a secondary heroine (*pratināyikā*), as well as the absence of verses in the Prakrit language.
All of this and more has been stated in detail in the Introduction composed in the English language; therefore, let us conclude here.
May there be auspiciousness for both the student and the teacher.
M.R. Kale. Śrīḥ!
*Mālatīmādhava*.
With joy: When the serpent-king, terrified by the young peacock summoned by the sound of the drum struck by Nandin’s hand, contracts his coils and enters the aperture at the tip of [Śiva’s] nose...

May the quivering movements of the faces of Ganesha, as he dances at the side of the Trident-wielder—making the quarters of the sky resonant with swarms of bees flying up from his temples—protect you for a long time with their cries of joy.

May Sthāṇu, who possesses the shimmering moon as his beautiful flower, whose sprouts are his intoxicating matted locks, and whose abode for his five fingers is the jewel of the proud and fierce serpent—
may he grant me abundant fruit, as if constantly assuming a divine state out of a longing for the flowing nectar melting from the moon-like face of Gaurī.
Having bowed to his gurus, who are preeminent in virtue, and having consulted the Viśva and other lexicons, the Bharata-śāstra, the science of grammar, the Veda,
the meters, the treatises on poetics, and the interpretation of meaning, the illustrious Jagaddhara composes this commentary.

In this sharp drama unfolding upon the throat of Śrīkaṇṭha, a commentary is being composed by me, even though my intellect is small; may this not lead to the laughter of the multitude of wicked men, for everyone desires a high station.

In this work, while composing the eight-line *nāndī*, the poet—seeking the unimpeded accomplishment of his desired aim—performs at the beginning of the play an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) in the form of a praise of Lambodara (Gaṇeśa), by means of the sudden display of the wild *tāṇḍava* dance of the Lord of Caṇḍī. "With joy," and so forth: may the shakes of the face of Vaināyaka protect you for a long time; that is to say, may the movements of the elephant-faced god’s countenance guard you for a long duration.
Thus the poet offers his benediction to the listeners and the members of the assembly.

He states the reason for shaking his head: "When the lord of serpents, the nāga Vāsuki, joyfully enters the aperture at the tip of the nose—the opening at the end of the trunk—here, 'nose' refers specifically to that of Vināyaka."

The sense is that there is joy due to the hope for life resulting from the terrified one’s sudden attainment of the opening at the top. For this very reason, there is no room for the objection as to how "joy" can be an adverb following immediately after "entry," because the intensity of joy arises precisely from the swift attainment of the opening at the top.
Just as there is joy for one who is terrified upon quickly reaching his home or similar place;
or rather, it should be construed as "may they protect [us] in such a way that it is accompanied by bliss";
or else, "sānadam" is an adjective qualifying [the act of protecting].
The compound is justified because it conveys meaning despite being dependent [on another word].
Precisely because it functions as an adverb (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), in the expression *sānandam*, there is the status of an object (*karman*), singular number, and neuter gender.

O you who cry out in distress! In the *Mālatīmādhava*, where one ought to say "here at the nostril," the use of the term "tip" (*agra*) is intended to indicate the joy arising from the sudden recovery of the terrified person.

Alternatively, since the entry of the tip [of the arrow] upon the entry of the shaft is already established by implication, its explicit mention through words constitutes the ornament *uktipoṣa* (enhancement of what has been said).
As Daṇḍin says:
"The ornament *uktipoṣa* occurs when that which is obtained through implication is explicitly mentioned by word."
Of what kind was the lord of serpents?
He was one who "possesses the contraction of his coils," meaning he possesses the contraction—either of his hoods or his body—of those coils (*bhoga*).
[The action took place] upon him.
In following the cavities, there is the contraction of the serpent’s coils; this is the rule of its nature.
By this, the suitability of the great body for entry through the tip of the nose is stated.

He states the cause for the entry: when the dance (*tāṇḍava*) of Śiva, the wielder of the trident, takes place, [the breath enters] out of fear of the young peacock—the peacock of Kārttikeya—summoned by the sound of the *muraja* drum struck by the hand of Nandin, a particular class of attendants (*gaṇa*).
Here, by the fact that the drum is struck by Nandi’s hand, its possession of a deep and loud sound is shown;
and by the peacock being devoured by a serpent, its terrifying nature is indicated.
Of what kind are the shakes?
Those [elephants] by which the quarters of the sky were made resonant— rendered noisy— by swarms of bees (*alimālā*) that had flown up from their temples (*gaṇḍa*);
likewise, they were accompanied by *cītkāra*, the cry of terror of frightened elephants,
because Vināyaka has the face of an elephant.
In this context, the possessive suffix (*matvartha*) signifies mere concomitance (*sāhityamātra*).
Thus, the intended meaning is that the shaking of the head and the shrieking occur simultaneously out of fear.
The poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) here is *jāti*.
Although lightning is insentient, it acts as a protector solely through the power of the presiding deity;
for this very reason, it is attributed with agency even toward one who is terrified.
Here, the fact that serpents seek out their holes out of fear of peacocks attracted by the sound of deep-drumming is a sign of the rainy season.
For this very reason, it is suggested that the events of this section take place only after experiencing the rainy season;
as he will state later: "Fragrant with the earth moistened by showers," and so forth.

By indicating the drumming through the striking of the *muraja* drum, the singing through the resonating of the quarters with swarms of bees, and the dancing through the shaking of the face, the threefold symphony (*tauryatrika*) is described.
By the sound of "cītkāra," even the explicit recitation [of the word] is indicated.
According to Amarasimha, "kumāraḥ krauñcāraṇaḥ" (the young one is the krauñca bird).
This [state] belonging to Kumāra is "kaumāram."
The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] in the sense of "this belongs to him.
"Mayūra, barhiṇa, barhin, nīlakaṇṭha, and bhujaṅgabhuk" [are synonyms for peacock], according to Amara.
Regarding the distinction between words: "nāsā, nāśā, and nāsikā" [are synonyms].
"Bhogaḥ [is used] in the sense of pleasure, the enjoyment of women and so forth, and the body of a serpent's hood," according to the Viśva-kośa.

The word *uḍḍīna* is derived from the root *ḍī* preceded by the prefix *ud*, with the suffix *kta*. By the rule "and [the roots] ending in *o*," the letter *n* is substituted for *t*. It is said: "The terms *praḍīna*, *uḍḍīna*, and *saṃḍīna* denote these various movements of birds."
Thus says Amara:
"The quarters are *kakubhaḥ* and *kāṣṭhāḥ*.
And: "*Tāṇḍavam*, *naṭanam*, *nāṭyam*, *lāsyam*, *nṛtyam*, and *nartanam* [are synonyms for dance]."
And thus:
"Vināyaka, Vighnarāja, Dvaimātura, and Gaṇādhipa.
And thus.
This belongs to Vināyaka; thus it is *vaināyakyam*.
According to the rule *tasyedam* ("this belongs to that"), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ-*.
"Vidhuti" is formed from the root *dhū* preceded by the prefix *vi*, with the suffix *ktin* applied in the feminine.
The engagement of discerning spectators in drama and similar works is purposeful.

As Bharata said: "There is no such knowledge, no such craft, no such science, no such arts, no such policy, and no such action that is not seen in drama. At the beginning of a drama, the *nāndī* should be performed to ward off obstacles.
As Bharata said: "Even though there are many constituent parts of the *pūrvaraṅga* in a drama, nevertheless, the *nāndī* must necessarily be performed for the pacification of obstacles."

And the definition of the *nāndī* is given by Bharata: "The wise should diligently compose the *nāndī*, preceded by words of blessing for the gods, the twice-born, the king, and others, and joined with a salutation."
The *nāndī* should be composed by poets, marked with these name-words: Gaṅgā, Nāgapati, Soma, Svadhā, Ānanda, Jaya, and Āśis.
This benediction (nāndī), composed with elegant phrasing, accompanied by the praise of the Moon, intent upon the eight directions,
and endowed with auspiciousness, should now be employed.
A certain *nāndī* of twelve lines—moreover:

**Act One** May the matted locks (*jaṭā*) of the Lord of Beings protect you—locks from which the waters of the Mandākinī flow in profusion, mingled with the mass of skulls worn as a crest; whose luster is blended with the light from the cavity of his forehead-eye that is like a flash of lightning; whose lovely crescent moons are obscured by the tips of his hair; and which are bound together by a garland of coiled serpent-creepers.
A certain eight-line verse is prescribed;
the stage director, established in the middle register, should recite it.
"Where the mention of the moon occurs, the highest aesthetic flavor (rasa) depends upon it;
when the moon is pleased, the beauty of rasa flourishes—thus says the wise man."
In this regard, some maintained that a *pada* is a word ending in a case-suffix,
while others stated that it is a portion of a verse (*padya*).
Thus, by adopting the latter position here, the *nāndī* consists of eight *padas*, being composed of two verses.
Fearing many obstacles and performing further auspicious rites to ward them off, he concludes the eight-line *nāndī* with the verse beginning "cūḍāpīḍa" and so forth:
"May the matted locks of Hara, the Lord of Beings, protect you, the foremost of the assembly. Of what nature are they?"

In their crests—the topknots—is a *āpīḍa*, a garland bound crosswise; these [streams] are filled (*saṃkula*) with *kapālas*, which are masses of dried skull-bones, and for that very reason, they possess the water of the Mandākinī—the Ganges—trickling down from them.
Here, the "garland" refers specifically to the skulls.
Alternatively, those whose ornaments are skulls may have crosswise garlands made of other bones, such as the collarbones or kneecaps, for the sake of decoration.
The meaning is that they are the skull-fragments connected to that [body].

Likewise, those whose splendor (*tviṭ*)—that is, their radiance—is blended with the light of the eye-socket (*locana-puṭa*) on the forehead, which is primarily lightning-like (*vidyut-prāya*), resembling lightning;
here, by the word "socket" (*puṭa*), the fact that the entire portion of the eye situated within it consists of light is expressed.
Those [clouds] in which the charming and lovely young moon is made doubtful—rendered uncertain—by the tip of a *ketakī* flower, whether it be hard, soft, or full;
for on the head of Hara, the thought "Is this the tip of a *ketakī*? is an impropriety.
Thus, the sense is that even this doubt is rooted in impropriety.

Likewise, the *bhujaṅgas* are serpents themselves, and the *vallīs* are creepers; these very [serpents and creepers] exist in the form of circular coils (*valayas*) which serve as garlands (*srajas*). Those [braids] in which the top portion of the braided hair (*jūḍa* or *jūṭaka*) is bound or tied with such garlands are so described.

Thus, by this [description], although the mass of matted hair (*jaṭājūṭa*) is brownish from incessant bathing, its form is concealed by being entwined with serpents; because of its extreme blackness, it suggests the rising of clouds, and thus indicates the movement of snakes. By the dripping of the Gaṅgā water, it suggests rainfall; by the garland of skulls (*kapālamālā*), a row of cranes (*balākāvali*); and by the flames of the fire from the eye on the forehead, the radiance of *kaitaka* flowers. [Note: *Cūḍā* refers to the crest. Beyond this, these two verses are recited by some:
Furthermore:
"In the rows of teeth, they are agitated by the turning back of the splashing sounds; in the cavities of the nostrils, eyes, and the hollows of the ears, they produce a stammering sound."
May the streams flowing from the cavernous skull-bowl of Śambhu—streams intensified by the throbbing of his forehead-tumor, the swelling of his goiter, and the wounds on his temples—protect you.
And furthermore:

May that third eye of Purañjaya, which burnt away Madana, protect you—the eye whose entire mass of rays is like a single speck of the tawny hue of a row of eyelashes; into which the Sacrificer of Time offered the entire universe as an oblation within its slightly opened bud; and whose corner was made resonant by the flow of nectar dripping from the moon upon his crest, which had been recently heated. At the conclusion of the *nāndī* in the *Mālatīmādhava*, the Stage Manager says: "Enough with this excessive prolixity."
Looking ahead:
Ah, the venerable sun, the lamp of all the islands of the world, has almost risen. Therefore, I shall offer my worship.
Having prostrated:

By its brilliance, it displays the flash of lightning; and by the young moon, which shows the likeness of a *ketaka* bud-tip, it indicates the season of thick clouds that kindle the intoxication of Love—thus, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) pervading this dramatic work is also hinted at.
One should note that the protection of the inanimate matted locks is due to the power of the deity.
In the phrase "a garland of encircling creeper-bands," the poetic figure is *rūpaka* (metaphor).
The etymological derivation is that the term *api ca* is employed where there is mutual dependence.
"Ending with the Nāndī."
The *nāndī* is the verse—such as those found at the beginning of a *nāṭaka* and other genres—possessing the characteristics already described.
It is called *nanda* because it causes joy (*nandayati*) through the employment of benedictions and so forth; the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for roots beginning with *pac*.
*Nanda* itself is *nānda*;
the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule beginning with *prajñādi*,
and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañj*.
The Nāndī.
And the definition of the Sūtradhāra is given in the *Bharata*: "That which constitutes the performance of the drama, together with its seed (the plot), is the *sūtra*;
one who performs the worship of the deities of the stage is called the Sūtradhāra."
Thus [it is said]. But surely, the phrase "at the end of the *nāndī*, the *sūtradhāra*" is inconsistent;
for the *sūtradhāra* does not enter the stage immediately after the recitation of the *nāndī*.
However, having entered, he recites it;
nor indeed should it be recited by anyone else,
because the *nāndī* has been stated as something to be recited specifically by the *sūtradhāra*.
"Because of the statement: 'The Sūtradhāra should recite the Nāndī while maintaining the middle pitch'—
thus it is said."
Having recited the *nāndī*, the *sūtradhāra* enters or recites it.
Since this [recitation] is heard as belonging to the *sūtradhāra* at the conclusion of the *nāndī*, it too must be recited by him alone.
It was not stated that "first the *sūtradhāra* enters."
Because the performance of salutations to the deities and so forth is prescribed specifically for the purpose of auspiciousness;
or alternatively, the *nāndī* should first be recited by the *sūtradhāra* himself immediately after entering the stage.
The term "staging director" (*sthāpaka*) is used for the actor because of his similarity to the *sūtradhāra*, as indicated by the phrase "at the end of the *nāndī*, the *sūtradhāra* [speaks]."
As Bharata said: "Having performed the *nāndī*, the *sūtradhāra* should exit along with his attendants;
thereafter, the *sthāpaka*, who possesses the qualities and appearance of the *sūtradhāra*, shall enter."
"Having first performed the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga), when the stage-manager (sūtradhāra) has departed,
another actor enters in a similar manner and establishes the play.
For this very reason, some read "the Sthāpaka" [instead of the Sūtradhāra] at the end of the Nāndī.

But surely, there are many constituent elements of drama (*nāṭyāṅga*) prior to the prologue (*prastāvanā*); why have they not been mentioned? As Bharata has said: "With verses sweet in their grace for the stage and indicative of the meaning of the poem, one should adopt a particular season and resort to the *Bhāratī* style."
Through various means accompanied by persuasive inducements, such as the petitioner, the jester, or the prologue,
the *sūtradhāra* addresses either the *māriṣa* or the *vidūṣaka*.
That which, through a striking expression, anticipates its own subsequent development is the *āmukha* (prologue).
Therefore he says, "Enough.
This is the intention: the other [elements] mentioned previously do not exist here; rather, they are for the purpose of attracting the audience.

If the audience itself has already paid close attention and is eager to behold the new drama, then even pride (māna) becomes a supreme obstacle to the aesthetic flavor (rasa); thus, there is no need to compose those [other elements].

Otherwise, it would be fruitless in the assembly. The particle *aye* expresses agitation arising from the sudden perception of something not previously perceived due to distraction or other causes, such as the unexpected sight of the rising sun. Then, one should recite a single verse with a deep tone.
Placing the hymn of praise to the deity at the forefront, for whomsoever this worship proceeds.
Thus, having assented to the opinion of Bharata, he introduces the verse to be recited at the entrance of the stage for the sake of auspiciousness, beginning with the word *udita*:
"He whose [orb] has risen most abundantly..."— that is,
the greater portion of it has risen.
The sense is that only a very small portion remains for its rising.
Here, because of the prohibition [found in the *Manusmṛti*], "one should not look at the sun as it rises," it is said that it has "mostly risen.

*Bhaga* is the perfection of knowledge and so forth; he who possesses that is *bhagavān*. Otherwise, there would be an interruption of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Enough, enough with this! [He gazes] toward the East—the very one, the jewel of the sky, the lamp, that very one... Act One.

O you whose form is the universe, you are the vessel of all auspicious glories; O Lord, bestow upon me abundantly the fortune that bears the burden of my goals, and be gracious. O Lord of the World, cast away whatever sin belongs to me as I bow before you; grant me every blessing, O Blessed One, for the sake of supreme well-being.

Looking toward the dressing room: My friend, the auspicious rites for the stage have been well-prepared, and a great assembly of people from various regions has gathered on the occasion of the festival of the holy Lord Kālapriyanātha.
Furthermore, I have been commanded by the assembly of learned men that we must entertain them with some unprecedented dramatic composition.
So why do the actors remain indifferent?
The meaning is "by means of a cow.
"I shall approach" (upatiṣṭhe); the word "with a verse" (ślokena) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
He says that very thing in the verse beginning with "of auspicious things," and so forth:
"O Viśvamūrti, O God who consists of all!
You are called 'Deva' because you shine; thus, O Radiant One!"
You are the vessel, the receptacle, of auspicious glories, blessings, and splendors;
therefore, be gracious, be well-pleased.
