is so called because "the word *parimala* denotes an auspicious fragrance," according to the *Viśva-kośa*.
It is *milan*, meaning "meeting" or "blending."

The row of *bakula* buds, dense and agitated, is a cluster of buds facing toward full bloom; it is that very thing which serves as a captivating ornament, and thus [the tree] is "delightful" (*ramaṇīya*) by means of it.
Alternatively, there is a compound meaning "sweet with the fragrance of wine" (*madirāmoda-madhura*).
By this, he states that the fragrance of wine acts as a *dohada* (a longing or stimulus) for the emergence of the *bakula* flowers.
By this [verse], the loveliness of the courtyard situated nearby—due to watering and so forth—is shown.

Here, in the word *aṅgana*, the hearing of the nasalized *ṇ* (ṇatva) is improper due to the absence of a rule providing for it; even the statement that the *ṇ* occurs by virtue of its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group is entirely without foundation.

On the contrary, since the *Viśvakośa* and other lexicons state, "The word *aṅgana* is understood to mean a courtyard, a lattice, or a beautiful woman (*kāminī*)," and because the *Śabdaprakāśa* states that *aṅgana* is simply formed with the fifth letter of the dental class (*tavarga*), it should be noted that it possesses only the final *na*.
The term *ālavāla* is known as *khala*; as Amarasimha states: "Ālavāla and āvāla are the names for that wherein water is held.
Regarding the word *vidagdha*:
The creation of the garland is for the purpose of demonstrating proficiency in the science of love (*kāmaśāstra*).
The intended meaning is that this is stated by the passage beginning with "the various methods of stringing a garland" and so forth.
Here, the garland is woven from *bakula* flowers because they surpass other flowers in their extreme delicacy, their power to captivate the minds of lovers, their fragrance, and their beauty.
For this very reason, even at Damayantī’s svayaṃvara and other such occasions, she accepted a wreath of madhūka flowers equal in beauty to a wreath of bakula blossoms.
She was a moving, ever-wandering banner of victory for Makarakeṭu, the god of love.
Her maidenhood was revealed by her bright, pure, and refined arrangement of ornaments for her young body, fashioned within the inner chambers of her residence.
The sense is that because she is a maiden, there is an absence of a veil or similar covering, and thus her [beauty] is revealed.
She is characterized by the power of the passion of one whose sole delight is in a person of great majesty.
"Atyudāra" means either very noble or very generous.

With great curiosity for the magnificent and grand sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*), Bakulamukha, having repeatedly gathered flowers from the blossoming *bakula* trees, fashioned a garland with a clever arrangement. In the *Mālatīmādhava*, [the poet says]: "She is either the presiding deity of the treasure-house of loveliness, or the abode where the essence of all beauty is gathered.
O friend, it is certain that the moon, nectar, lotus-stalks, moonlight, and the god of love were the causes of her creation."
Being entreated by her affectionate female attendants, who were delighted by the sport of gathering dense clusters of flowers, she came to that very spot beneath the *viṅkuḷa* tree.
And there, we observed in her—a being born of great fortune—a transformation caused by the anguish of love that seemed to have been accumulating for many days;
for as the lexicon states: "atha" [is used] in the sense of "then."
The courtesy of the attendants is to be understood through their bringing [the deity] into presence;
for that very reason, it occurs right there.

He speaks of the praise of her qualities, beginning with "She" (*sā*): that woman is the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*)—the presiding power—of the treasure (*nidhi*), which is the repository of loveliness (*rāmaṇīyaka*), that is, of charm.
Alternatively, loveliness itself is the treasure, and she is its presiding deity, its protector.
Or, she is the abode, the very home, of the collection of the essence of beauty, which is a flood of the distillate of splendor.
The coreferentiality [of the two terms] is possible because "niketana" (abode) is not fixed in gender.
The sense is that both "manoharatvam" (attractiveness) and "kāntimattvam" (splendor) are observed in that very place.
"Vā" (or) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Or "yadvā" signifies an alternative (*vikalpa*); its meaning here is that it cannot be determined. Or "yadvā" is used in the sense of "indeed" (*eva*).
The meaning is "like a deity who is a treasure-trove of loveliness.
According to the Viśva lexicon: "The word *vā* may be used in the sense of an alternative, a comparison, the particle *iva*, or even in a collective sense.
Alternatively, *rāmaṇīyaka* refers to the perfection of form and so forth; she is the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) of that treasure-trove.
By this, *śobhā* (splendor) is described.
As it is said: "The splendor of the limbs, augmented by the enjoyment of form, youth, and beauty, is proclaimed as *śobhā*. By the words beginning with *saundarya*, *kānti* (loveliness) is described.
As it is said: "Beauty itself, when filled by the wielder of the flower-arrow [Kāma], is called luster (kānti). Therefore, there is a distinction between these two.
Beholding her, who is exceedingly distinct [from ordinary beauty], he conceives this poetic fancy:
"Surely, the moon, nectar, lotus stalks, moonlight, and so forth, must have been her material cause (samavāyikāraṇa)."
The moon is for her face; the lotus-stalk is for her nectar-bearing lips; and the moonlight is for her loveliness and so forth—this is the intended meaning.
By the word "and so forth" (ādipadena), it should be understood that the lotus is for her feet and the tender sprouts are for her toes.
The sense is that this [comparison] is composed of all the materials used for metaphors.
Thus, Madana alone was her creator and fashioner;
the word "alone" (eva) is used for emphasis.
The sense is that the ancient Brahmā, who is dull-witted regarding the Vedas, possesses no skill in creation here.
Here, one should not ask "how" because desire is not heard of as the creator; rather,
it is because she is imagined to be produced by desire, which is skilled in deluding,
since such a thing has never been seen before— an observation that is favorable to the poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
Because the superimposition of what is non-existent constitutes *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
A fixed word (*niyatapada*) is the indicator of *utprekṣā*, according to the statement: "By means of words such as *nūnam* (surely), etc."
*Praṇayinī* means affectionate;
*anucarī* means a female attendant or servant;
*sañcayaḥ* means a collection or multitude.
*Avacaya* means plucking;
*dohada* means longing.
He says with joy: "That very one... etc.
He states his own position with the words "in some [case]":
"bhāgadheyam" means "fortune," according to Amara.
Here, the *garbhasandhi* (the "embryo-junction") in the form of inference is indicated by the phrase "in some [case]."
As it has been said: "Inference is declared to be the cognition of the pervader through the pervaded."

He describes the signs of transformation: "The maiden, constantly curious and longing, has somehow managed to sustain her body—which is withered like a crushed lotus stalk—through the entreaties of her attendants for various activities; moreover, her cheek, pale as a fresh slice of ivory, bears the beauty of the moon when it is free from clouds. Act One.

Furthermore, from the moment of my first sight of her, she has produced an incomparable bliss in my eyes like a wick of nectar, and she has drawn my inner heart toward herself like a piece of a magnet-stone draws iron; this is so in every respect.
What more need be said?
This mind of mine, regardless of its cause, is attached to her for the sake of a great calamity consisting of a continuous succession of torments.
Generally, it is destiny alone—the all-devouring goddess—that ordains both the auspicious and the inauspicious for a living being.
"Completely crushed": just as her limb has been thoroughly crushed—that is, subjected to pressure—so too is it withered like a lotus stalk (*mṛṇālī*).
Regarding activities such as chewing betel and so forth, she manages to engage in them only with great difficulty through the entreaties of her attendants.
Here, by the word *mṛṇālī* (lotus-stalk), leanness is expressed; by *mlānyā* (fading) and *kathamapi nidrācchedaḥ* (sleeplessness somehow), the withdrawal from sense objects is stated.
Leanness, fading, and dullness express languor (*glāni*).

As it has been said: "In languor, there is the indication of leanness, discoloration, dullness, and so forth. Now, one might ask: how can a transformation of love be inferred through transitory states such as leanness? To this, he says: "she perceives" (*kalayati*).
Its forehead bears the splendor of the moon;
by this, its paleness is indicated.
Of what sort is it?
"White as a piece of the tusk of a newly-tamed elephant"—
the word *cheda* means a "cut" or "fragment.
Here, by the use of the term "newly," the presence of horripilation (*sapulakatva*) is suggested (*dhvanita*).
And thus, the sense is that her state is inferred through such signs as the paleness of her cheeks and the bristling of her hair, which are pervaded by the transformations of love.
Paleness also occurs during separation;
as it is said: "The lack of physical grace, feverish heat, paleness, emaciation, and longing [are the signs of love]."
A line of collyrium for the eyes;
a magnet, a gem that attracts iron;
and iron ore, a substance in the form of iron.
The internal organ is the mind (*manas*). The meaning is that she has drawn my internal organ [toward her].
By the phrase "what need of more," there is an indication of a sorrowful sigh.
"Saṃtāpa-petyādi" means that my mind is attached to her as its object and is clinging to it on all sides.
A succession of torments (*saṃtāpa-paramparā*) itself constitutes a great calamity; [the compound] is for the sake of that.
The dative case is used here in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*).

By the word *santati* (lineage), it is stated that there shall be no interruption for as long as she lives until Mālatī is obtained, and that in the event of her not being found, her life will perish.
Of what kind [is he]?
It is independent of external causes.
By this, it is stated that even when the object is not obtained, his joy is innate.
As it is said: "From practice, from self-conceit, and likewise from conviction..."
"And those who know reality recognize four kinds of pleasure derived from sense objects. By this, even his own unrestrained nature is refuted.
For this very reason, he says "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*).
Generally, the divine destiny—the inevitable power of past karma—ordains both the auspicious and the inauspicious for living beings.
For this very reason, she is "all-consuming" (sarvekaṣā) and "all-destroying" (sarvaharā).
Thus, the sense is: "My suffering is inevitable, but you should act as is appropriate.
[The word *āsaktā* is derived from the root *ṣac* with the prefix *āṅ*, meaning "to assemble" or "to adhere."]

From the very moment of seeing him, she has incessantly drawn an ocean of bliss into her eyes. In the *Mālatīmādhava*, Makaranda says: "Friend Mādhava, that affection should depend upon external causes—this is a contradiction.
Behold:
An internal cause of some kind unites all things; indeed, affections do not rely upon external conditions."
For the white lotus blossoms at the rising of the sun, and the moonstone melts when the cool-rayed moon has ascended.
And then what happened?
Mādhava: And then, having first playfully raised her eyebrows there, she looked at me as if with recognition;
and then, by her friends, who were expert in reading each other's feelings, glances were cast toward her, sweet with the nectar of smiles.
In this context, the suffix *khac* is applied [to the root] by the rule "sarvakaṣa," and because it is marked with *khi*, the augment *muṭ* is inserted.
Makaranda explains the causelessness of the affection described by Mādhava with the words, "Affection," etc.
Here, the cause is twofold: external and internal.

Therefore, in this context, affection that depends upon external causes is indeed unstable; for when the cause ceases, the cessation of that affection is inevitable. Thus, the intended meaning is that affection must depend solely upon internal causes.
"Contradictory" (*vipratiṣiddha*) means opposed.
The sense is that there is a contradiction in relation to external causes.
He states the reasoning for his own position with the words beginning "it interweaves" (*vyatiṣajati*).
There exists some internal, ineffable cause that interweaves—and particularly unites—entities such as men and women;
for this reason, affections do not depend upon, nor do they intensely rely upon, external conditions or external causes such as beauty and the like.
By the word "some" (ko'pi), there is an allusion to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by experiences in previous births.
By the word "not indeed" (*na khalu*), there is the determination [of the meaning] through the negation of all worldly conditions—seen, heard, or inferred.

For this very reason, the prefix (*upasarga*) [in *ā-ās*], by means of two prefixes that indicate excellence of distinction, expresses that the life of the lotus extends until the end of its existence.
He confirms what has been stated: because the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) blossoms at the rising of the sun (*pataṅga*).

When the moon has risen, the moonstone melts and flows; likewise, upon the rising of the sun with its sharp rays, the delicate lotus petals expand, and upon the rising of the nectar-rayed moon, stones are split asunder—thus the cause is indeed spontaneously established. What external cause is perceived here?
The sense is that, similarly, in the present case as well, affection is indeed natural. Here, the word *puṇḍarīka* refers simply to a lotus.
This is an instance of the figure of speech *arthāntaranyāsa*.
"From there, from there"—this is the manner of commencing a narrative.
Mādhava:
At that place.
[The passage beginning with] "With a play of the eyebrows," and so forth.

Then, her companions, having said "This is he," looked at me as if with recognition and as if I were someone seen before; they cast side-long glances with various playful movements of their eyebrows and contractions of their brows.
By this, it is expressed that the side-long glances convey the form of recognizing one previously seen. Of what kind [were they]?

"By one who understands their mutual intentions"—by this, the heroine's excellence of proficiency is expressed. Of what sort are they? They are charming through that nectar which is a slight smile (*smita*).
"It is understood by means of cheeks slightly blossoming; thus it is called 'īṣat' (slightly). [End of] First Act.

Makaranda—(To himself) How indeed could he have recognized me? Mādhava—Then they, with playful grace, their lotus-hands raised in rhythmic clapping causing their rows of bracelets to jingle, their gait as charming as that of startled, intoxicated swans, and their movement accompanied by the tinkling of anklets and the resonant chiming of their girdles and clusters of small bells, turned around and cried out: "O Princess, by good fortune we are prospering!"
"Someone is standing right here for someone," they told me with a playful gesture of their fingers. Makaranda (to himself):
Ah, what a manifestation of long-standing affection!
The smile of noble women is considered to be one accompanied by graceful side-glances, yet without the blossoms of visible teeth.
Thus says Bharata.
Here, the word *iva* is used in the sense of a conjecture based on one's own conduct.
[Regarding the phrase] "having observed":

This is the *lalitā* (graceful) gaze. As it is said: "The gaze that is sweet, with slightly contracted pupils, accompanied by a side-long glance and a smile, and possessing the stirrings of passion—that is considered the *lalitā*."

But here, because of joy and so forth, this [lalitā] is appropriate, as it is said: "Lalitā occurs in concealment and in joy. By the phrase "play of the eyebrows," *moṭṭāyita* (the feigned anger of love) is also implied.
Makaranda:
Recognition consists in the specific combination of "that-ness" and "this-ness" regarding a single object;
its very form is expressed as "This is that."
The word *nāma* is used in the sense of "supposition.
The meaning is that because [Mādhava] has not been seen before, his recognition is impossible.
He clarifies this very point with the words "Now" (*atha*).

Immediately thereafter, those friends said, "O Princess, O daughter of our lord, we are filled with joy because someone is staying right here in this very place," and having spoken thus, they indicated me with a playful gesture of their fingers.
Having done what?
Having turned back with graceful and amorous movements.
Bharata states: "The playful movements of women are *līlā*.
*Uttāla* means intense or formidable.
*Vibhrama* refers to gracefulness or a particular kind of swaying motion.
*Mañju* means charming or pleasing.
*Mañjīra* means an anklet.
*Rasitānuviddha* means accompanied by sound or permeated with resonance.
A cluster of the girdle is a *guccha*.
Alternatively, it refers to the small bells (*kiṅkiṇī*) belonging to both the girdle (*mekhalā*) and the cluster (*kalāpa*).
The girdle (*mekhalā*) and the hair-ornament (*kalāpa*) constitute the decoration for the hips;
the *kāñcī* consists of a single string, while the *mekhalā* consists of eight strings.
The girdle is known to have sixteen [strings], and the bundle consists of twenty-five.
Thus says Bharata.
All of this is an adverbial modifier of the action of turning back.
This gait is deficient.
As it is said: “In moments of agitation, in joy, and when the body is possessed by haste—in these instances, a wise person should employ a faltering gait. Thus:
“The King is the venerable Lord; his daughter is the noble lady.”
The term "king" (*rājapada*) refers merely to a sovereign;
therefore, it should be understood that even the daughter of a minister is addressed as "the princess" (*bhartṛdārikā*).
By the phrase "some [man] to some [woman]," their cleverness is expressed through this subtle manner of presentation.
For this very reason, because of the general indication "of someone" (*kasyāpi*), its neuter gender is used;
otherwise, there would have been an indication in the feminine gender.
The masculine indication "someone" (*ko'pi*), however, is for the sake of clarity.
The sense is that if it were described otherwise as "something," there would be doubt due to the possibility of it being understood as flowers and so forth.
By the phrase "petal-like fingers," a playful narration is expressed, or rather, a concise narration is suggested;
this narration is a word of jest.
As it is said: "The wise do not desire speech that consists mostly of laughter."

"O you who are throbbing with longing, having turned back, you flourish! You have indeed shown yourself as the first among those who are dear to someone. Mādhava: (Listening) How is it that this conversation concerning women is so full of sweet and charming continuity? Makaranda: What followed after that? What followed after that? Kalahaṃsa: (Listening) How is it that this conversation concerning women is so full of sweet and charming continuity? (*kathaṃ sarasaramaṇijjāṇubandhiṇī itthīaṇakahā*) Makaranda: Then what? Then what? (*tatastataḥ*)

Mādhava: In the meantime, there appeared a certain victorious manifestation of the power of Love, belonging to the lotus-eyed maiden—a display of wonder that transcends the reach of words, which, through its weight of involuntary emotional transformations, cast aside all self-restraint.
I became the recipient of various glances— staring and wide-open, with throbbing eyebrows, smooth and closed like buds,
spreading toward the corners, and slightly contracted when falling upon my eyes.
Makaranda: Ah, joy!
"Udbheda" means manifestation or disclosure.
Kalahaṃsa:
It is continuous and implied.
"At this juncture," and so forth.

At the very moment of the friends' appearance, that instruction—the teaching—pertaining to the lotus-eyed maiden, which was born of the god of love (Mānmatha), manifested; that is, it became manifest. Of what sort was it?
It was such that its wonderful variety (*vaicitrya*) surpassed and exceeded the power of speech—that is, the expansion of words—and was therefore indescribable.

That in which there is an exuberant and arisen *vibhrama*—a variety of emotional state—is described as follows: "The instability of the mind's fluctuations born of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is called *vibhrama*;
its three varieties, characterized by great persistence and known as *karkaśya*, have been declared by the learned."
Thus says Bharata:
"That [drama] in which there is abundant (*bhūri*) or profuse (*pracura*) *sāttvika-vikāra* (emotional transformation arising from the quality of *sattva*).
*Sattva* is a certain state of mind; that which is produced by it is the *sāttvika-bhāva*."

As it has been said: "Those states that arise when the mind is dominated by *sattva* are declared by the ancient poets to be *sāttvika*. And they are: perspiration, paralysis, horripilation, change of voice, trembling, change of color, tears, and fainting—these eight are considered the *sāttvika* [states]."
Thus:
that by which steadfastness has been cast away or discarded;
the sense is that this is due to a disregard for noble lineage and other such qualities.
"Victorious" means unimpeded everywhere;
the sense is that even for a young girl, there is victory due to her childhood.
By the phrase "lotus-eyed," the *hāva* (a graceful gesture) consisting of pleasure arising from various types of eye-movements is expressed here.
As it is said: "That which indicates the form of the erotic sentiment through the modifications of the eyebrows, eyes, and so forth..."
The permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva) is established as the gesture (hāva), arising from both jealousy and affection.

In this verse, *vilāsa* (graceful playfulness) is described. As it has been said: "That particularity in bodily movements arising from the sight of a beloved and so forth, accompanied by amorous gestures, is declared to be *vilāsa*."
Now, according to Bharata’s rule that "playful sport (*helā*) arises from amorous gesture (*hāva*)," he describes *helā* following *hāva*: "Stimite... and so forth.
"The surge of emotion among women, manifested through their own nature by means of longing for a lover, shame, timidity, and curiosity, is proclaimed as *helā*."
Thus says Bharata.
As for the meaning of the verse: "I have become, I have been, the worthy recipient (*pātram*)—that is, the fit object—for her *ālokitas*, her sudden glances.
It is said that a glance which occurs suddenly is called an *ālokita*.
Thus says Bharata.
Of what kind [are they]?
By means of the wonder arising from the discernment of the forms of the *mardāya* [dance].
Stimite means motionless; vikasite means blossomed with joy. This gaze of theirs is wonderful.
Of these two—[the one] standing near Dhātṛvṛti—in the mind of the large-eyed woman, there arose delight, and from that...
And by them.
Act One.
With eyes languidly turned, lovely, tender, motionless, and slow; with pupils smiling from within with wonder as they open at the sight of the sun.
My heart, finding no refuge, has been carried away, pierced, drunk up, and uprooted by the side-long glances of that long-lashed-eyed woman.
As it is said: "The gaze called 'wonderful' (adbhutā) has its eyelashes slightly contracted, its pupils raised with astonishment, and is gentle with wide-open corners."
Alternatively, the sense is that there is a gradual unfolding, like a slow or gentle blooming, of those [eyes] first revealed by the sight of the hero.
By this, a desire for further successive sightings is indicated.
[The phrase refers to] those in whom there is a flickering, tremulous play of the eyebrows.
The *rūpaka* (metaphor) is by virtue of its length;
by this, the "lovely" (*kāntā*) glance is described. As it is said: "The 'lovely' [glance] is produced by joy and clarity, exceedingly full of passion."
In the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), the gaze is considered to be one accompanied by the knitting of the eyebrows and side-long glances.
"Smooth, soft, and closed out of modesty—this is their 'mukulita' (bud-like) gaze.
Regarding this, Bharata states: "The 'mugdha' (charming) gaze has its corners closed; such a gaze is considered 'mukula' (bud-like)."
Alternatively, it refers to those [eyes] which are closed gently and softly through the cultivation of bliss;
by this, the culmination in the abundance of joy born from seeing is indicated.
Furthermore, they are expansive at both the outer corners and the inner vicinity due to being drawn obliquely with a desire to see again and again.

This is the apprehensive glance (*śaṅkitā dṛṣṭi*). As it is said: "Slightly moving yet steady, slightly lowered, extended obliquely, with the pupils hidden and startled—this is called the apprehensive glance. By this, the culmination of the sidelong glance (*kaṭākṣa*) is expressed.
When the fall of her eyes was directed toward him as he approached from the opposite direction, they were slightly contracted and closed out of modesty and eagerness to see;
this is the "contracted" (ākuñcitā) gaze.
As it has been said: "With the tips of the lashes uncontracted and the lids likewise contracted..."
And when the pupil is contracted and the gaze is narrowed, it is called the "contracted" (kuñcita) look.

Nor should it be argued that the mention of the "contracted glance" (*kuñcitadṛṣṭi*) here is improper because Bharata restricts its use to cases of loss, difficulty of sight, or eye-pain—according to the rule: "The *kuñcita* [glance] is indicated in cases of loss, difficulty of sight, and eye-pain.
For, due to her modesty, it is possible for Mādhava to be difficult for her to look upon.
What kind of vessel?
Various, of many kinds.
Even when employing a steady gaze, the meaning is that I too employed a gaze in exactly the same manner.
"Yogya and bhājana both mean 'a worthy recipient' (pātra)," according to Amara.
The form "abhūvam" is the third person singular aorist (luṅ) of the root *bhū* with the suffix *sic*.
"Alas," and so forth.
By those glances of the long-lashed one—glances endowed with beautiful lashes that have attained the state of side-long looks (*kaṭākṣa*)—my heart has been stolen, that is, brought under her control.
Here, because of the abundance of guards, or due to haste in departing, or out of apprehension, it is said that the very glances constitute side-long looks.
The side-glance consists of a sidelong look;
its meaning is that it causes all the stages of amorous passion by moving the pupils near the ears.
Likewise, "apaviddha" means churned or agitated due to its steadiness.
Because it was in a state of being intermediate and liquid in form, it was drunk;
for that very reason, it was uprooted.
The meaning is: "At that time, nothing at all was known by me."
For this very reason, it has become shelterless, devoid of a protector.

From that [state], from that [state], it moved; even the outflow [of its effects]. Immediately following this, this verse is found in another manuscript: "Your eyes are sprinkled with the nectar of a smile, and so is your speech; there is that braid, those arms so perfectly straight, and that gait languid with grace.
'She is thin,' 'she is she,' 'O she'—with our minds constantly bound in meditation upon her, there is neither censure, nor delight, nor even detachment; the mind remains empty."

In the *Mālatīmādhava*, although I was thus brought under her control by the anticipated essence of affection from her—who is so captivating to the heart in every way—I nevertheless desired to conceal my own agitation and somehow managed to finish weaving the remainder of the bakula-garland. Then, [the King says: "The meaning is that you should act as is appropriate for the matter previously introduced, now that the cane-weapon has been joined. By what means? [He continues: *Malatimadhavam*: Thus, though I was brought under her sway by the anticipated flavor of affection from her who is so heart-captivating in every aspect, I desired to conceal my own agitation and somehow indeed finished weaving the remainder of the bakula-garland. Then, [the King says: "The sense is: 'Act according to the merit of the matter previously introduced, now that the cane-weapon has been joined.
Of what kind?"
With eyes languid with shame, turned back by curiosity, and then moving forward; charming with their budding [expression], lovely,
and affectionate with love.

The meaning is that [the eyes] are slow due to dejection—caused by the wonder of seeing her form and the thought [of what she might be]—and are motionless and unblinking as one wonders, "Who is this who is to be seen?
This is the dejected gaze (*viṣādinī dṛṣṭi*). As it is said: "The dejected gaze has wide-open lids, with the corners turned upward and is unblinking."
"And with pupils slightly fixed, the gaze of a woman is not poisonous. Alternatively, it is turned slowly and languidly.
This is the gaze free from emotional agitation (*nirvikārā*). As it is said: "That which is graceful (*lalitā*), contracted (*kuñcitā*), and that which looks steadfastly (*dhīrāvalokinī*)."
She was free from change, eightfold, and truly virtuous in the concealment of her outward form.

Thus, because of the perception of specific details now, compared to their first sight, those whose eyes are more intensely smiling with an inner wonder blooming even further—this gaze is affectionate (*snigdha*). As it has been said: "It is as if accompanied by a slight smile, joined with wonder, the raising of the eyebrows, and side-long glances."
In this context, a gaze that is exceedingly tender, solely intent on passion, and born of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) is prescribed.
Alternatively, by the phrase "my heart has been stolen by her side-glances," affection is expressed;
for even in another person, there is indeed a captivating quality that causes delight to the eyes.
By the word "cast away" (*apaviddha*), attachment of the mind is expressed.
The intention is that the term *apavyādhi* signifies absolute non-attachment.
"Drunk" (*pīta*) means brought under one's own control;
by this, the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is expressed.
The meaning is that this is because mental activity is under one's own control.

By the word "uprooted" (*unmūlita*), the cessation of objects is indicated. By the word "without refuge" (*aśaraṇa*), the absence of anyone to prevent the mind from being carried away and so forth is stated.
The faultless beauty of the heroine is also indicated:

by the word *alasa* (sluggish), the breaking forth of sleep is shown; by *valita* (turned), the disappearance of bashfulness; by *mugdha* (charming), sweetness; by *snigdha* (glossy), longing; by *niṣpanda* (motionless), the turning away from contraction because the object of desire is the focus of affection; by *manda* (slow), joy; and by the phrase beginning with *adhika* (excessive), the smiling pupils expanding within.
Thus, she has been captivated by these sluggish and turned glances.
For even a thief or the like who steals something turns back very slowly; this is the sense.

It was "cast down" (apaviddham)—meaning thrown away or defeated—by those who are "deluded" (mugdhaiḥ), meaning possessed by extreme infatuation at the sight of his natural beauty, and "affectionate" (snigdhaiḥ), meaning characterized by gestures indicating their love for me as their object.
"Viddha, kṣipta, and īrita are synonyms," according to Amara.

By this, the lack of control over the mind is shown. Now, one might ask: why was meditation on Him or similar practices—which ward off mental distraction—not performed? To this he replies: "It was drunk by [the senses] that were motionless, withdrawn, and resting solely in Me; that is, they were made devoid of any connection with anything other than That."
And thus, the sense is that there can be no talk of cultivating other objects [of meditation].
It has been "uprooted by the passing days.
By this, it is indicated that there is an absence of restraint over the mind and that there is no occasion for the instruction of a friend.
In this case, there is no redundancy of meaning with the preceding verse,
because there is a distinction between the state of a mere glance (*ālokita*) and the state of a side-long look (*kaṭākṣa*),
or because the hero’s mind is already captivated by aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

"Thus" means that through the sight of such a state, it is possible for [the matter] to reach the heart; the sense is that even in the absence of a cause, one suspects what is undesirable on account of love.
"Intention" (abhisaṃdhi) means purpose (ābhiprāya). "In whatever way" means that the mind has been carried away by that; such is the sense.
The eunuchs (*varṣavara*) were mostly of that [eunuch] sort and were the principal attendants.
Having been brought within range by their proximity, she somehow or other concealed the *bakula* flower—[End of] the First Act.
Surrounded by a retinue of men who were mostly eunuchs, the moon-faced lady mounted an elephant-cow and set out upon the road leading to the city.
And then, as she departed, repeatedly turning her neck and bearing a face like a lotus with its stalk bent back—
the side-glance of that long-lashed-eyed woman, smeared as it were with both nectar and poison, was deeply embedded in my heart.
From that time forward, [this state] has transcended all demarcation and lies beyond the scope of every word; it is something that has not been experienced even for a moment in this present birth.
A certain transformation, dense with great delusion accumulated through the destruction of discernment, numbs the inner self and brings forth torment.
Moreover:
"Or rather, those who are ill-behaved, all beings who are by nature impotent,
and those who are not at fault by birth— they are indeed considered to be eunuchs (varṣavara)."
Thus were the eunuchs instructed.
By Mālatī’s mounting of the female elephant and so forth, her status as a woman of the highest rank is indicated through her birth in a noble lineage;
alternatively, by her mounting of the female elephant, her ability to see from afar due to the extreme height of the mount is indicated.

Even there, the mention of a female elephant (*hastinī*) is intended to indicate a slow gait; for even within the species of elephants, the female possesses a slow movement. The implication is that both of these [qualities] are due to her long-standing longing to behold Mādhava.
"Yāntyā" and so forth:
by that long-lashed-eyed woman, as she was departing, a side-glance was cast as if it were deeply buried or fixed within my heart.
The meaning is that at that time, the sight of her became, as it were, stuck in my heart.
By the word "planted" (*nikhāta*), the unbearable nature of the sidelong glance is expressed. Of what kind [of woman]? Of one who bears that face.
Of what sort? That in which the neck—the throat—is repeatedly bent or turned;
that which is twisting back and forth from moment to moment.
The meaning is "beholding.
That which has a revolved stalk—that is, a bent stem—is the hundred-petaled lotus (*śatapatra*); that from which there is unsurpassed luster or radiance is [the object].
Or, it may mean "resembling that," i.e., equal to it.
By revolving starting from the stalk, the unfolding of the lotus is accomplished.
Of what nature is it?
First, it is smeared—that is, augmented—by nectar because it is a cause of bliss; afterwards, due to the interruption of the bliss of seeing [the face], it is smeared by poison.
From that time forward, beginning from that point; "pariccheda" and so forth:
the transformation born of desire is a state that internally numbs, deludes, produces heat, and causes anguish.

When there is the thought of attaining that [state], then there is the experience of an effect other than dullness; and when there is the thought of its absence, then there is heat. Thus, due to the difference in time, there is no contradiction between dullness and heat.
Anticipating the objection that the entity producing both might not exist, he says: "some" (*kaścit*)—meaning specifically indefinable, beyond measure or limitation, and impossible to describe.
The sense is that because it has not entered the path of experience in this life, it is therefore impossible to delimit or define.

Anticipating the objection—"Why is that pair [of discernment and knowledge] not practiced now through that very experience?"—he says: "Because of the destruction of discernment (*viveka*), there is an absence of excellent knowledge; thus, one is enveloped in a dense thicket of great delusion, a state of extreme peril.
The sense is that at that time, discernment is absent.

By this, [the heroine] is surrounded by a retinue of *vetravārakas* (staff-bearers), like a female elephant (*kareṇukā*) on the city road; she torments her senses at every step and spreads [her influence] throughout the *Mālatīmādhava*.
There is no clear discernment even regarding an object standing before one; likewise, there is remembrance of what has been practiced, yet it is devoid of its true nature.
There is no cessation of distress in either a lake of snow or the moon; the mind, empty of resolution, wanders about and sketches something indistinct.
Kalahaṃsa: He has certainly been carried off by someone;
could it possibly be Mālatī herself?
He has certainly been carried off by someone.
"Could that woman named Mālatī be she?
Makaranda—(to himself): Oh, what an attachment!
So why should I forbid my friend?
Or rather—may he not indeed lose his senses; may your mind not become clouded by the density of impure transformations.
And so forth; but indeed, this [objection] here is entirely pointless, because both desire, with its fully blossomed qualities, and fresh youth are present.
[Aloud:
Friend, have you learned the name of his lineage?
[She replies: It has been shown.

"Discernment (*pariccheda*) is manifestation (*vyakti*)," and so forth. Even when a jar or similar object is in close proximity, discernment—that is, the manifestation of a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*)—does not occur. The meaning is that one is unable even to determine the jar and such objects.
By this, the withdrawal of the external sense faculties from their objects is stated.
Even regarding that which has been practiced and repeatedly experienced, memory occurs as "not being so"—that is, fragmented, broken, and flavorless (virasa), possessing a sense of distaste.
By this, the dullness of the mind is expressed.
This is the state of *anusmṛti* (recollection).

He says that even by resorting to cooling things, the torment does not depart because of the withdrawal from sense objects: "In a cool lake, or in the moon with its rays like those of nectar, there is no removal of my torment.
The word *candramas* (moon) is used here figuratively to denote its own rays;
this is a state of agitation.
As it is said: "Whether on a seat or in a bed, he neither stands nor finds contentment;
there is constant restlessness and a state of perpetual agitation."
"The mind, devoid of resolution and lacking fortitude, wanders due to its own frailty;
it sketches some desire and embraces it.
By this, the state of madness is described.
Kalahamsa:
He has been abducted, that is, brought under control;
the particle "api" is used here in the sense of possibility or emphasis.
The term *nāma* is used in the sense of manifestation.
Regarding "to oneself" (*svagatam*):
Bharata states, "That which is to be heard by [the character] alone and not by everyone is here called *svagatam*."
*Abhiṣvaṅga* is a mental defeat consisting of attachment;
as Śāśvata states: "The word *abhiṣvaṅga* is known [to apply] to insults, curses, and overcomings."
"Do not be bewildered. Indeed, it was Kāma, who is born of no other source, that utterly bewildered her; he did not produce a derangement of the mind accompanied by physical illness.

Thus, the prohibitive statement beginning with "let not your mind become dense and thick with the impure transformation born of desire" is indeed meaningless here; for it is a non sequitur. This is because [the subject] is one whose bowstring—the string (guṇa)—is drawn and coiled, that is, [the bow] is strung.
Or, desire is one whose qualities have expanded and whose activity has increased;
and fresh youth is that in which the qualities have expanded—
meaning that its form and other attributes are manifest.
Therefore, the meaning is that this [person], being dependent on that [other], cannot be restrained.
"Publicly"—that which is audible to all people is intended here as "public. Otherwise, there would be an improper connection; it is highly disagreeable, in which even a friend... [End of First Act].
Mādhava: Friend, listen.

Then, at the very moment she was about to mount the female elephant, a certain courtesan from the circle of the noble lady’s friends drew near while gathering young *bakula* flowers; having approached and bowed, she spoke thus to me under the pretext of offering a floral wreath: "Noble sir, this arrangement of your flowers is beautiful due to its well-knit qualities.
Furthermore, our mistress is curious regarding this matter."

"Let his novel and wonderful activity among the flowers be successful; let the cleverness of his art attain its purpose; let the Creator’s beauty of craftsmanship bear fruit; and let this [garland], full of aesthetic flavor, obtain the high value of being suspended around the neck of our noble lady.
Makaranda: "Oh, what ingenuity!
Thus says Bharata.
Lineage is the family line.
Mādhava:
A female elephant is a *kareṇukā*;
it is one of many.
The suffix *tamap* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*).
Alternatively, the word *anyatama* is an underived (*avyutpanna*) synonym for "one. A courtesan is a *vārayoṣit*.
Because of her being such as this, there is here the taking up [of the action]:
having become alone after a delay,
and having become nearby, that is, situated in close proximity.
"In both cases, it should be understood as being by way of plucking flowers.
"Under the pretext of a garland of flowers" means by means of a floral wreath.
The sense is that she says "Do not [do this]" under the pretext of fear of her request being rejected.
And yet, Kāma, who is crowned with flowers (*kusumāpīḍa*), torments me even with a flower; the meaning is that he pays homage to me under that pretext. O highly fortunate one, O one of great merit!
The *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *bhāga* is used in the senses of both fortune (*bhāgya*) and a portion (*artha*).
By virtue of its well-knit qualities, it is like a well-fastened thread.
*Saṃniveśa* refers to a specific arrangement or composition.
*Kutūhalinī* means curious regarding the *puṣpadāman* (flower-garland). By the term *bhartṛdārikā* (the daughter of the master), her eagerness to see [him] due to her maidenhood is expressed.
Alternatively, since Bharata accepts that a maiden is a fit object for confidence, she is indicated here as being a maiden.
"Exquisite" means transcendent, wonderful, and of many kinds.
"Occupation with flowers" refers to the arrangement and composition of blossoms. By this, it is said that she possesses a marvelous skill and curiosity born from her proficiency in weaving garlands.
The meaning is: "of cleverness," that is, of skill in composition; "fulfillment of purpose" means having achieved one's objective. The underlying sense is that she praises this clever beloved.
May it bear fruit and be successful through its gift to a person of refined taste;
for the arrangement of the garland remains fresh and unfading.
"High value" means great worth.
In this context, "your" (*vaḥ*) refers to your assembly or union; it is delightful through mutual compatibility and the like, worthy of sport, and indeed fit for honor.
Here, the plural form *vaṃ* (for *yuṣmad*) is used out of respect, according to the rule: "For some [grammarians], the plural is used for *yuṣmad* when expressing respect."
Among the assembly of messengers, she was full of curiosity and longing; she was unprecedented and novel due to her exclusive devotion to him alone;
she was wonderful and excellent.
Or, he is a source of wonder because he causes various transformations;
the activity of the flower-arrowed Kāma is delusion,
which is the meaningfulness of his cleverness— that is, his proficiency in all the arts.
Because it generates delight for the wise;
"the loveliness of its creation" refers to the beauty of its composition;
"may it bear fruit" through association with a worthy person.
The sense is that, if this were not so, everything would be in vain.
*Rasa* means either the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) or passion (*anurāga*).
*Kaṇṭhāvalambana* means embracing.
"High value" means being difficult to obtain.
Thus, it is suggested here that the operation of the female messenger proceeds once she has understood both the proficiency of the hero and his intention through this double-entendre.
Makaranda:
The sense is that there is ingenuity (*vaidagdhyam*) due to the employment of punning words (*śliṣṭapadaprayogāt*). Then, the young girl remains steadfast (*dhīrā*).

[She says: "To her... [Kusumeṣu: "O woman skilled in the art of love! [Kadambā: "It was told to me by Mādhava in the *Mālatīmādhava*, and by her, who was questioned by me: 'This is Mālatī, the daughter of the minister Bhūrivasu; and I am Lavaṅgikā, the foster-sister and favorite of the princess. Kalahaṃsa: [With joy] "What! Her name is Mālatī?"
By good fortune, the divine Lord of the Flower-Arrows has indeed manifested his power!
We have triumphed!
What indeed is this called "Mālatī"?
"By good fortune, the blessed god with the flower-bow has indeed displayed his prowess;

victory is mine! Makaranda (to himself): That she is the daughter of the minister Bhūrivasu is no small matter for my great respect. Moreover, the venerable Kāmandakī rejoices, saying, "Mālatī, Mālatī."
And it is rumored that she is being sought after for the delight of the King.
Mādhava: And being thus entreated by her, I took that Bakula garland from my own neck and gave it to her.

Furthermore, with a fixed gaze, she—distraught by the sight of Mālatī’s face—highly esteemed that very [garland], which had its parts unevenly arranged, and accepted it, thinking, "This is a great favor.
Immediately thereafter, when the crowd had dispersed due to the throng of the great multitude of citizens moving out for the festival procession, I arrived.
Makaranda: Friend, this is well-suited, given that affection is also seen in Mālatī.
For that intense passion of hers, which was previously indicated by signs such as the paleness of her cheeks and which has now grown strong, is clearly centered on you alone.
However, this remains unknown: who among her friends has been seen by her before?
Indeed, maidens of such great fortune do not, having set their hearts elsewhere, become blind in one eye for another.
Moreover: Mādhava—
by her who was questioned, that is, asked.
"Offspring is progeny;
it is the ground of favor, the locus of trust, for her.
And you are the ground of favor, the object of compassion, because of the gift of the garland."
Kalahaṃsa: Here, "vilasitam" means manifested;
the sense is that this has arisen from the mutual passion between these two.
Makaranda:
The "insufficiency" (aparyāpti) of great honor—that is, its lack of limit—is due to its being endowed with qualities such as being unassailable and inviolable; this is the intended meaning.
Mādhava:
Though repeatedly entreated and earnestly besought by her, she— this girl from Aṅga— remains obstinate,
despite my efforts being directed toward her with great persistence.
"By being bewildered and agitated. "This is a great favor"—
the sense is that love is not for the object itself, but rather for its qualities.
Makaranda:
It is well-joined and certain.
He has been seen before; he was previously seen.
Such [women] are born of noble lineage.

According to the doctrine of Bharata, the objects of visual attraction (*cakṣūrāga*) and passionate love (*anurāga*) are one and the same. Furthermore, [he] seeks that jewel of a daughter, who has been won by him; and having pursued her, he entreats her. Regarding the citizens and merchants, there was previously an affection marked by signs of attachment, born of their devotion.
And they are full of affection. [The Kalahaṃsa bird] points it out.
First Act.
This is the sign of her prior affection for you, seen by her friends whose eyes are fixed upon one another.
And this clever speech of the nurse’s daughter was reported: "Someone has said something to someone."
Having approached, they both look at the painting, saying: "This is it! This is it!"
Makaranda: Kalahaṃsaka, by whom was this portrait of Mādhava painted?
Kalahaṃsa: By the very same one who stole his heart.
Jeṇa jevva se hiaaṃ avaharidaṃ.
Makaranda: And what of Mālatī? Kalahamsa: Indeed so;
it is she.
Friend Makaranda, your conjecture is almost certain.
Makaranda: Kalahaṃsaka, from where was this obtained?
From the *kāśa* grass.
Kalahamsaka: First from Mandārikā’s hand;
and by her, too, from Lavaṅgikā’s presence.
Makaranda: What then did Mandārikā say regarding Mālatī’s purpose for the portrait of Mādhava?
Kalahamsa:
"To dispel longing," he says—*ukkaṇṭhāviṇoda*.
Makaranda: Friend Mādhava, take heart by all means!
He states the sign of her passion with the words beginning "anyonya" (mutual), etc.
The sign of her prior passion for you is indeed manifest.
How so?
This is a singular report from friends whose glances are met with one another, saying "it is someone's [affair]";
otherwise, how could the circle of friends look at you with side-long glances, or how could they speak thus? Furthermore, this is the articulate speech of Lavaṅgikā.
The sense is: how else could she speak thus, beginning with "kutūhalinī" (full of curiosity)?
According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "In the case of *saṃgata*, when it is split, it becomes *bhinna*."
Kalahamsa: The meaning is that it refers to the person by whom [the object] was stolen,
and upon whom his transformation of passion is based.
Makaranda: This means it was written by Mālatī.
Kalahamsa: Indeed, that is so; [the word] "atha kim" expresses acceptance.
Mādhava:
Vitarka means conjecture or deliberation.
Makaranda: [End of sentence].
Realization is attainment.
Kalahaṃsa:
"As a diversion for her longing.
The meaning is that Mālatī, being enamored of Mādhava, finds delight even in gazing at him depicted in a painting, though she has not yet attained him in person.
"Is he not indeed worthy?"—this was his intention. After this, Mādhava says: "And what else?

Makaranda—[is it] for the Creator? Some say [it refers to] "this heart. [In the *Mālatīmādhava*: "That moonlight which is well-born for your eyes—you too, O friend, are the kinsman of her heart’s longing.
There is no doubt regarding our union, O friend, in which both Fate and Love have exerted their efforts."
Moreover, her very form as it appears to you is the cause of this transformation; therefore, let Mālatī be drawn right here.
Mādhava: Whatever pleases my friend. Then, bring the picture-board, the paints, and the brushes.
Makaranda brings [the writing materials].
Mādhava— (writing)—
Friend Makaranda, again and again a flood of tears obstructs the emergence of my vision, and my body reaches a state of paralysis through the numbness induced by thoughts of her.
Sweating instantly, with fingers trembling from incessant quivering, this hand of mine is utterly unable to proceed with the drawing; what am I to do?
"Yetyādi" and so forth.
O friend, there is no doubt at all regarding that union; for the "kaumadī"—the moonlight—of your eyes causes [me] great joy.

You, too, who are of noble birth and the beloved friend of her heart's desires, are the one to fulfill her longing. Indeed, even when there is mutual affection, success does not occur due to the aversion of Fate and Kāma; therefore, he says: "In this union, both Fate and Kāma have exerted their efforts.
The meaning is that Kāma has made his effort through the pleasure of the eyes, while Fate has made his effort by bringing her to this place.
And from an assault, there is the acquisition of a maiden;
as it is said: "For from an assault, the acquisition of a maiden is indeed certain."
Citra inflames Mādhava’s passion with the words, "She is to be seen.
Regarding Mādhava: in the phrase "to his friend" (*vayasyāya*), the status of recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is established by the rule *'rucyarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ'* (Pāṇini 1.4.33).
Now, with a joyful mind, he describes a *sāttvika* emotion through the verse beginning with "Again and again," and so forth:
"This hand of mine remains entirely intent upon the rules of drawing and the creation of paintings, yet it does not write.
What am I to do in this matter?"
The meaning is: "I shall write in whatever manner [possible].
In the reading "natarām," the meaning is that it does not exist at all.
For the flood of tears—the flow of tears of joy arising from meditating upon him—repeatedly obstructs, that is, covers, the movement of the eyes.
By her resolve—that is, by her thought—her body, whose numbness consists in the inability to perform any action, attains a state of paralysis, an immobility.
Bharata states: "Paralysis is that which arises from joy, fear, disease, wonder, despondency, or the defect of intoxication.
Of what sort is it?
At the very moment she began to write,
her fingers became trembling due to incessant and excessive shaking;
by the fact that her fingers were used for writing, their restlessness indicates that she was unable to write.
Thus, here tears, paralysis, perspiration, and trembling have been mentioned;
however, horripilation and the like have not been mentioned,
because they are not incompatible with writing.
All of this arises from joy and is characterized by *sattva*.
As it has been said: "Sweat may arise from anger, fear, joy, shame, sorrow, fatigue, disease, feverish affliction, exertion, trepidation, and so forth, as well as from physical pressure."
Trembling arises from cold, fear, joy, suppression, contact, old age, and disease.
Thus [it is said].
Now, Mālatī, behold this marvel! Thus ends the first act of that venerable [work].
Nevertheless, I am weary.
Having finally finished painting it, he shows it.
Makaranda—
[Gazing at the painting] It is indeed fitting that your lordship’s affection should be directed toward this.
[With curiosity]
How was this verse composed and written down so quickly?
"Those various objects such as the crescent of the new moon, which are naturally sweet and victorious in the world, certainly exist and delight the mind;
yet for me, she alone—who is like moonlight to my eyes—is the one great festival in this life, since she has come within the range of my vision."
Entering quickly, Mandārikā says: "O Kailahaṃsaka, you have been found by following your footprints.
She writes this verse, *jagati* and so forth, which contains both affection and reproach, thinking that Mādhava will see it:

"Those various states and objects, such as the crescent of the new moon, are victorious; they are everywhere unimpeded in producing intoxication, naturally charming, and there are indeed others that intoxicate the mind."
The sense is that for me, however, these things are not causes of intoxication; on the contrary, they are indeed causes of burning.

Here, by the word "victorious" (*jayinaḥ*), it is stated that those who possess victory at a particular time and place are givers of a mass of bliss. They are called "objects" (*bhāvāḥ*) because they are cultivated (*bhāvyante*) or are worthy of contemplation (*bhāvanām arhanti*) due to their beauty.
"Those [beings] distinguished by *mālatī* flowers, who gladden the hearts of the connoisseurs"—
by means of this repetition (*vīpsā*), it is shown that the moon and so forth, as well as the gods and so forth, are indeed well-known.
Furthermore, by means of the pronoun (*sarvanāman*), it is suggested (*dhvanita*) that those things upon which the mind is fixed in a particular place are what are grasped therein.
By the word "tu" (but), it is stated that the same applies to others through the medium of their mutual agreement.

What, then, is the cause of his pride? To this he says: "But for me, this Mālatī, painted here in a picture, is the moonlight for my eyes; that she has come within the range of my vision is itself the sole great festival of this life.
Here, the underlying passion is expressed by the thought: "What more could there be than this, such as actual union and so forth?"
That itself is a great festival.
The reproach— "whether there be passion or not"—
is intended to demonstrate Mālatī’s absolute passion for him.
Even if others appear at another time, they do not possess the quality of producing bliss;
for this very reason, that quality is nourished by the phrase "that very same [one].
By the general designation "in birth," it is suggested that throughout all births there is no one equal to Mālatī.

This is the verbal rasa (vācika-rasa). As it is said: "The verbal rasa is said to consist of conversations, verses, sentences, and words that correspond to the [emotional] flavor (rasa) and are endowed with various poetic ornaments (alaṃkāra)."
Thus [it is said].
Here, although [the jasmine] is naturally sweet, because it produces intoxication specifically in Mālatī, there is the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction).
Because it conveys what is dear, it is the figure of speech *priya* (the dear).
"Vilocanacandrikā" (Moonlight for the Eyes) is a metaphor (*rūpaka*).
Nor should it be argued that "navendukalā" refers to the crescent of the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad-candrakalā*), and that such a crescent is not a cause of intoxication;
for the word *nava* is derived from the root *nū* (to praise). Thus, it means "praiseworthy."
The meaning is "one with a praiseworthy moon.
Alternatively, it is a *dvandva* compound meaning "the new [moon] and the digits of the moon, etc. Or else, it means "new," having just emerged from the ocean.
The meaning is that it is indeed full.
Regarding "having entered": where the entrance occurs with the dropping of the curtain, there is the expression "having entered. "Anusāra" means following after.

These too, who were painted upon the picture-board—having observed them here with great reverence as a single entity, my mind became deeply absorbed; yet, with the sudden tossing of the curtain of my desires, I cry out, "Kalahamsa! Kalahamsa! Thief! Thief! [In the *Mālatīmādhava*: Beholding the two in the distance, [Makaranda says] with shame: "How is it that even these two noble souls are right here?"
