"Extremely long" means of very great length. "Revolution" (*parivartanā*) refers to going back and forth repeatedly; therein, "playfulness" (*vilāsa*) is a specific activity of the gaze, by which the "creeping vine of the eyebrows" (*bhrūlatā*) is made to dance—that is, to perform a rhythmic movement. By this, the "grace of the deer-marked bow of the Bodiless One" (*anaṅgaśāraṅgavibhrama*)—the playful charm of the god of love’s bow—is "imitated," meaning it is rendered equal to it. Thus, the word "skillful" (*vidagdha*) is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
[The verse continues: "The movements of walking, sitting, hands, and feet, as well as the specific actions of the eyes and eyebrows..."
That which is performed effortlessly upon the arrival of the beloved is surely called *vilāsa*.
Thus says Bharata;
because of the usage "śarata," the *repha* [the letter *r*] in "śāraṅga" is distinct.
"Śāraṅga is known as a bow," according to Śāśvata.
Therefore, the intended meaning here is that your state of longing due to not seeing you is the cause of the necklace's beauty.
Mālatī:
"Ām" signifies acceptance of what was said. In the reading "ammo," it expresses either joy or wonder.

Deceived, O Māruta-pālakā (O protector of the wind), you have been moved; restrained, you have become self-controlled; made to blossom with grace, you have overflowed with joy. [The words] *hetukāḥ* mean causes; *vipralambhitakāḥ* means those who have been deceived. (From the *Mālatīmādhava*). [Laṅkeśvara], laughing as if with indignation:
"You too, by your very nature, were made to dance without music on that occasion. "You too, by your very nature, were made to dance without music on that occasion. (In the *Mālatīmādhava*, Act 10).
Mālatī—smiling bashfully: Hum, and then? Hum, and then?
Lava: Then, when he had been hidden by the crowd of people returning from the pilgrimage, I went to Mandārikā’s house.
Indeed, her picture-board had been taken into my hands at dawn. Therefore, when he was hidden by the crowd of people returning from the pilgrimage, I went to Mandārikā’s house.
Indeed, that picture-board was made by her at dawn.
Mālatī: For what purpose? For what reason? (Kiṃṇimittam)
Lava: Indeed, one named Kalahaṃsaka, an attendant of Mādhava, desires her;
she will show her to him.
Consequently, Mandārikā has become a bearer of pleasant news.
"Indeed, a follower of Mādhava named Kalahaṃsaka desires her;
she will show her to him.
Then Mandārikā, the bearer of pleasant news, departed.
Mālatī: Surely that Kalahaṃsaka must have shown his master that portrait of her as well.
[Aloud] Friend, what is pleasing to you now?
Surely that portrait must have been shown by Kalahaṃsa to his master as well.

Friend, what is pleasing to you now? Lavaṅgikā: This very portrait of yours is indeed a momentary relief for my heart, which is being consumed by the unbearable distress of unattainable desires—an affliction that brings further torment to one already tormented.
Thus he shows it to Citra.
"This is indeed a portrait of you, brought here to provide a momentary relief for one whose mind is distressed by the onset of a rare longing and who is tormented by the heat of love.
[It is presented.]
The suffix *itac* is applied because [the word *tāraka*] belongs to the *tārakādi* group; from that, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the same meaning (*svārthe*).
Here, the word *ādu* is a synonym for *aho* or *ahosvit*.
Because character (*śīla*) is something to be known over a long period of time, there arises the thought of deception when it is present for only a mere moment.
The sense is that it is impossible to know whether this alteration of the eyes and so forth is natural or born of passion;
in the reading *vippalambhaittakāḥ*, it should be understood as "those who contemplate deception."
Lavaṅgikā: Here, "by Manmatha" is the ellipsis.
The meaning is that you were made to dance in such a way as to be a silent dance (*asaṃgītaka*), that is, a quiet dance.
"With resentment," meaning accompanied by hatred for another; "Mālatī";
"hum" [expresses] a touch of affectionate anger.
Lavaṅgikā: Here, "kāmayate" means she desires. Lavaṅgikā.

[To himself, with joy: Here, upon you who are so difficult to attain, there is this intense longing; and because of that unbearable anguish, my heart is being consumed by fire—yet for even a moment, this [longing] does not exist anywhere else. [Aside, with joy: Thus, the picture-board of the noble lord, the master, is yours to see. [The second act. Mālatī (gazing with delight): Oh! Even now my heart remains unattached, since I suspect that even such a consolation is merely a deception.
"How even the syllables [are so well-chosen]!
Thus he recites. Having read what was previously stated, beginning with "The Victors in the World," he says with joy:
"O noble one, your speech truly appears to be as sweet as your very form."
Furthermore, this sight, though enchanting for the moment, is terrible with its long-lasting suffering in its ultimate transformation.
Truly fortunate are those maidens who do not behold you; having beheld you, they no longer have mastery over their own hearts.
Thus she weeps:
"Alas! Even now my heart remains unattached, since I consider even this consolation to be a deception.
How is it that even the syllables [of his name]..."
O noble one, your speech is indeed worthy of your noble birth because of its sweetness;
however, the sight of you is charming for the moment but cruel with long-lasting torment in the end. Truly blessed are those mothers who do not behold you.
Or rather, they are the masters of their own hearts.
Lava: Friend, why is there no comfort for you even in this? Friend, why is it so that there is no comfort?
Mālatī: How so? Like what?

Lavangikā: He for whose sake you languish—your play-leaf like one severed from its stem, exhausted and unable to bear the fresh *mālatī* blossoms—is he too made aware by the divine Love-god of the unbearable nature of this torment?

Even he, for whose sake you are being wasted—like a *kaṅkelli* sprout whose stalks are severed, and who is unable to endure the *nomālikā* flowers—has been made to know by the blessed Cupid the unbearable nature of this torment.
Thus [it is] "the extinguisher."
Mālatī:
Here, "lack of attachment" means a lack of confidence.
The intention is that Lavaṅgikā herself has written this and is making it known as having been written by Mādhava.
"Similar" means that the speech is similar to the sweetness of his physical form.
The meaning is that just as your form is sweet, so too is your speech sweet.
This is an inquiry preceded by a reproach: "How can one whose speech is such as this have a vision [of reality] like this?
As it is said: "Wherein one perceives oneself or another as endowed with meditative cultivation (bhāvanā)..."
It expresses its meaning as if it were asking; therefore, it is called "the question" (pṛcchā).
"By the very nature of dramatic convention (*nāṭyadharmatva*), even that which is beyond the senses is made manifest to the eye.
As it has been said: 'Even when absent, a lover should be addressed by a woman as if he were present before her.'"
The word *ammakā* is a regional term (*deśī*) used for a woman or a girl.
Lavaṅgikā: Here, "utkhaṇḍita" means cut;
"bandhana" refers to the connection between the stalk and the branch; and "kaṅkelli" is the Aśoka tree.

With joy, for a long time, wondrously; with a sigh of great delight. "Breathlessness" (*an-āśvāsaḥ*) is inferred (*saṃbhāvyate*); it is perceived (*lakṣyate*). "Charming women. This [phrase] does not exist in another manuscript; how then [does it read]? "Holding your heart like a *kaṅka* bird [longing for its mate], you, exhausted by the flower-arrowed god (*Kusumāyuḥ*), shall be overcome"—thus [it reads]. In the *Mālatīmādhava*, Mālatī says: "May there now be well-being for that noble one. But for me, however, consolation is difficult to obtain. [She speaks] tearfully:
"Especially today, dear friend, may there be well-being for that noble one."
But for me, hope is exceedingly difficult to find.
Friend, today—relying on the Sanskrit—[I feel]:
"The intense passion of longing spreads incessantly like a virulent poison; it is tormenting, like a smokeless fire that blazes when fanned."
Like a severe fever, it afflicts every limb; neither my father, nor my mother, nor you, my lady, are able to protect me from this.

In this very way, encounters with virtuous people grant immediate happiness but are difficult to endure when their absence brings suffering. Moreover, for one who, even at the sight of them through a window for a mere moment, experiences an extraordinary rising of the full moon that acts like a fiercely kindled fire—yet who is simultaneously unable to bear the slightest suspicion of the pitiless workings of love—it is exactly thus: [the heart] becomes utterly helpless and incapable.
"Having exhausted yourself, you are wasting away.
By this, the state of attenuation (*tanutā*) in the stage of desire is described.
Mālatī: "Asram" means tears. [The text] is in Sanskrit.

The woman’s recourse to Sanskrit is for the purpose of manifesting a natural transformation due to her imminent death; or else, because it is taught that at the time of death, recollecting the vernacular results in birth in an inferior womb, she resorts to Sanskrit at that moment;
or else, it is for the purpose of manifesting her cleverness.
As it has been said: "In drama, the speech of women is generally praised when composed in Sanskrit;
however, in certain instances, it is commended for the purpose of awakening discernment."
"Passion of the mind," and so forth.
"O dear friend, neither my father, nor my mother, nor you are able to protect me today. Why is that?"
The passion of the mind (*manorāga*), which is an unceasing anxiety, agitating and causing agitation, spreads and pervades just like a potent poison;
that is to say, just as poison pervades the bodily elements, the skin, and so forth, so does this mental distress pervade the limbs.

Alternatively, due to the perception of something specific, the attachment of the mind—a particular form of desire—spreads and pervades the mind just as intensely, like a poison, because it causes a burning sensation.
Just as a fire that has been fanned and then kindled blazes forth, becoming smokeless through that very fanning, so too does that same passion blaze up, becoming filled with garlands of flames.
It strikes and afflicts every limb here and there, like a severe fever.
The sense is that, having abandoned him, your mental distress cannot be composed by you.
Or rather, my father was unable to protect [me],
because he gave me to Mādhava by rejecting Nandana;
nor was my mother able to do so either.
For there was no prohibition against his father acting in such a manner;
furthermore, the inclusion of Ladaṅgikā alongside those two on equal terms was intended to manifest his own independent view according to his own will.
Lavaṅgikā: [The meaning is that] it is indeed appropriate to say this here.

For one whose indistinct sight of the moon produces the state of fire and a danger to life, what is surprising in this—that his distinct sight should produce the kind of feverish heat you have described?
The cutting off of sleep is said to result from perceiving the moon as fire.
In this [state], which is delicate, there is a lack of compassion due to its causing extreme pain.
Its activity consists of ten stages.

What can be said here, O friend? For one of such great power, this intense mental affliction is like a spreading fever, smokeless yet most powerful, accompanied by a second [element], and it has reached its full intensity.

Your physical condition, which has brought your life to the brink of extinction, and the fact that you are now tormented after having obtained a special sight of him—what more is there to say in this matter?

Therefore, dear friend, we know only this: that for the world of the living, the attainment of a beloved of noble character who corresponds to one’s deep affection is a praiseworthy fruit of a rare wish.
In this very way, meetings with good people grant manifest happiness while making the suffering of their absence unbearable.

Moreover, since your physical condition— tormented by merciless love, its life-breath hanging by a thread, and resembling the full moon’s light when it is consumed by a fiercely blazing forest fire even during the brief moment of seeing him from afar— is such that you now grieve upon having attained the opportunity for close proximity, what more need be said here?
Friend, we know this much: that in the world of the living, a meeting with a noble beloved such as this, characterized by profound affection, is praiseworthy and the fruit of a rare wish.
Mālatī—Friend, you who speak of such rashness regarding the life of my beloved Mālatī! Begone! (With tears.)
Or rather, it is I alone who, looking again and again, have offended here by my lack of modesty— a mere trifle of ill-breeding— relying on a fortitude established through sheer misery.
Nevertheless, dear friend,
O you who have offered this act of courage for the life of Mālatī, go away!

Or rather, it was I myself who, looking again and again, was established in suffering; by my own heart, which was devoid of shame due to its arrogance and its lack of self-restraint, I have committed an offense here as one light-minded through insolence. Nevertheless, dear friend—(then returning to Sanskrit: *aha vā ahaṃ jevva vāraṃvāraṃ viloaantī dukkhevvavatthā vidadhīrattaṇāvambheṇa attaṇo hiaeṇa dūraviṃalidalajjeṇa duvviṇaalahuā ettha avaraddhammi | tahāvi piasahi | bhūyaḥ saṃskṛtamāśritya |* "Or rather, it was I myself who, looking again and again, was established in suffering; by my own heart, which was devoid of shame due to its arrogance and its lack of self-restraint, I have committed an offense here as one light-minded through insolence. Nevertheless, dear friend—" (then returning to Sanskrit:)
Let the moon with its unbroken digits blaze in the sky night after night; let Madana burn me; or what can he do beyond death?
To me, my beloved father is praiseworthy, and my mother of stainless lineage; but neither this person nor life itself is so.
To this he says: "That" (tat).
Thus, the sense is that the fruit of such intense passion is that the union with the beloved must be brought about through the mediation of a female friend.
Mālatī:
Here, "dayitam" means beloved. "Sāhasam" refers to a rash act [committed] out of fear of bringing disgrace upon a noble family.
For this very reason there is weeping.
And so [she says], "You, depart; go away.
To the question, "Why do I revile you, who speak so sweetly? Should not I myself be the one censured here? she replies with "Or rather" (athavā).

The meaning is this: here, the steadfastness that was established with difficulty due to being distracted by glancing at him moment by moment—its support being non-existent—is merely a superimposition upon it. It has become "light," having attained lightness;
the sense is: "I am at fault in this matter," since you have proposed such a rash course of action.
Nevertheless, dear friend, now, keeping in mind the non-performance of a rash act, she speaks with dejection, beginning with "Let it burn," and so forth.
The sense is: "Let the full moon burn—that is, let it heat—every night; nevertheless, I shall not commit a rash act."

By the word "sky" (*gagana*), its unattainability and the fact that it cannot be approached have been stated. Then, O Kāma, [why do you torment me]? Now, at this very moment—on this most auspicious full moon night—because of seeing her today... what is appropriate here? [It is] like one who flees and then stops; by that which is light due to far-reaching misconduct; by that which has dissolved through the vanishing of shame. (From the *Mālatīmādhava*). Lavaṅgikā—(to herself): *Note on the Sanskrit fragments:* * *apāgamanīyatā*: the state of being unfit for approach. * *edam*: this (referring to Mālatī). * *dūsahāāsakāriṇo*: of one who causes unbearable distress. * *muhuttamatta susame*: in this most beautiful moment. * *puṇṇacaṃ saṃpadaṃ*: now, at the present time, on the full moon day. * *sāṃprataṃ*: currently. * *daṃsaṇādo ajja*: because of seeing her today. * *tā ettha jaṃ sarisaṃ*: therefore, in this matter, what is fitting? * *palāantapaḍiṭhṭhāṣida*: fleeing and then standing firm. * *dūrabijjambhamāṇaduvviṇaalahuraṇa*: by that which is made light by far-extending wickedness. * *dūraṃ vijjambhantalajjatteṇa vilīyamānalajjātvena*: by the state of shame dissolving as it spreads far away.
* *lava – svagatam*: Lavaṅgikā—(speaking to herself).
Now, what is the remedy here? What indeed is the means now?
Then, a female doorkeeper, having entered halfway from behind the scenes, says: "This is the venerable Kāmandakī."
This is the venerable Kāmandakī.
Both: Is it the venerable lady? Is it the venerable lady?
Pratī: I have come wishing to see the lady of the house.
Both: Then why is there any delay? Why is it being postponed?
[The curtain falls. The female doorkeeper exits.
Mālatī covers the painting.
—To myself:
A truly well-wished-for thing has indeed come to pass. [A truly well-wished-for thing. Then Kāmandakī and Avalokitā enter.
Kāmandakī: Well said, friend Bhūrivasu! Well said!
You have offered words that are not in conflict with either world, namely, "The Great King has authority over his own daughter.
Moreover:
Today, through the events at the Garden of Manmatha, I perceive even the favor of the Lord Creator himself.
Thinking that Bakula will be adorned, he says:
"Let Madana burn."
What will he do after death—that is, after dying?
The sense is that since suffering is abandoned when death occurs, that [death] is indeed desirable.
Regarding the word "by another" (pareṇa):
The third case ending [is used] according to the rule "an addition [should be made] for *prakṛti* and so forth.
This is the heroines' fortitude born of her essential nature (*sattva*).

As it is said: "The mind that is not carried away by fickleness is called fortitude. Now, one might argue that following Mādhava alone is better for the removal of suffering; therefore, he says: "But to me, my father is dear—that is, beloved.
Of what sort?
Laudable, being the object of all praise."
A mother of stainless lineage is desired; a pure family is desired;
but this person dwelling in the heart, Mādhava, is by no means desired.
The phrase "by means of a rash act" is to be understood as the ellipsis. If so, how is there life? To this he says: "And life is not desired.
Here, there is a state of agitation due to hatred for life.
As it has been said: "That aversion toward what ought to be lived for is known as *udvega* (agitation) by the wise."
Lavaṅgikā: Reflecting on a means to dispel her agitation, Lavaṅgikā says: "What remedy is there now for this?"
Doorkeeper: This is the venerable Kāmandakī; the sense is that she is the means for Mālatī’s survival.

By the word *pratīhārī* (female doorkeeper), the establishment of the connection [between the characters] is indicated. As it has been said: "Those who report matters concerning peace and war, along with various customs and practices, are considered *pratīhārīs*."
In the word *pratīhārī*, the long vowel occurs even when referring to a human being due to the rule of frequent usage (*bahulavacana*). This applies to both sentences.
The meaning is: "For what purpose have you come?"
For this very reason, her activity is described in the subsequent sentence.
Lavaṅgikā: Indeed, a most desirable thing has come to pass.
Now, the sense is that [this refers to] Kāmandakī’s arrival.
Kāmandakī says: "Both."
"Not contrary to this world" means it is not explicitly forbidden, as it does not provoke the king's wrath. "A picture-board. "Well-composed. "Your Majesty, the reply. Act Two.
The wonderful curiosity of the arrangement involving the folding of the picture-board arouses a joy rooted in amazement.
For a man’s passion for another woman is the most excellent auspicious omen for a wicked deed;
and this point has been sung by Aṅgiras: "In her upon whom one's mind and eyes are fixed, there is prosperity.
Here she is—Mālatī.

This is Mālatī. (Gazing at her) Oh, Kāmandakī! Her limbs are exceedingly emaciated, yet she is as beautiful as the core of a fresh plantain tree; like the form of the moon when only a single digit remains, she brings a festival of joy to the eyes.
Having fallen into this state, distressed by the intense burning of the fire of passion, this auspicious lady both delights our minds and makes them tremble.
Moreover: Bearing a face with cheeks pale and dusty, she has attained an even more captivating beauty;
for the playful power of Love triumphs over a person of such lovely birth.
Through a fixed method of mental construction, a union with the beloved is experienced.
For indeed, her loosening of the knot of her garment, the quivering of her lower lip, the languor of her arms, perspiration, a soft and sweet glaze in her eyes,

the smooth charm of her hands, the stiffness of her limbs, the swelling of her bud-like breasts, trembling, a mass of horripilation upon the expanse of her cheeks, and even fainting and consciousness [all manifest].

The meaning is that the phrase "not for another" is stated in a general sense to avoid uttering an untruth; for the master’s responsibility regarding his own daughters extends to their welfare in the next world, whereas it does not extend to that of others.
"Vyatikara" means meeting, and its nature constitutes the arrangement. "Dārakarmaṇi" refers to marriage.
*Parārdhya* means most excellent;
*anubandha* means attachment or pleasure;
*ṛddhi* means increase or prosperity.
"Exceedingly," and so forth.
This very day delights our minds.
Why?
Her limbs are exceedingly emaciated;
"sarasam" means moist,
that is to say, not stale.
Like the core or pith of a plantain tree, she is beautiful despite her emaciation and paleness;
here, the word "core" (garbha) indicates extreme paleness.
She is like the form of the moon when only a digit remains, like the second crescent of the moon.
For this very reason, she delights [the heart] by accomplishing the task at hand;
yet, having fallen into a state of agitation due to a fierce burning (*uddāha*), she causes the mind to tremble—
the sense being that this is because of the excessive pain and the resulting apprehension of the undesirable.
Here, the stage of passion known as "attenuation" (tanutā) is indicated.
"Parītyādi" and so forth.
"Pāṃsula" means rough.
Even with cheeks and face pale and rough, she is beautiful.
For when a person of pleasing birth undergoes whatever transformation of their body, that very transformation, being desired, becomes victorious.
*Saṃkalpa* is a mental operation.
Regarding "the knot" (*nīvī*) and so forth:

the knot of the garment on the hips is some wonderful bond of marriage; it is passion; it is prosperity—success. Having seen it, there is no madness, nor is it unrestrained. Then, quivering, or rather, with the fatigue of the beloved restrained, [she approaches] with eyes slightly closed and squinting, [a voice] high-pitched and sweet from her two breasts. Thus she approaches.
In the *Mālatīmādhava*, Lavaṅgikā rouses Mālatī.
Both rise. Mālatī: "O Blessed One, I bow to you. Bhavabhūti: "I bow to you."
O Kaumudī-mahābhāgā, may you become a recipient of your desired fruits.
Here is a well-prepared seat;
may the Blessed Lady sit here.
The seat has been well prepared;
let the Blessed One sit here.
(All sit down. Mālatī: Is the Blessed One well?
"May it be well with the lady. (Sighing) "It is as if it were well."
Kāmandakī (to herself):
This is indeed the prologue to the drama of deception;
the "nīvī" is the seed.
The loosening of that knot of her garment is its slackening;
it arises from both the relaxation of the cloth and from passion.
As it has been said: "Sweat, trembling, and paralysis [occur], as does the loosening of the lower garment."
It manifests for women whose souls are under the sway of passion.
Trembling of the lower lip is the shaking of the lower lip;
this, however, occurs during a throbbing kiss.
As it has been said: "She who desires to seize the teeth that are entering the lip..."
When one's own lower lip trembles and quivers, that is considered the kiss.
Lassitude in the arms results from the pleasure of embracing;
perspiration from exertion; "masṛṇa" means soft.
It is sweet and graceful;
it is longing because that which is obtained through mere thought is difficult to behold;
and it is tender due to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
The eye is bewildered by the cultivation of pleasure;
it is a sidelong glance due to the presence of envy toward the beloved, who is obtained through mere thought.
A sidelong glance occurs in the context of envy.
As it is said: "The oblique glance (jihyā) is described as having its lids gracefully contracted, slowly gliding sideways, with the pupil partially hidden and partially revealed."
When [the object] has been obtained, it is *lalita* (graceful) due to steadfastness and joy;
its definition has indeed already been stated.
[The term] *ākekarā* [is used] in the context of a dense gaze, in separation, and when [loved ones] have gone abroad.
With her eyelids slightly contracted, she gazed with half-closed eyes that did not blink.
A gaze in which the pupils repeatedly roll back and forth is considered ākekarā.
There is a distinction between the words *dordoṣā*, *bhujā*, and *bhuja*.
*Gātrastambha* is the rigidity of the body;
it arises from excessive joy.
As it has been said: "Stiffness arises from excessive joy, fear, anger, and passion."
Because they have the shape of buds, the breasts themselves are the "buds. The "continuous tremor" refers to a vibration that lacks interruption,
resulting from the lover's firm embrace.
Upon the expanse of her cheeks, within the circle of her face, there appeared a mass of horripilation— a cluster of bristling hairs—
due to the thought of her beloved’s kiss;
the use of the word *paṭala* (cluster/mass) is intended to convey its extreme intensity.

*Mūrcchanā* is a state of swoon, resulting from union with unsurpassed bliss. As it has been said: "Lassitude of the body, closing of the eyes, and *mūrcchanā* are the characteristics of attaining the height of passion."
And her consciousness was intermittently present through the mental construction of amorous play.
Mālatī:

It is the established custom among Buddhists to say "I salute" (vandāmi) when approaching one who has gone forth into the religious life; or rather, it may simply be a general salutation, as in "I salute" (vanda).
Kāmandakī says "the vessel" (*bhājanam*) in order to divert Mālatī’s mind and to demonstrate her own steadfastness regarding that object. Lavaṅgikā:
Deceit itself is a drama.
Having moved [her] here... Kāma—sighing—O child; of the fruit of being born with great fortune. O you of desired fruit, the state of the fruit. Venerable lady, this seat is thus purified. Second Act.
Now, the venerable lady [speaks] aloud.
His voice is altogether changed—his throat is choked by a flood of heavy tears, and his sighs are closely entangled within him.
What could now be the cause of such distress?
This is surely a prelude to some deceptive drama.
"O Guru, because my throat is choked with such agitation, I cannot clearly utter the words of the venerable lady; they seem quite different today.
So, what could possibly be the cause for this distress?
Is it not indeed this very familiarity that is at odds with her tattered rags?"
Kāmandakī: Lava—How so?
How indeed? Ayī! Do you not know even this?
This body, the victorious weapon of Love and the very foundation of innate grace,
will become pitiable through its union with an unworthy husband, its excellence of virtues rendered fruitless.

Mālatī gesticulates her distress. Lavaṅgikā: It is true that because the Minister, acting in accordance with the King’s command, has promised Mālatī to Nandana, all the people are loathing the Minister. It is true that because the Minister, acting in accordance with the King’s command, has promised Mālatī to Nandana, all the people are loathing the Minister.
Mālatī – (To herself) How is it that my father has made me an offering to the King? How is it that I have been offered as a gift to the King by my father?
Kāma: Oh, how wonderful! Kāma: "Bāṣpa" refers to tears;
"stambha" refers to paralysis or obstruction.
*Mandharita* means made slow or slackened;
that [state] in which the breath is clinging to such a throat.
Kāmandakī: Familiarity with Mālatī and her attachment to her—this is the cause of distress; such is the ellipsis.
"This," and so forth:

Buddharakṣitā: Indeed, by the command of the Blessed One, during various confidential conversations, my dear friend Madayantika has been led far astray by such and such talk regarding Makaranda, developing a secret passion for him. And even her heart’s desire was this: "O, that I might behold him!"
This is my heart's desire: that I might indeed behold her.
(He faints.)
Avalokitā:
Here, indeed, because the purpose of increasing one's good fortune serves as a pretext for that which is false;
thus it is said.
The meaning is that one should worship the deities with flowers plucked by hand.
Regarding the phrase "he will bring":
the intention of the Blessed One is that, through the unexpected sight of Mālatī and Mādhava in a secluded place, their mutual passion may increase.
Buddharakṣitā:
Having been invited and summoned here,
I am going.
The remainder of the sentence is "at Madayantikā’s location.
Avalokitā [asks]: "What has transpired regarding the marriage of Makaranda and Madayantikā? This is the intended meaning.

Buddharakṣitā: Here, "deception" means trust—that such-and-such [person] is like Makaranda. Avalokitā, what will happen? To my mother? To Saṅkaraura? Then, so far away... [Mādhava and Mālatī]. Avalokitā: Excellent, Buddharakṣitā! Excellent, excellent, Buddharakṣitā! Excellent! Buddharakṣitā: Come, let us go.
"Come, let us go! Thus they both exit. Interlude.
Then Kāmandakī enters.
Kāmandakī: Although she was so humble by nature, I have, through various means, led Mālatī in a few days to a state where she may be enjoyed with the confidence of a friend.
For at this moment:

In separation she falls into distress; in my presence she is serene; in private she delights with affection; she speaks with love and follows my will. At the time of my departure, clinging to my neck and holding me back again and again, she immediately seeks my return through oaths and prostrations.
And this is the strongest ground for hope in this matter:
having heard from incidental conversations the legendary tales of Śakuntalā and others, she remains for a long time motionless with thought, her limbs resting upon my lap.
"Nam" means "indeed.
Of that Madayantikā;
him, Makaranda.
Avalokitā:
The sense is that you have lightened the burden of the Blessed Lady.
"Thus," and so forth.

In that manner—that is, by means of a method such as the story of Śakuntalā and others—Mālatī, who was bowed down with humility and devoid of arrogance, was brought by me, within a few days, to a state of serviceability through the instillation of a sense of confidence as if she were a friend, thereby leading her to abandon her bashfulness and other such traits.
The word "api" (also) has the sense of "eva" (indeed).
Alternatively, there is an elision of the vowel *a* in the word *avinayanamrā* (not bowed down by lack of discipline).
Regarding the phrase *katipayāhobhiḥ*, the rule for the compound-ending suffix does not apply because *ahar* here refers to the genus (*jāti*).
She indicates the sign of her friend with the words beginning "she goes" (*vrajati*), and so forth:
"Now, because she departs from us in our absence, she becomes cheerful in our presence;
she delights in solitude."
The word "with me" (*mayā saha*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Out of affection, she gives a reply that is a gift accompanied by a jest;
or else, she gives a gift such as camphor and other such items.
At the time of departure, she follows me, trailing behind;
then, clinging to my neck, she repeatedly restrains me with oaths and, having prostrated, begs for a return at that very moment.
My friends do the same.

Therefore, the sense is: "Having become her friend, she will carry out what is in my mind. Regarding the word *dāya*, Medinīkara states: "The word *dāya* may mean that which is to be given or a gift; it also refers to sarcastic speech (*solluṇṭhabhāṣaṇa*)."
"Excellent, very well!
'Nibandhana' means the cause.
'Śākuntalādīn' and so forth..."
She introduces historical narratives such as that of Śakuntalā and other ancient accounts through words seemingly directed elsewhere, in the course of another conversation.

[She says: “O father, enough with Śakuntalā and the rest! Come, go! (Having walked about: “In just a few days, there will be a change. He speaks of the inheritance and forcibly restrains me. (With longing: “The Third Act.”
Therefore, today I shall commence my reply in the presence of Mādhava. (Looking toward the tiring-room) Child, this way, this way!
Then Mālatī and Lavaṅgikā enter. Mālatī (to herself): "How have I been made an offering? How have I been made an offering? She recites the aforementioned passage beginning with these words.

Lavaṅgikā: Friend, here indeed is the garden breeze from Kusumākarodyāna embracing you—a breeze charming with the fragrance of Campaka flowers whose petals are torn asunder by the swarms of restless bees flying up from the tops of mango trees, which are agitated by the clamor of flocks of cuckoos warbling sweetly and passionately over their clusters of fresh, glistening blossoms; a breeze whose gentle movement is faltered by the weight of thighs heavy and slow from supporting the fullness of a female swan’s fleshy hips, and whose cool touch acts like sandalwood upon your lovely moon-like face, where droplets of perspiration have been removed and now resemble drops of nectar. Come, let us enter.

My dear friend, here is the breeze from the Kusumākara garden—charming with the fragrance of campaka trees whose petals are slightly opened as they are brushed by the restless swarms of bees that have flown up from the tops of sahakāra trees, which are filled with the tumultuous clamor of flocks of cuckoos eager for the sport of sipping the clusters of blossoms dripping with the essence of sweet honey; it is a breeze whose touch is as cool as sandalwood paste applied to the moon-like face of a young woman, her cheeks moist with drops of perspiration brought on by the slow gait of one whose heavy thighs are burdened by the weight of hips as fleshy as those of a peacock, and who stumbles slightly as she moves. Come, let us enter.
Having walked around, the two enter.
The meaning is that she asks me, "O Blessed One, is it true that you have given yourself away regardless [of my request]?

Here, by the word "other" (anya), it is indicated that the desire to hear the description of the hunting grounds and the hermitage, as well as the intention to commit a rash act, are present in her mind as the direct objectives.
Having heard "so be it," she places her body upon my lap due to the remembrance of the Leader held in her heart.
Then, she remains for a long time in a state of stillness and immobility, characterized by the thought, "What shall I do now?
The word "thought" (cintā) is used here as an illustration.
The meaning is that she is characterized even by her sighs and so forth;
or else, "mad" is the ablative case,
meaning she acts thus only after having heard it from me.
"Samakṣam" means "in the presence of" or "directly perceived. "Uttaram" refers to the subsequent action or duty.
The ellipsis is "let him come from here."
Lavaṅgikā: The connection is that the breeze from the Kusumākarodyāna garden is indeed embracing you right here.

Of what nature is it? It is captivating due to the fragrance—the scent of the campaka flower whose petals have opened wide and which is thus uneven [in its blooming]—and this is brought about by contact with a charming swarm of bees that have flown up from the very fragrant tops of mango trees because they were agitated by the clamor of a flock of cuckoos making indistinct sounds (*kala*) in their play (*keli*), that is, their sport, while devouring—that is, eating—an extremely fresh cluster of blossoms (*mañjarī*) with its exceedingly sweet nectar.
By this, coolness and fragrance are indicated.
The state of being swarmed by cuckoos [is a quality] of mango blossoms; the reason for the bee’s abandonment of them is [their lack of these qualities].
"Marāla" refers to either an elephant or a swan.

The sense is that your two thighs are slow and languid due to supporting the fullness of her fleshy hips. Because of their weight, as she moves with a faltering and uneven step, she proceeds slowly and gently—she who is dark like a *karāla* (a type of black bee), whose speech is sweet, who sports with her mouth, whose hips are like those of a swan (*marāla*), and who is brought forth by the movement [of her gait]. (She speaks) in a voice clear with tears, saying: "Sister, let us proceed this way. —From the *Mālatīmādhava*.
Then Mādhava enters.
Mādhava (with joy):
Ah, the venerable lady has arrived!
For as this [moonlight] appears, it first makes the heart of my beloved breathe freely,
like a flash of lightning before the rain for a young peacock scorched by the heat.
Having seen Lavaṅgikā alone here, Mālatī too said:
"It is a marvel! Due to the proximity of this lotus-eyed one’s stainless moon-like face, my mind repeatedly attains a state of numbness;
thus, a liquid transformation is sustained within my heart, just as a mountain of moonstone is melted by the presence of a genuine moon."
By that movement brought about by him, [there was] upon your charming moon-like face— which, by implication, is yours— is like drops of nectar from the spray of perspiration;
it possesses a touch as cool as sandalwood paste.
By this, both languor and coolness are also suggested.
"The *sahakāra* is exceedingly fragrant," according to Amara;
"the *cañcarīka* is used for a bee and for movement," according to Dharaṇi.
‘Karāla’ means jagged; thus says Amara.
‘Marāla’ refers to a swan or an elephant, and also to something extensive or auspicious; thus says Viśva.
Therefore, it should be construed as "of that which is extensive and auspicious like a swan," or simply "of the extensive and auspicious."
"Smooth, glossy, and even" — thus says Amara.
Mādhava: Ah, what joy!
She has arrived.
"Āviḥ" and so forth:
this Blessed Lady, appearing before my beloved, first causes my heart to expand. Of what kind [of heart]?
For one scorched by torment, consumed by the fire of desire—
just as a flash of lightning appearing before a young peacock brings relief and a sigh of hope to its heart—
the mention of a "youth" heated by the summer heat is intended to illustrate the cause of his madness.

In the expression *priyāyāḥ*, the genitive case is used according to the rule *ṣaṣṭhī atasarthapratyayena* (Pāṇini 2.3.30). For this very reason, the construction *priyāyāḥ prathamam* is not tenable; for when joined with a word denoting "first" (*prathama*), the genitive case is prohibited.
By this it was indicated that his beloved would also arrive.
In the word "mālatī," the particle *api* is used to express respect,
since indeclinables possess multiple meanings.
[This refers to the passage beginning with] "it is a marvel," and so forth.

In the presence of the spotless moon-like face of this lotus-eyed woman, my mind repeatedly attains a state of dullness characterized by an inability to perform any action; through that very dullness, as its instrument, a transformation—a change from its natural state—is maintained.
Of what nature is it? It is, as it were, composed of liquid.

Because her heart is melted and she possesses perspiration and other signs, it is a marvel that this transformation consisting of melting occurs in her through his mere presence, whereas for another woman it would result from actual union; for one observes such an excellence of action. As Bharata said: "The arising of wonder is produced by an excellence of action."

"He is to be won over at the places of accomplishment by means of great joy, horripilation, and so forth. Just as in the presence of the stainless moon, a mountain [of moonstone] attains a state of dullness through coldness, and by that very coldness, the liquid transformation of the stone—its fluidity—is maintained;
here, by the simile of the mountain, the abundance of Mādhava’s firmness and other qualities is expressed.
In the reading "jātyena," it means "by that which possesses the genus" (i.e., genuine).
"By the most excellent" means up to that point.
This should be understood as a further qualification of the term "candrakāntena" (by the moonstone).
Alternatively:
This is also a qualification of the mind.
O noble lady, by good fortune, Mādhava—the very essence of the mind—has surely returned from his journey, having dispelled the dullness caused by the heat of the summer season. Act Three.
At present, Mālatī is even more beautiful.
She kindles the fire of passion, intoxicates the heart, and fulfills the eyes with her limbs,
languid and lovely with the grace of a garland of crushed campaka flowers.
Mālatī: Friend, let us gather flowers in this bower of *kubjaka* trees.
Friend, let us gather flowers in this bower of *kubjaka* trees.
Now, with my hair standing on end from hearing the first words of my beloved, I am being mocked by myself.
The splendor of the kadamba trees was intensified at that moment by the sudden sprinkling of fresh water from dense rows of clouds.
—Friend, let us do so. Friend, let us do so.
(Lava and Puṣpā act out gathering flowers.)
Mādhava: The teaching of the Blessed Lady is of immeasurable wonder.
Mālatī: Friend, let us gather [flowers] elsewhere from here as well. Friend, let us both gather elsewhere.
Nor even by one of noble birth; the word "even" (api) is to be supplied here. For this very reason, it is a marvel.
Regarding "saṃprati" (now): formerly she was beautiful through the state of the sprouting of the impulse of passion; but now, because that impulse has put forth shoots, she is even more beautiful.
This very point he clarifies with the words "it inflames," and so forth.
Now, she kindles the fire of passion with the limbs of Mālatī;
she makes her heart frantic.
He ordains that the eye has fulfilled its purpose;
"mine" is the understood remainder.
Of what kind [is it]?
The meaning is that [the women] were like crushed campaka garlands due to their graceful charms (*vilāsa*), which were languid, slow, and restrained by modesty.
"Grace" (*vilāsa*) is defined by the wise as that specific quality arising from the movements of the eyes, face, and so forth, during walking, standing, sitting, and other such actions.
Thus says Bharata:
That which is performed by the graceful arrangement of hands, feet, and limbs, as well as by the eyebrows, eyes, and lips,
according to a delicate method, is called *lalita* (the graceful).
Thus says Bharata.
Or alternatively:
"mlānāni" means those whose beauty is like that of a crushed campaka garland.
"Lalita" means cast here and there;
"alasāni" means slow.
Thus, it is a three-word *karmadhāraya* compound.
And the root *dhā* is used in the sense of "unsteadiness" as well, because roots have multiple meanings. In the reading *lulitālasaiḥ*, the meaning is "shaken and tossed here and there."
"First," and so forth.
Now, by means of the fresh sprinkling of water from a mass of clouds, I am adopting the splendor—or rather, the elaborate display—of a *nīpa* tree that has just begun to bud.
Of what kind [of tree]?
From hearing the words of her first beloved, with his hair standing on end clearly visible;
if the reading is *saṃstava*, then *saṃstava* means familiarity.
By this illustration, the horripilation covering all his limbs and its steadfastness are expressed.
"Clouds are called *mudira*," according to Amara.
Mādhava: "Immeasurable," and so forth.

At the time of plucking the flowers, Mādhava’s manifestation of satisfaction through a flood of bliss arises from seeing the budding breasts of Mālatī and others; thus, Kubja first takes hold [of this]. In the *Mālatīmādhava*, Kāmandakī—embracing Mālatī—says:
"O child, stop, stop!"
You have become exhausted;
for indeed,
your speech falters, each limb of yours droops, and beads of sweat arise, shining upon your moon-like face.
O fair-browed one, your eyes are closing; exhaustion manifests in you in every way, equal to the longing gaze of a lover.
Mālatī gesticulates bashfulness. Lavaṅgikā: What the venerable lady has commanded is excellent; what the venerable lady has commanded is excellent.
Mādhava: A heart-warming jest!
Kāmandakī: Therefore, please be seated;
I wish to tell you something that must be told.
They all sit down.
[Mālatī] raises her chin.
Listen, O fortunate one, to this wonder!
Kāmandakī: Mālatī— I am attentive. Kāmandakī:
Now, on one occasion, in the course of conversation, I have already mentioned a prince named Mādhava, who, like you, is a second bond for my heart.
We remember; we remember well.
This is the state of Lava.
Under the pretext of mentioning fatigue, Kāmandakī addresses Mālatī—who is unaware of Mādhava’s presence—with a word of playful irony, beginning with "Ayī" and so forth.
"Niḥsahā" means you are exhausted; therefore, "virama," which implies "cease from your distress. Alternatively, it may mean "cease from gathering flowers."

The sense is: "Sit down. In the alternative sense, you have become exhausted from passion; therefore, enjoy yourself intensely. The *loṭ* suffix is used here in the sense of expressing a wish (*āśaṃsā*).
"Skhalayati" and so forth:
O fair-browed one (subhru), fatigue manifests itself—that is, performs its own function—in you simultaneously with the gazing upon your beloved;
the sense is that as there is the gazing upon the beloved, so too is there fatigue.
In one sense, there is the gazing by the beloved and [in another] distress;
for this very reason, the phrase "in every way" indicates their equality.
He expresses that very point: "Distress causes your speech to falter."
He clings to every limb with restraint; in the reading "he causes to slip," it means he loosens them.
He produces beads of perspiration emerging from the moon of his face, and he causes his two eyes to close like buds.
At the end of sexual union, during fatigue, in the state of experiencing pleasure,
and in response to fragrance, touch, and joy, the *mukulā* gaze is prescribed.
Thus says Bharata. This occurs even upon beholding one's beloved; the meaning here is that the beholding of the beloved resides within you.
Lavaṅgikā:
The intention is that [the conversation] should be stopped.
Kāmandakī: Raising and lifting up the chin— that part of the body below the lower lip—
she implies by the word "fortunate" that because you have captivated Mādhava’s heart, you alone are truly blessed with good fortune.
Kāmandakī:
By the word "prince" (kumāra), astonishment is expressed. For: he blushes while conversing; this is strange due to the context. End of the third act.
Kāmandakī: Indeed, ever since the day of the excursion to the Madana garden, he has been dejected, as if no longer master of his own body due to its torment.
For instance:
That which brings him no joy in the moon nor in his beloved person, that very thing now reveals his inner anguish, even though he is exceedingly steadfast. It is a grievous state.
Although his body is naturally dark like the priyaṅgu plant, he bears a form that is exceedingly pale, sweet, and emaciated, yet he remains beautiful.

Lava: At that very moment, Avalokitā, urging the Blessed Lady to hasten, had exclaimed, "Mādhava’s body is unwell! Kāmandakī: As long as Mālatī herself is not here—Mālatī alone [is the remedy] for him; that is my firm conviction.
Why?
Because it is the cause of the madness of love.
For the moon of his face inevitably brought about this indignation in that great-souled one, as he spoke of his own experience.
The mind, agitated and trembling with longing, is like the water of the great ocean when it is still.
Mādhava: Oh, what purity of argument!
Oh, what effort in attributing greatness!
Or rather—
Mastery of the scriptures, innate understanding, confidence, speech refined by practice,
timely comprehension, and eloquence— these qualities are like wish-fulfilling cows for all undertakings.
Wealth is the object [of desire].
Kāmandakī:
One who is dependent is not independent.

"Yadityādi" and so forth. Because of the torment of his body, he is as if dependent on others; for this reason, he does not experience—that is, he does not obtain—joy or affection toward the moon or toward a beloved person.
It is so;
nevertheless, even though he is endowed with fortitude, he reveals an inner torment that is difficult to bear.
And although his bodily nature is dark like the *phalinī* creeper, he bears a body that is pale, sweet, slightly wan, charming, and exceedingly emaciated—just as it is, so it is.
And it becomes beautiful.
The word "api" (also/even) expresses wonder; the word "ca" (and) serves as a conjunction for accumulation.
The word *api ca* is used either as a compound or as a conjunction for the purpose of accumulation (*samuccaye*).
Therefore, the intended meaning here is: "In this state of passion, act as is appropriate.
According to Amara, *priyaṅgu* means *phalinī*.
Kāmandakī: "As for 'in order to ascertain'—the meaning is that I heard it to be exactly this: that Mālatī alone is the cause."
I have heard; I have listened.
"Anubhavam," and so forth.
This moon of his face has certainly attained—that is, reached—the experience of this Great Soul;
for that reason, the mind of this steady and composed one has been moved.
Thus, my resolve is also exactly that;
what is it like?
It is restless with longing.
Just as the water of the great, unfathomable ocean—which is normally still and motionless—becomes agitated by the experience of the moon, its waters becoming restless with waves;
as Medinīkara says: "The term *utkalikā* refers to longing (*utkaṇṭhā*) and the playful ripples of water (*helā-salila-vīci*)."
Mādhava: Purity is the state of being untroubled.

Regarding the qualities of the messenger (*dūtī*), he says: "In the scriptures," and so forth. [She is] one who is devoted to this, charming, and pleasing to the mind. Just as his... up to "I am indeed... [her] intellect is such that, oh, she is for me like the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmaduh*) in accordance with the time. In the *Mālatīmādhava*, Kāmandakī says: "By him, who is trembling at the thought of life, nothing is left undone, however difficult it may be.
For he fixes his eye upon the budding young mango tree where the cuckoo warbles; he casts his body along the path of the breeze filled with the fragrance of the *bakula*."
With her body fainting from the heat of her longing, separated from him by no more than a single leaf of a fresh lotus, she repeatedly resorts to the rays of the moon for her own death.
Mādhava: A truly unprecedented manner of discourse for the lady.
Mālatī (to herself): She performs what is exceedingly difficult.
*Atidukkarāṃ karedi*.
This is the conclusion:
therein, innate awakening is natural knowledge;
when knowledge exists, there is boldness or eloquence.
Speech in which qualities such as *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and the like are practiced;

or alternatively, speech that accords with what has been practiced—that is, with repeated cultivation (*abhyāsa*). Knowledge of time (*kālāvabodha*) means the understanding of the proper occasion (*samaya*).
"Appropriate eloquence" refers to the power of instantaneous recollection and the possession thereof.
These qualities, when applied to all tasks—whether in general contexts or specifically in matters concerning female messengers (*dūtī*)—are like wish-fulfilling cows, bestowing whatever is desired.

Among these, proficiency is said to arise from mastery of the sciences; boldness from confidence; audacity from the presence of creative intuition (*pratibhāna*); and the ability to discern gestures from the qualities of a messenger.
As it is said: "Cleverness, boldness, knowledge of gestures, the ability to deceive, and knowledge of place and time—these are considered the qualities required for the duties of a female messenger."
In the word *kāmaduh*, the suffix *kvip* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.61] *sati* and so forth.
Kāmandakī:
"By one who is weary of life"—this follows the definition by Bharata: "Aversion toward living beings.
With the reading "is not done," there is a shaking of the head [in disapproval].
He speaks of what is indeed difficult: "They bear," and so forth.
By that, a difficult task is performed;
for this [person] bears his eye toward death—that is, toward dying—amidst fresh mango blossoms and warbling cuckoos.
She casts her body and places it upon the path of the wind, the kinsman of the Bakula fragrance.
Here, by the word "path" (*mārga*), that route by which the yet-to-arrive wind must come is indicated.

By the term "Bakula fragrance," her capacity for her own task is expressed; by the word "womb" (*garbha*), the firmness of her internal and external state is stated; and through her "love for the forest fire" (*dāvaprema*), she repeatedly resorts to the moonbeams out of affection for the forest conflagration.
By this, the burning quality of the moonbeams is expressed.

Here, by the word "love" (*prema*), the absence of any conflicting reflection regarding the heroine's passion is suggested; and by the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), their status as the cause for physical contact is also implied.
Of what nature [is he]?
With his body wasting away, separated from him by nothing more than the leaves of a lotus pond;
the phrase "death is everywhere" is to be applied here.
Thus, the sense is that he has made an effort toward death.
When there is an obstacle— that is, a hindrance to death—
in that context, the lotus leaf serves as the cause.
Here, by being a cause of harm through its nature as an arouser of passion, the moonbeams and so forth indicate the excellence of the *vipralambha* (love-in-separation).
Furthermore, by stating that mental transformation is produced by the senses, the pacification of the senses is effected:
through the sight of the fresh mango, the eye [is calmed];
for the mango, by virtue of its being covered and its budding state, causes extreme suffering.
By hearing the song of the cuckoo, the sense of hearing [is purified];
by contact with the fragrance of the bakula flower, the sense of smell;
and by the touch of the wind and moonbeams, the sense of touch.
Mādhava:
An unbroken manner of narration—a sequence of telling not experienced by others.
Mālatī:
Because it causes such intense pain from the mere sight of the young mango tree, it is called *mālayati*. For instance: [She] covers her upper garment... in this way he acts. (End of the third act.
Thus, this youth is by nature so delicate that this poor fellow has never before experienced such suffering elsewhere.
"Now he is even capable of experiencing death.

Mālatī (aside): "Friend, because I suspected something on account of myself regarding him who is the ornament of all the world, the Venerable Lady acted as if she were afraid. So, what shall I do now in this situation?"
My friend, because of my own actions toward her—who is the ornament of the entire world—I have been made to tremble by the venerable lady’s affection.
So, what shall I do now in this situation?
Mādhava: By good fortune, I have been shown compassion by the venerable lady.
Rikālava: The Blessed One is reported to have spoken thus.

Even for us, O mistress, she—who has been seen by us many times as she graced for a moment the entrance to the street near our house—though her beauty is made even more enchanting by the pangs of love manifested through limbs as lovely as the core of a lotus bud untouched by the sun’s rays, yet she distresses her attendants;
she takes no delight in playful diversions.
She passes the day with her cheeks resting upon her lovely hands, which resemble lotuses;

moreover, she languishes before the breeze that blows from the edges of the palace garden—breezes as beautiful as the flow of nectar from blooming lotuses, carrying a mass of honey-drops from the *kunda* and *mākanda* blossoms.
Thus it is said that the lady speaks in this manner.
The meaning is that even for us, the princess has spoken thus out of love for you;
this is what Kāmandakī intends by saying "elsewhere" and so forth, thereby demonstrating that he was first attached to you alone.
"A *tapasvin* is to be pitied.
According to the *Viśvakośa*, "the word *tapasvin* applies to an ascetic and to one who is to be pitied.
By this, it is stated that he says this because "this poor fellow is a stranger," and not for some other reason.
"It is possible" means:
"In that way, you should become full of passion."
Mālatī:
"In this matter, of myself"—that is, of me. "Something" means death, which is not to be spoken of because it is inauspicious.
In the word *bhītāyitā*, the suffix *kyaṅ* is used in the sense of "acting like" (*ācāre*). As for the question "Why?":

the meaning is that although it would have been appropriate to say, "I too feel affection for him there in order to remain alive," she did not say so because she is still a maiden; therefore, [the speaker] intends her to speak.
[To Kāmandakī:
This is whispered aside;
[and Mādhava is concealed.]
Having heard this, he says, "By good fortune," and so forth. Lavaṅgikā:

How indeed does she—whose pleasure in sleep has been lost; whose body, like a sprout, is as if smeared with the juice of red lac from her slipping anklets; whose thick thighs tremble so that the knot of her lower garment is undone; whose lotus-like breasts heave unevenly with sighs surging from her agitated heart; whose slender arms are bound together by her disheveled tresses; who, at the moment of awakening, closes her eyes in a swoon due to the realization of the empty bed caused by the blow of her distressed gaze; and who, with only a long sigh remaining as life departs, is rendered a mere object of pity for her bewildered friends who have rushed to her aid to break her fainting fit—is she not making me, alas, a person to whom the end of my own desired life is imminent through the intervention of irresistible and ill-fated destiny? This one, an inhabitant of the earth, has emerged from the monastery and performs a display of playful sport, terrifying all the people gathered there with his formidable physical presence. I feel as if I have been bathed, as if immersed, by a copious, unsurpassed, or continuous stream of milk—a flow of milky water. In this context, by the first word (*tāraka*), the tremulousness of the pupils is indicated; by the second, the mobility of the eyeballs; by the third, the expansion of the eyelids and their playfulness; and by the fourth, the possession of merit is established upon the attainment of these three qualities.

Lava—(Aside): "Venerable lady, since these side-glances of theirs—which are beautiful with the overflowing wonder and joy filling their hearts, and charming as their composure wavers—spread about, they intoxicate me; for they resemble a garland of crushed blue lotuses to Kāma and Karandaka. The King: *(Observing them)* Ah, how wonderful! This pair of youthful maidens possesses a beauty that rivals the loveliness of the two Aśoka trees in full bloom. For, like those two trees, they possess limbs that are tender and yet firm, marked by the play of youth; they are adorned with the fresh blossoms of smiles, and their eyes are like the petals of a blooming lotus. Just as those two trees are graced by the presence of the God of Love, so too are these two maidens graced by the presence of the God of Love himself. Indeed, they are the very personification of the God of Love’s own form. *(Reflecting)* Or rather, this is not surprising. For the Creator, who fashioned the world, surely drew his materials from the very essence of the ocean of nectar. Otherwise, how could such a pair of jewels have come into being? *(Looking at them again)* But why do I think thus? It is because of the following: The Creator first fashioned the moon, which is the very essence of the nectar of the ocean of nectar, and then created her face. He then fashioned the blue lotus, which is the very essence of the moon, and then created her eyes. And finally, he fashioned the spring season, which is the very essence of the blue lotus, and then created her body. Thus, she is composed of the quintessence of all things. *(Aloud)* Noble lady, what is the name of this maiden? And whose daughter is she? Mādhava: King, this is the daughter of the illustrious Śarvilaka, the minister of the King of Magadha. She is named Mālatī. Kāmandakī: And who is this other one? Mādhava: This is her dear friend, Madayantikā, the daughter of the illustrious Bhūrivasu, the minister of the King of Ujjayinī. Kāmandakī: (With a smile) Oh, how well-matched they are! Truly, the Creator has made a perfect union of these two. For, just as the moonlight is enhanced by the presence of the moon, and the moon is enhanced by the presence of the moonlight, so too are these two maidens mutually enhancing one another’s beauty. *(To herself)* Oh, how my heart leaps up! Alas, alas! My mind is being torn asunder by the conflicting emotions of hope and fear. For on one hand, I am filled with joy at the sight of this union; yet on the other hand, I am struck with anxiety, fearing that some obstacle may arise. What shall I do? How can I ensure that this auspicious union is brought to fruition? *(Reflecting)* Ah, I have it! I shall employ the power of my spells and mantras to bring about their union. But first, I must ascertain the true nature of their affection for one another. *(Aloud)* Dear child, let us go to the temple of the Goddess Gaurī. There, we shall perform the rites of the *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage) for you both. *(They all rise and move about.)* Mādhava: (Aside) How strange! As I gaze upon these two maidens, who are like two celestial nymphs descended to earth, my heart is filled with a longing that is both sweet and painful. For, while I am captivated by their beauty, I am simultaneously tormented by the memory of my beloved Makaranda, who is likewise separated from his own beloved. Oh, how the sight of these two intensifies my own sorrow! *(Reflecting)* Yet, even in this state of distress, there is a certain inexplicable sweetness in my heart. It is as if a drop of nectar has fallen into a cup of poison. What is this strange transformation within me? Is it love, or is it something else? Or perhaps it is simply the power of destiny, which has brought these two together in such a way that they mirror my own condition. *(Looking at them again)* Ah, how they look at each other! Their glances are like the first rays of the morning sun, tender and full of longing. They seem to be whispering secrets to one another without words, their hearts beating in unison. Truly
