This eightfold sovereignty of Śambhu is not known by everyone, even though it is sought by some; as it has been said: "Even among the perfected ones who strive, only someone knows Me in truth."
Thus [it is said].

Alternatively, "the bestower of success upon those who know them" means he is the giver of success—that is, the giver of desired accomplishments—to those who, through the knowledge of the means, place, time, measure, and procedure, understand those [accomplishments].

He states the perfection of yoga regarding the self in the verse beginning with "nityam" (always), etc. [The meaning is: "I have now arrived"—by implication—from Śrīparvata, having come toward the desired place; of what sort am I?
She perceives the Self as having the nature of Śiva through one-pointedness of mind by virtue of absorption;
by this, the manifestation of all other things is set aside.
Of what nature?

Eternal and indestructible. It is that which has been placed—meaning deposited through the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*)—within the wheel, that is, the collection, of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) assigned to the body: the heart, head, crest, eyes, armor, and weapon. It is established and superimposed by means of the ritual placement of mantras.
As it is said: "This six-limbed [practice], which bestows all accomplishments, has been taught;
the practitioner, whose soul is endowed with devotion and who contemplates knowledge, should indeed perform the placement."

The wise one should place [the mantras] upon the body either three times a day or at a single time; by this, the covering of the limbs (*aṅgāvaraṇa*) is explained. In the reading *nityanyasta*, the meaning is "placed daily" (i.e., every day).
In the center of the heart-lotus—that is, in the pericarp of the heart-lotus—it has arisen like the sun through the practice of meditation.
As it is said: "The heart is seen there to have a shape resembling a lotus;
for the subtle Puruṣa, the Supreme Self, is to be known as residing in the heart."

Through practice, one perceives the Sun, the Supreme Self, by means of the self. By means of the sequence of the rising of the previously mentioned channels, such as *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, and through the process of filling [them] with breath; and from that attraction—by the power of yogic *siddhis*—of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), namely earth, water, fire, air, and ether, which constitute the world-body; she is the one by whom fatigue has not been incurred through leaping or traveling through the sky. Alternatively, "nectar" (*amṛta*) is like actual nectar, because it is the cause for the maintenance of the body.

Furthermore, that [nectar] is either the specific essence flowing from the stimulation of Kuṇḍalinī at the station of the *bindu*, or the specific essence flowing from the aperture situated below the tongue;
for it is designated by the five names because of its pervasiveness,
due to its being drawn upward.

Alternatively, there are five nectars of the world—that is, of the body—which consist of the nature of Śiva and Śakti, characterized by form, taste, smell, touch, and sound; they are eternal and serve to nourish the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) of the gross material elements.

The sense is that through the utilization of these by the Yoginīs, their powers and other qualities arise by means of their extraction. Nor should it be argued that flight is impossible because [the body] is inactive due to being subject to dissolution (*laya*).
Because its capacity exists even elsewhere when one is in a state of repose (laya).

As it is said: "Even when the mind is directed elsewhere and the eye is cast elsewhere, the yoga of yogis is nevertheless proclaimed to be uninterrupted. Indeed, by the very majesty of her flight and other such powers, she splits asunder the clouds standing before her in the sky. Furthermore, in the *Mālatīmādhava*: api ca | [She continues:]...and moreover:

With the garland of skulls on his neck jostling and tumbling in the violent surge, and the small bells on his skeleton frame tinkling from their friction, the momentum of his flight through the expanse of the sky perfectly combines in me a state that is both beautiful and terrifying.
For instance:

the mass of matted locks, though bound with tight knots, sways in every direction; the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), its bells ringing shrilly from long-standing habitual practice, rattles loudly;
and the wind, whistling through the groves of rows of open human skulls, shakes the banners aloft, providing the cause for the incessant tinkling of the small bells.
Regarding the reading *agre nabhaḥ*, it means "shattering the clouds in the sky before [her]";
nor is the word *nabhaḥ* (sky) redundant.
For even in the presence of clouds over forests, mountains, and so forth, their dispersal does not demonstrate an excellence of ascending into the sky.
Or rather:
"In front, she disperses the clouds in the sky."
The word *agre* is an indeclinable particle (*nipāta*) that resembles a case ending. It forms an adverbial compound (*avyayībhāva*) in the sense of a case ending.
By these two verses, the aesthetic sentiment of tranquility (*śānta-rasa*) has been expressed.
On this point, Bharata also says: "The ninth rasa is the peaceful (śānta).
And that arises from a distaste for sense objects.
As he said:
“Once again, the supreme flavor of the object arises as peaceful.
Thus [it is said].
He establishes the previously mentioned terrifying and radiant nature of Kapālakuṇḍalā with the verse beginning "ullole" (tossing).

The speed of her movement through the expanse of the sky brings together in me all that is both beautiful and formidable—where "ramaṇīyatva" means loveliness or charm, and "ḍāmaratva" means terror, ferocity, or intensity filled with the fervor of sport. [The lexicon states: "The words *ḍāmara* and *uḍḍāmara* denote the terrible, as well as that which is intense with the fervor of play."

Thus ends the *Ratnakośa*. [The compound is explained as follows: It is that [place] where the small bells (*kṣudraghaṇṭikā*) are "terrible" (*karāla*) and "mute" (*mūka*). They are "mute" because, due to the loud sound of the garland of skulls (*kapālamālā*) on the neck—[a garland] which is jingling through its movement back and forth by being tossed up with force—the sound of those [small bells] is not heard, owing to the clashing of the skulls against one another. It is as if they were mute because their own sound is drowned out by the high-pitched noise of the skull-garland.
Or rather, it is that [necklace] upon which there is a *kiṅkiṇī*— a small bell— that is *karālā*, meaning jagged or uneven, due to its such-like tinkling sound.
The state of bliss for the *kulayoginīs* arises from the sound of small bells (*kiṅkiṇī*) and other such instruments.

As it is said: "Through the sounds of the ocean’s roar, the multitude of *kiṅkiṇīs*, and the ringing of small bells, the yogi shall be ever-blissful; for him there is neither sleep, nor hunger, nor thirst."
Thus [it is said].
He says that very thing with the word "viṣvak":
the mass or collection of matted locks (*jaṭā*), though tied together firmly and tightly, moves about while pervading all directions (*viṣvagvṛtti*).
This is because of the speed of its movement through the sky; such is the implied meaning.
The word *viṣvak* has various meanings and is listed among the words beginning with *suṣamā*; by virtue of this, there is the substitution of *ṣ*.

Having performed the circumambulation (*kṛtāvṛttiḥ*), having gone and returned (*kṛtagatāgatā*), and having completed the rotation around the mandala (*kṛtamaṇḍalabhramaṇā*), the bell (*ghaṇṭā*) together with the *khaṭvāṅga* resounds—meaning it makes sound—in a manner that is long, sharp, and beautiful, through the resonance (*kkāṇa*) produced by its refinement (*saṃskāra*) and continuous succession (*saṃtāna*).
By this, its terrifying nature (*ḍāmaratva*) is expressed.
*Khaṭṭāṅga* is a type of musical instrument.
The wind blows upward, causing the banner to flutter; that is, it causes it to shake. The root *dhūñ* means "to shake."
The reason for the long vowel at the end is stated by the author of the *Nyāsa* in the sūtra beginning with "svarati" and so forth.
Of what sort [is it]?
It resounds—that is, makes a humming sound—within the thickets, those dense regions, of the rows or lines of those skulls which are wide open due to being devoid of flesh.

For this very reason, the shrill sound of small bells is loud and fierce, and their incessant tinkling is tumultuous and overflowing. [Looking around and sniffing the scent: This, then, is the temple of Karālā, situated near the great cemetery enclosure that is made manifest before us by the smoke of funeral pyres—smelling of garlic being fried in old neem oil—where, by the command of our preceptor Aghoraghaṇṭa, who has completed his mantra-attainments, I must today especially prepare the materials for worship. [The Fifth Act] (Walking about, looking around, and smelling the air) This, then, is the temple of Karālā, situated near the great cemetery enclosure that is made manifest before us by the smoke of funeral pyres—smelling of garlic being fried in old neem oil—where, by the command of our preceptor Aghoraghaṇṭa, who has completed his mantra-attainments, I must today especially prepare the materials for worship.

And it was said to me by my teacher, O dear Kapālakuṇḍalā: "Today, a jewel among women must be offered as a prior vow to the blessed goddess Karālā; she resides right here in this city. Therefore, I shall search for her. (Looking ahead with curiosity) Who is this person of such profoundly deep and sweet appearance, with his curly locks tied up, descending into the cemetery grounds with a sword in hand?
He who, though dark as the petal of a blue water-lily, possesses limbs that are perfectly pale; whose gait is graceful, who is glorious, and whose face resembles the moon;
and whose left hand—displaying audacity, dripping with the mud of blood, and clutching a dangling human leg—strikes down all decorum.
And the cause [of this]. By this, its loveliness is expressed.
"Nikkāṇa, nikkaṇa, kkāṇa, kvaṇa, and also kvaṇana."
Thus says Amara. Alternatively, the beauty [of the banner] is expressed here by its sharp rattling, and its terrifying nature by the fluttering of the flag.
"This first," etc., refers to the description of the nature of the funeral pyre's smoke by means of the words beginning with "ancient" (*purāṇa*).
"Anointed" (*akta*) means smeared (*mrakṣita*).
*Paribharjana* is the process of cooking by placing [the substance] in the midst of fire. *Rasona*,
which possesses five tastes with the exception of one— the sour taste—
is known as garlic (*lasūna*).
A *vāṭa* is that by which one is enclosed or surrounded (*vaṭyate veṣṭyate*). The suffix *ghañ* is applied according to the rule *halaca*.
Bhāguri states: "A *patha* is a *vāṭa*; a *patha* is a *mātha*."
*Nedīyaḥ* means near.
*Paryavasitam* means finished, completed, and destroyed.
*Mantrasādhanam* refers to the practice of mantra, such as the preliminary recitation (*puraścaraṇa*) and so forth.

*Saṃbhāraḥ* means a collection or multitude. *Upayācitam* refers to that which is undertaken for the sake of a desired object. Regarding this, it is said: "That which is given to the gods for the fulfillment of one's heart's desire is called an *upayācitakam*; they also designate it as a *dohada*."
Thus says the *Hārāvalī*.
Regarding "a jewel among women" (*strīratnam*):
"That which is most excellent within each respective class is indeed called a *ratna* (jewel)."
Thus [says] the *Viśva* lexicon.
In the reading "viditam," "upalabdham," and "vicintitam," the meaning is "sought after.
Regarding the passage beginning with "gambhīra" and so forth:
That state in which innate transformations of joy, anger, fear,
and so forth are not perceived during various emotional conditions is declared to be "depth" (gāmbhīrya).
"Thus it is said:
'From practice, however, the integration of the instruments arises;
even in great transformations, that sweetness is proclaimed.'"
Thus says Bharata:
he is one whose curly, crooked, and wavy hair (*kuntala*) is tied up and fixed in the form of a topknot (*juṭākāra*).
By this, his possession of the *raudra-rasa* (the Furious sentiment) is expressed.
"Kuvalaya," and so forth.
He who, though naturally dark-complexioned like the petal of a blue lotus (*nīlanalina*), now bears a body that is pale all over due to separation (*vipralambha*);
he whose bodily form (*nyāsa*) is alternately graceful and lovely, yet formidable and terrifying.
Gracefulness arises from its own nature;
ferocity arises from the *raudra* [sentiment].
Alternatively, "placement" (*nyāsa*) refers to the movement of the hands, feet, and so forth.

He is glorious and exceedingly beautiful. His face possesses a splendor that surpasses the moon; for this very reason, the word "moon" (mṛgāṅka) is employed [in the original] for the purpose of indicating its inferiority.
Whose left hand carries away—that is, removes—discipline;
here he states the reason: "with mud of flowing blood," meaning with a mire of streaming gore.
Garlic juice. Below. Indeed, today by me... searched. [Observing the mass of matted hair, grey and disheveled] Ah!
This is that very Mādhava, the son of Kāmandakī’s friend, who is offering human flesh for sale.
So, what is the use of him?
Let it be; I shall accomplish what you desire.
The time for the evening twilight is almost at its end.
For thus it is:

Now the horizons of the sky are being enveloped by creeping vines of darkness, as if by clusters of *tāpiccha* blossoms; through its encroachment upon the edges, the earth seems to sink into fresh waters.

At its very onset, the night brings forth its own deep blue hue within the forests, where it takes on the appearance of thick, swirling columns of smoke spreading in all directions with the force of a whirlwind.
Having walked around, they exit. This concludes the *viṣkambhaka*. Then Mādhava enters as previously described.
Mādhava (with longing):
May those various gestures of the lovely-eyed one—touching with love, arising from intimacy, born of deep passion, and naturally sweet—manifest toward me;
for even when merely imagined through longing, they bring about in an instant a dense absorption of bliss that obstructs the activity of the external senses within my heart.
Where there is human flesh, which is "mahāmāṃsa" (great meat), it is "lalat" (graceful) yet "cañcalam" (fickle/unsteady);
for one who is disciplined does not carry blood and great meat.
Here, gracefulness (*lalatva*) is expressed by the first half-verse, and the grotesque (*vikaṭatva*) by the second half-verse.
For this very reason, he is one who has committed a manifest act of rashness.
By his bearing of "great flesh" (mahāmāṃsa), the heroic (*vīra*) and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) sentiments are expressed.
As it is said: "From energy, resolve, wonder, joy, and delusion..."
From the remainder of various fragrances, that which is called the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa) arises.

"The aesthetic flavor of the loathsome (bībhatsa-rasa) arises from the sight of what is undesirable, from defects in smell, taste, touch, and sound, and from many kinds of stimulations. Regarding the word *dadhat*, there is a prohibition of the *num* augment according to the rule *nābhyastāc chatur* [Pāṇini 7.1.78].
According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *jāṅgala* refers to a deserted place in all three genders, and to meat in the masculine and neuter genders."
*Paṇāyitā* means a seller;
*vigalitaprāyaḥ* means almost fallen away or nearly lost.
"Of the sky," and so forth: the edges of the firmament are pervaded by creepers of darkness, as if by clusters of *tamāla* flowers.
And thus, with its submerged portion, the earth seems to sink into the fresh water;
this is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
"Triyāmā" means night.
Even at the very beginning of nightfall, it makes its own blueness appear fresh within the forests.

Of what sort? It is like a mass of smoke or mist—similar to a *dhūmyā*, which is a collection of smoke or frost—that is spread out, expanded, and coiled in a circular form in all four directions by the force of the swirling gusts of wind (*vātyā*).
Thus, the meaning is that twilight has almost passed away due to the approach of darkness.
Dharaṇi states: "The word *dhūmyā* refers both to a mass of smoke and to mist."
"Sāśaṃsam" means with longing or prayer.
Regarding the passage beginning with "prema" (love):
may those various experienced gestures of the lovely-eyed Mālatī—such as kisses and so forth during sexual union—occur in me once again.

"Specific gestures in sexual union, such as kissing, embracing, and so forth—thus, according to the context, they generally come to an end through contact. [This is] the play of pure objects; there is apprehension regarding the dense arising [of passion]. Furthermore: Act Five."
May I lie upon that body of my beloved, which is rendered fragrant by the constant application of the garland of *atimukta* filaments woven with *madayantī* flowers,
and upon which her face is nestled within the hollow of her ear as she turns toward me.
Or rather, let that be far from us for now;
this much I pray for:
may those joys which, when united, expand into a supreme abundance within the mind, and wherein a festival for the eyes initiates delight as they descend upon the path of vision.
Or rather, may I behold once again her face—that auspicious abode of the bodiless god of love—which seems as if fashioned from the very essence gathered from the rising moonbeams of her childhood.
The Neck Ornament (*kaṇṭhābharaṇa*). Of what nature are they?
First, they are like the joy of sexual union through love, because they produce horripilation and other signs that serve as the cause for the alleviation of distress.
Then, having gained confidence, they touched the clarity of their hearts;
then, through familiarity, they became invincible by pleasant weapons and possessed an intense surge of passion;
they were naturally sweet and inherently charming.

The meaning is that the mind dissolves into those activities in which, even when they are brought about by mere expectation, an absorption characterized by an intense mass of unsurpassed bliss occurs in an instant. Of what nature is [that mind]?
It is the nature of the internal organ, the mind, to restrain the activity of the external senses.
The meaning is that because my mind is entirely absorbed in Mālatī, it does not engage with external objects.
Therefore, the implication is that even though that place was crowded with many doubts and terrors, Mādhava experienced not even the slightest trepidation or fear.
Or rather, those various gestures which she performed toward Bakulavathī and others—may those very same ones be directed toward me;
for it is precisely because they are so difficult to obtain that they are worthy of longing.
He prays for an embrace because it is the cause of the first joy—beginning with the words "atimukta" and so forth:
"May I too obtain a turning upon that lap together with my beloved. This means a state of being situated in every way upon her lap, in her embrace.

The meaning is an embrace of the heart; it follows the sequence from the armpits. Or rather, by turning upon her lap in an upward-and-downward sequence, I shall attain the *puruṣāyita* (the male position).
Of what sort?
That in which my beloved has placed her face at the root of my ear (the *karṇajāha*).
That [same state] is mine as well.

In the first case, he is one by whom the face has been placed at the root of the ear (*karṇamūla*). Regarding the word *mūla*, the suffix *jāhac* is applied according to the rule: "After words beginning with *pīlu* and *karṇa*, the suffixes *kuṇap* and *jāhac* are added [to form a compound denoting a part].
She is *atimuktā*, meaning she by whom the pearls have been surpassed or released.
"Having cast aside the pearl necklace, there is a transgression because of its offering [to him];
or rather, she is 'atimuktā' (freed from restraint) due to her intense absorption in gazing at the *mālatī* flower.

This is an adverbial phrase describing the act: 'wherein the breast offered is beautiful and fragrant due to the constant perfuming by that very *kesarāvalī* (saffron garland) which was woven by me.'"
The reading *avimukta* is not compelling;
for since constant dwelling is already attained precisely because of being *aviyukta*, the inclusion of the term *sata* (constant) would be redundant.
"Having come together," and so forth.
"I pray for nothing other than this: that I may behold her face once again"—the sense being that the attainment of her lap is difficult to achieve.
Of what sort? It is the house for the sake of Kāma’s auspiciousness;
the meaning is that Kāma dwells there joyfully.
Alternatively, it is the auspicious golden house of Kāma;
for the Viśvaprakāśa states: "One should know that *kalyāṇa*, *maṅgala*, and gold are synonymous.
Or else, it is the abode of the auspicious factors—such as delicacy and so forth—which serve as the causes for the accumulation of the limbs of Anaṅga (the bodiless god).
For this very reason, he imagines:

"O child, my throat is constricted by the pressure of the seal; let there be first a reversal of the embrace, brought about by the moonrise and intensified by [the rising] of passion. In the *Mālatīmādhava*, there is no distinction [between the two].

Indeed, it is true that for me now, this continuous stream of cognitions consisting of memories of my beloved—arising from the incessant awakening of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the extraordinary perception of her in the past, which, though very slight, expands because its flow is not obstructed by other dissimilar cognitions—makes my consciousness itself seem composed of her alone through the conformity of its internal activity.
For instance: she seems as if dissolved, as if reflected, as if painted, as if carved in form, as if inlaid, as if joined with adamantine cement, and as if deeply engraved within.

"It was produced from the essences gathered from the rising digit of the moon"—here, by the word "from the rising" (*udayāt*), there is an implied reference to the substance; thus the meaning is: "as if produced from the essences gathered from the new moon's digit.
The intended sense is that it is more enchanting than even the digit of the new moon, which delights all people.
Alternatively, the ablative case is used with the elision of a verbal suffix (lyablope);

thus, the meaning is "gathered after reaching the rising of the crescent moon's digit. Or else, it means "gathered starting from the rising of the digit of the new moon—that is, from the first day of the lunar fortnight—until the full moon."
The sense of "beginning with" (ārabhya) is obtained precisely from the ablative case;
thus, the similarity of the face to the full moon is established.
In some places, the reading is "from the accumulation of parts" (kaloccayāt).
In that context, "from the accumulation" means from the collection;
wherein, when the face is turned toward one, the joys become the agents [of that turning].
As if having gathered together, they expand a supreme abundance and vastness within the mind.
By this, internal joy is expressed;
the word "iva" (as if) indicates a poetic conceit (utprekṣā).
In this reading, the word *eva* expresses astonishment.

He describes outward joy: the "festival for the eyes"—the pride of having obtained what was unobtainable—announces and pours forth passion (*anurāga*), because it is the very essence of sexual delight (*rati*).
Concentration is an ornament.
He expresses the extreme intensity of his mental longing with the words "mama hi" (for me).

My own stream of consciousness—the continuous succession of transformations arising from the cognition consisting of the remembrance of my beloved—is itself of the nature of memory; it makes my very consciousness, the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*), as if composed of her, meaning it makes it consist of Mālatī.
Of what sort is it?
"Stretching out" means becoming long.
The reason for this is the intensification (*udreka*) of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), that is, its awakening to an extraordinary degree. Of what kind of latent impression?

It establishes that the experience of the previous time continues in the bakula-avenue precisely because it is superior, respectful, or its form is not indistinct: "its activity is not obstructed by other cognitions whose objects are dissimilar to it and distinct from Mālatī.
Thus, the sense is that because no other object flashes forth in the interval, there is no interruption of the stream.
Now, since the reality of the Self is untainted like a lotus leaf, how can it consist of Mālatī? To this he says: "within."
The term "within" (*antaḥ*) here refers to the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*).

And thus, because that activity of the principle of intellect—the innate, established operation—appears within the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*) due to the non-apprehension of their difference, [it is said to be "within"].
This is because, in the Sāṃkhya system, the intellect (*buddhi*) is the experiencer.
Alternatively, the term *antarvṛtti* emphasizes the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*).

Thus, the similarity between the self and the cognition consists in their internal functioning, that is, their abiding within; for this reason, it is as we have already stated: "she has dissolved," and so forth. That beloved is *lagna*—that is, attached or bound—to our minds.
He states the possible modes regarding the state of being connected: "as if dissolved," "as if concealed.
Where a connected thing is not perceived by direct observation, it is said to be "dissolved" (*līna*) therein;
for example, salt dissolved in water.

He demonstrates here that the state of being fixed (*lagnatva*) arises everywhere through a distinction in its mode: "because of awakening"; "now there is no vision"—even a slight difference is perceived by one who has cultivated the self through powers dissimilar [to ordinary ones]; this creates the activity of the written record. —The Fifth Act.
That beloved is as if nailed to our hearts by the five arrows of the Mind-born God; she remains fixed, as if tightly sewn by the web of threads consisting of a continuous stream of anxiety.
Nor is there a distinction from a simile, because each preceding [simile] is unsatisfactory;
for instance,
since the state of being merged does not appear, he says "as if reflected" in order to convey a clear appearance.
When the eye, struck by a transparent substance, turns back and perceives another object, that [object] is said to be reflected therein—
just as a red flower [is reflected] in a crystal.
Since a reflection (*praticchāyā*) is not innate because it depends upon contact with another entity, he says "as if inscribed" (*likhiteva*) in order to describe its innate nature.
That which is fashioned upon a solid substance by means of a substance whose constituent parts are loosely joined, and which possesses a specific configuration, is said to be "written" thereon;
for example, writing on a leaf.
Since that which is written is not long-lasting due to its susceptibility to destruction by contact with water and other elements, he says—referring to this purpose—"as if carved in form."
If, in this case, some separation of parts is produced in a dense substance by such [an action], then that is "penetrated" (*utkarṇita*) there;
for example, stone and the like by a hammer or similar tool.
Since this too exists in only one part, he says "as if inlaid" (*pratyupteva*) in order to indicate its existence throughout the whole.
"Set in" (pratyupta) means half-set.
Whatever here is in contact with another substance is "set in" therein;
for example, a gem and so forth in a ring.
Because this [connection] could also be removed, he speaks of a "dense connection" (nibiḍasaṃbandha): "as if joined by adamantine glue" (vajralepaghaṭiteva).

Whatever here is not the substratum of conjunctions and disjunctions produced by action, which is itself produced by the impact of a solid substance, is there "joined by adamantine glue," such as a diamond and the like.
Nevertheless, because the ointment exists on the exterior, he says "as if buried within" in order to indicate internal contact.
That which is connected here [within] and held by means of upward and downward conjunction and so forth, yet is not perceived, is said to be "buried" there;
as, for example, a radish or similar root in the earth.

The distinction between these two is that "being dug in" (*nikhātatva*) refers to complete planting, while "being sown" (*uptatva*) refers to partial planting. He says—“as if nailed by the five arrows of Kāma”—to show that even what is dug in can be extracted with extreme persistence, yet it is difficult to distinguish [and remove] because of its deep roots. To show that what is nailed cannot be uprooted because it must first be countered by another nail, he says—“as if firmly sewn by the multitude of threads that are the succession of anxieties. By this sewing with a dense net, his state of being impossible to sever is expressed.
It should be noted here that although the substrate (*upadheya*) is non-different, there is no tautology due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);

for a single entity indeed becomes the object of different cognitions through its association with various adjuncts, just as in the cases of "one who has a staff" (*daṇḍin*) or "one who wears earrings" (*kuṇḍalin*).
Alternatively, it means that she is firmly fixed—that is, closely bound—in our hearts.
The object that has become fixed (*lagnapadārtha*) is precisely that which is firmly bound;
for this is observed in such instances as "the arrow is fixed" (*śaro lagnaḥ*).
That which is firmly bound is then stabilized in various ways.
She is as if pinned down by the five arrows of Kama;
she is as if sewn together by the continuous thread of the stream of her thoughts.
But surely, neither of these two [metaphors] is appropriate.

Because there is no connection between that [object] and the internal consciousness, the relationship between the object and the subject must therefore be of the very nature of their identity; thus, the view of the Yogācāra school is stated by this. The phrase "as if reflected" indicates the Sāṃkhya position.
The phrase "as if written" (*likhita iva*) demonstrates the Sautrāntika position.
For in that view, knowledge deposits its own form upon the object, thereby manifesting that particular form;
this similarity to writing is like [the impression of] a horse or other figures on stone and such.

"In the manner of being carved" means that here, the modification of consciousness (*caitanya*) into the form of an object constitutes "the state of being carved. This is the doctrine of the Tridaṇḍins.

"As if inlaid" means that through the concealment of its prior form and the manifestation of another form—just as in the case of vessels fashioned from gold—the transformation of knowledge occurs by assuming the respective forms of various objects; this is the doctrine of Patañjali.
The view of the Naiyāyikas is that [the relation] is as if forged with adamantine cement (*vajralepa*).
For the distinction of nature (*svabhāvabheda*) belonging solely to that [consciousness], which constitutes the subject-object relationship (*viṣayaviṣayibhāva*) of manifestation,
does not differ from being forged with adamantine cement due to its stability as long as the object exists.
In the *Mālatīmādhava*, amidst a tumultuous noise behind the scenes, Mādhava listens and says:
"Ah! At this moment, the cremation ground is truly terrifying with its burgeoning swarm of jackals."
For here, the dense mass of darkness, thick with its obstruction of the horizon, reveals through its own excellence a dull luster of funeral pyre fires that is formidable in its vast extent;
meanwhile, the Katapūtanas and other spirits, engaged in frenzied play and exultant with joy, raise a resonant clamor of "kila-kila" shouts.
"He eats indeed" is an illustration of the position of the Vijñānavādins;
for in their view, because consciousness is buried within, there is no existence of external objects.
Here too, it is the same.
And these conceptual constructions regarding the relationship between object and subject revolve within Mādhava’s mind because they are modes of his contemplation;
thus, there is a connection with the mind.
Afterwards, through either piercing or sewing, it becomes firmly bound—that is, adhered.
The sense is this: what is there to wonder at in his having that vision experienced by great beings?
Here, by the word "by the five," he indicates his own state of being subject to the arrows of Kāma all at once, thereby suggesting that he is beset by an unbearable condition.

"According to my ability, according to logic, according to my reach, according to my intelligence, according to what I have heard, and according to right policy— this has been analyzed by me."
Mādhava:
A "kauṇapanikāya" is a multitude of *rākṣasas*; "raudratā" is the state of being terrifying.
"paryanta... and so forth.
Darkness, acting as the agent, manifests—that is, makes evident—the brilliance of the funeral pyres' flames by means of their "parabhāga," that is, through the imparting of an excellence of quality.
The sense is that when darkness is present, the excellence of the luster of luminous bodies becomes manifest.
What kind of darkness? Terrifying due to its expansive fullness;
obstructive in the vicinity of the circle of light from the funeral pyres; thick and glossy with its mass or accumulation; and dense.
Alternatively,

The corpses (*kaṭāḥ*), *pūtanā* demons, and other such beings dwelling there, such as jackals and the like, raise a clamor of mutual challenge through their *kilakila*-like cries.
From *saṃmada* means from joy or exhilaration. *Uttālāḥ* means lofty, formidable, or flickering;
they have emerged from the *tāla* (rhythm).
This is a *sup-sup* compound (a compound of two nouns). Alternatively, it means "those who clap their hands against one another.

Or else, they are those whose play is "clinging" (*saṃsakta*) with their "clan" (*kula*), meaning their own herd; in this case, because it is a three-membered *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is no substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) due to the absence of the status of being a final member (*uttarapada*).
According to Amara, *medura* means "thick" (*sāndra*) and "glossy" (*snigdha*).
*Kilakilā* is an indistinct sound.

There is vṛddhi of the initial vowel.

This is because the word *hā* expresses grief (*śoka*), and that word governs the use of the nominative case in its address (*saṃbodhana*).

From the fear of Mālatī, there was a loud cry;

And my acquaintance took place in the house of Śaṅkara. If you ask how it is that this is confirmed by what we have heard, he says:

I praise your playful sport, which caused the stability of the cosmic egg to dissolve through the trembling of the tortoise as its shell was bent under the pressure of the earth being whirled in the agitation of the forceful Anishumbha; and which cast the seven oceans into the cavities of your cheeks that rivaled the underworld, while your true power was manifested in the assembly of the delighted Nilakantha.
Moreover:

"O Malatī, [you who are] amidst a multitude of spirits engaged in loud praise, with fierce, boisterous laughter emanating from the row of skull-bowls still containing life—bowls from which nectar flows as it oozes from the moon split by the blows of claws shimmering at the edges of flapping elephant hides!
Here, the words "O venerable Kāmandakī" are to be supplied.
For a long time, for a great duration.

Mādhava:
"Hanta" expresses the attainment of certainty.
The two Kāpālikas: [speak].
"Resolute," and so forth.

With pride, he performs a mercilessly forceful *niśumbha* (a specific wrestling maneuver); from that, due to his agitation, the earth-sphere—the wheel of the world—is so compressed that the shell, the backbone, of the Tortoise supporting it sinks downward. By the trembling—that is, the movement of the limbs—of that Tortoise, the stability of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is falling away and collapsing; such is the state [of the universe]. O Goddess, may your wild *tāṇḍava* dance be for our desired destruction of inauspiciousness and for your satisfaction, O Mother! O you who are difficult to attain, O you who are not easily endured, O auspicious one, O intoxicating one, destroy [all obstacles] now! Thus indeed may I also honor you. Suddenly! O Blessed Cāmuṇḍā! Clearly yours! O Aghorā! In the *Mālatīmādhava*: [He sees her] with a mountain cast down by the mass of her outstretched arms, which are agitated and terrifying due to the expansion of the fiery poison issuing from the broad, fully blossomed surfaces of her hoods—hoods swollen by the pressure of the knots on her armlets formed by the coils of hissing black serpents.

O Goddess, may that *tāṇḍava* dance bring about our desired welfare and joy—a dance in which the quarters of the sky are stitched together by the whirling of firebrands set in motion by the rapid revolutions of heads made terrifying by the flash of eyes tawny with blazing fire; a dance where clusters of stars are scattered by the brandishing of the tips of lofty skull-topped staffs; and a dance that delights the Three-Eyed Lord, whose mind rejoices in the firm embrace of Gaurī as she is bewildered by the loud clapping of joyful *kaṭapūtanas* and frantic *vetālas*.
Thus [it is said] by way of dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*).
And may there be bliss!
Regarding the reading *ariṣṭyai*: *riṣṭi* is misfortune; the absence thereof is *ariṣṭi*, and [the word refers] to that.

By this, the "staff" (daṇḍa) which indicates a future undesirable event is also described. As it has been said: "That which occurs at the end of speech—unexpectedly connected and as if meaningful—that shall be the 'staff,' indicating a future undesirable event."
Medinīkara states: "The word *ṛṣṭiḥ* refers to a sword or to misfortune (when feminine).

Alternatively, according to the lexicon stating "the letter *ṛ* is the mother of the gods," from the word *ṛ*, in the vocative case with the application of *guṇa*, one has "O *aḥ*, O Mother of the Gods! The meaning is: "May there be *iṣṭiḥ* [fulfillment] for the sake of the desired (*abhīṣṭyai*)."
Of what sort?

It is that in which a hymn of praise has been commenced by many hosts of spirits who are terrified by the fierce, loud laughter [of the Goddess], released from rows of skulls—skulls that remain alive through the drenching and immersion in the nectar flowing from the moon situated on the Goddess’s head, which has split open and burst asunder due to the blows of her curved claws upon the edges of the moving hide of the demon Gajāsura.
Or rather, it is that in which a hymn of praise has been set in motion and performed by the hosts of spirits.
The causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is implied within the root. Alternatively, it is a locative bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that in which there is a covering in the form of a moving elephant hide";

Likewise, there is that [place] where mountains have been cast down by the mass of his arms—which are long and extended—by those black serpents who are panting from the exertion of the grand display of their *tāṇḍava* dance; where, through the pressure upon the knots of their bodies formed in the shape of armlets, there is a violent springing up with gaping mouths, or a throbbing expansion of the mass of their limbs like a blossoming flower, resulting in a broad hood-base (*phaṇāpīṭha*). This is expressed through a metaphor (*rūpaka*) by means of the expanded base. Then, due to the bursting forth and intensity of the fire of poison issuing from that [hood], it is most formidable (*ujjṛmbhaṇa*), whether terrifying, fierce, or agitated, moving hither and thither, spreading wide; and by that collection of arm-segments, the mountains were overturned and hurled away.
Because the Goddess possesses many arms, the term *doḥ-khaṇḍa* (arm-cluster) is used;
as Amara states: "The word *khaṇḍa* is masculine when referring to a cluster of lotuses and the like.

Likewise, the eye on her forehead is tawny (*piṅgala*) due to the blazing fire; the *chaṭā* is the spreading outflow of its flames. Through the *sāṭa*, or expansion, of that [eye], the head (*uttamāṅga*) becomes formidable. The *bhrami* is the whirling of that head in a circular motion (*maṇḍalākāra*). By means of this, the *prastuta*—meaning commenced—is the action of a *alātacakra* (fire-brand wheel), a specific act involving half-burnt wood set ablaze by fire. By this, the quarters of space (*digbhāgāḥ*) appear as if sewn together, as if bound into one. This is the description of that [place].

Thus, where the host of stars is scattered here and there by the trembling of the exceedingly great banner-top of the *khaṭvāṅga* (skull-topped staff), and where the Three-Eyed One, Śiva, whose heart rejoices through the firm embrace of Gaurī— who is agitated, terrified, or rushing along because her ears are pierced by the rhythmic clamor (*tāla*) of the joyful *kaṭapūtana* and fierce *vetāla* spirits— he exceedingly gladdens [her]. The *Viśvakośa* states: "Sāṭa means a bower (*nikuñja*), expansion (*vistāra*). Here, there is a blending of the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and the heroic (vīra) sentiments.

For now, by chance, I have encountered my beloved as she moves before the face of this robber, like a digit of the moon caught within the mouth of Rāhu, as he is about to sever her from the reach of his sword-blade."
How can the mind exist—distraught with anxiety, hurried by compassion, agitated by wonder, inflamed by anger, and blossomed with joy?

Aghora: "O wretched Brahmin child! By the logic of the deer distressed for its mother who has been snatched by a tiger, you—O sinner, who delight in violence and dwell in the sacrificial pavilion of animal offerings—have come within my range.

Therefore, I shall now slay you, the very one who caused the slaughter of living beings in my previous life, with my sword-blows severing your neck until it flows with a torrent of blood from the opening of the wound."
Mādhava:
(In amazement) Oh, how extraordinary! This is a "crow-and-palmyra" coincidence, occurring unexpectedly and without having been anticipated.
The meaning is that this too occurs by chance, just as the simultaneous occurrence of a crow's arrival and a palm fruit's falling depends on fate.
Regarding the passage beginning with "of Rāhu":
having attained or reached [the conjunction] by fate, that is, by the power of destiny.
The meaning is:

"How shall my heart fare as I draw away this beloved one from the reach of the sword-stroke of this robber-thief? Because of the arising of ever-new aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), I do not know [how it will feel]. This is the sense.
Like what?
Like a digit of the moon moving within the mouth of Rāhu.

Regarding the reading "kṛpāṇapātaviṣayām" (within the range of the sword's fall), the construction is as follows: having obtained such a beloved—one who is the object (*viṣaya*) or locus (*āśraya*) of the falling of the sword—how can my heart remain steady? Such is the connection of the words.
Or rather, of what sort [is he]?
Of one who is "seizing," that is, intent on cutting [her] in two;
[his] "beloved," according to the sense.
The implication is that, consequently, there is an absolute absence of livelihood for her.

thus, in this passage, the cause is stated in the first half-verse.

With the second verse, he states the result: although for one who is naturally courageous (*sāttvika*), there is no fear that is impaired by *ātaṅka*—which is a mental agitation—nevertheless, because of the attainment of his beloved, fear is entirely appropriate due to his dependence on life;
whereas previously, due to his independence from life, there was fearlessness, so *ātaṅka* was indeed nothing but fear.
The comparison with Rāhu is the cause of that fear.
It is "melted with compassion" because she, who brings a festival to the eyes of the world like a digit of the moon, has fallen into calamity;

and it is "blazing with anger" because of the word "robber," implying that this thief is intent on killing Mālatī.
"Of one who was snatching away his beloved"—this refers to [the face] being bright with joy at the successful preservation of his dear wife's life.

or, according to the reading *mayūramecakanibhaiḥ*, by those whose splendor is unsurpassed like the dark-blue eye-spots (*candraka*) of a dancing peacock with many feathers.
The *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *mecaka* is seen to mean an eye-spot (*candraka*), as well as something glossy and dark-blue."

"‘Bhūri’ means gold and also abundance; it is a word whose gender varies according to its referent," says Medinīkara. [The rays were] as if mingled with, or joined by, the shadow of the wings—meaning the luster of the feathers—of the blue jay (*cāṣa*), a species of bird, which had flown up and spread its wings.
Of what kind were they?
They were as if covered by a spread or a bed-covering of cloth produced in the land of China, featuring variegated patterns;
for the *Hārāvalī* states: "A spread is called a *śayyā*.
Here, "jewels" (*maṇi*) refers to gems set in ornaments.
Kalahamsaka:
Here, she is cast aside with a sidelong glance.
Kanaka means gold.
*Kaladhauta* means silver;
according to the *Viśva* lexicon, "kaladhauta" refers to both gold and silver.
*Paṅkena* means by means of a coating or plaster.
A cane-creeper is a small cane-staff.
It was encircled, that is, fashioned. "The mandala was fashioned."
The sense is that no one should go outside of this circle;
[this applies] to Mālatī from afar, as implied by the context.

She is one who wears as an ornament a *nakṣatramālā*—either a garland of twenty-seven pearls or a specific type of elephant decoration—which is slightly reddened and dyed by the glow of twilight, which is like a vast mass of vermilion, and which is flickering, restless, swaying, and hanging down.

In the context of night, "nakṣatramālā" means a garland of stars. "Kareṇu" means a female elephant; thus, it refers to that very night. The compound [manoharā] is formed as "that which is visible (dṛśyamānā) and charming (manoharā)."
She is one whose bodily luster is pale, ashen, withered, and exceedingly emaciated;
by this, her similarity to a digit of the moon is expressed.
By the word "visible" (dṛśyamānā), it is indicated that for others there is merely the act of seeing, whereas for you alone is the full enjoyment of Mālatī.
By the words beginning with "pāṇḍurā," the internal agitation within Mālatī is expressed. "Kiñcid antaram" means a short distance; "prasṛtā" means she has gone.

In the reading *kaladhauta-ṭaṅkapatra*, *ṭaṅkapatra* means a gold leaf-strip. [She is] clearly smeared with red, flickering, and thick paste... standing at a distance... In the *Mālatīmādhava*: "Adorning a female elephant that wears ornaments of strings of pearls, Mālatī has moved a little further along, her lovely beauty of a body—pale and emaciated—visible to the world from head to foot as she turns her face in curiosity, bearing the grace of a crescent moon. Madhura-gholanta Makaranda: "Friend, look, look!"
Adorned with ornaments yet possessing limbs pale and emaciated, bearing flowers like a young creeper that is beginning to wither,
this woman of noble form bears the lovely and rising splendor of the great festival of marriage, while simultaneously manifesting the deep-seated anguish of her heart.
"How has the female elephant been seated?
Mādhava (with joy): "How wonderful!
She has already begun her course from here together with the venerable lady and Lavaṅgikā."
Then enter Kāmandakī, Mālatī, and Lavaṅgikā.
Kāmandakī (joyfully, aside):
May the Creator grant us prosperity for this pleasing course of events; may the gods be obedient and bring about a most desirable conclusion.
May I become one who has fulfilled her purpose through this marriage with my beloved friend’s husband; may this entire effort bear fruit, and may there be supreme well-being.
"This," and so forth.
This woman of excellent hips (*varārohā*), possessing beautiful buttocks, bears a most exquisite and lovely perfection of the great festival of marriage,
owing to her innate loveliness.
And she reveals a deep and intense anguish of heart;
of what sort? Adorned with ornaments that are pale and emaciated due to her limbs.
The sense is that, because of their extreme loveliness, these very [limbs] are adorned by ornaments.
She is parched within;
for this very reason, her limbs have become pale and emaciated.
She is one by whom flowers have been gathered and worn.
A young girl sixteen years of age;
by the phrase "with her limbs," it is indicated that she possesses a pervasive paleness throughout her entire body;
like a creeper.
The meaning is that just as a young creeper, though well-flowered through the influence of spring and other seasons, may undergo internal withering due to some deformity, so too does this [woman].
She was "seated" (niṣāditā), meaning she was made to sit;
this is for the purpose of bringing her down [from her state].
Kāmandakī:
(With joy) The sense is that this is due to the fulfillment of her desired wish.
"By the Creator," and so forth.

May the Creator grant us—us who are desirous of—that which is pleasing to our minds, residing in our hearts, namely the undertaking, the activity, the present marriage; may He grant what is auspicious, well-being, and free from obstacles.
In the word *vidhaye*, the dative case is used either in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*) or according to the rule *kriyārthopapadasya*.

Fearing some undesirable outcome due to opposition from the king even though the task has been accomplished, she says: "May the gods grant me this supreme, most beautiful, and non-conflicting ultimate purification.
She also states the fruit for herself: "May I be one who has fulfilled her purpose," since this entire effort may bear fruit in the marriage of Mālatī and Mādhava.
The meaning is: "May it become a giver of fruit through purity at the subsequent time.
"May it become a giver of Śiva through purity of transformation"; the meaning is: "May it be auspicious."

With a face sweet with a smile, her limbs revealing the pangs of love through the beauty of her blossoming countenance, she laughs like the newly risen crescent moon. She is somehow—something indescribable. Like a circle of weary friends, or as if born of joy, she is lovely and filled with wonder. By this marriage, she has fulfilled her purpose; thus, the effort in the heart that was desired through exertion becomes a giver of auspiciousness. — Act Six. Mālatī (to herself):
But by what means now shall I find an interval between life and the extinction of death?
Even death is difficult to attain for those of ill fortune, as it is said that even death is desired by the unfortunate.
By what means, then, shall I now find an opportunity for the extinction of death?
Even death is difficult to attain for those of ill fortune, as it is said that even death is desired by the unfortunate.

Lavaṅgikā (to herself): My dear friend has indeed been greatly distressed by this favorable yet deceptive separation. (Entering with Pālaka’s hand) The female door-keeper: Blessed lady, the minister says that Mālatī must be adorned before the deities with these wedding garments sent by the King. Blessed lady, the minister says:
"Mālatī must be adorned before the deities with these wedding garments sent by the King."
Kāmandakī: The minister speaks rightly;
for that place is auspicious.
Therefore, show it to us.
Pratī—This, first of all, is the white silk bodice, and this is the upper garment of red-colored silk;
these are the ornaments for every limb;
and this necklace of pearls—let it be so, according to the reading "śivatātiḥ," which means "that which brings about auspiciousness."

While the suffix *tāti* following words such as *sarva*, *deva*, and *atta* is being applied, the suffix *tāti* is added here according to the rule "after *śiva*, *śama*, and *ariṣṭa*, when [the word refers to] the hand.

In this context, death itself—by virtue of its capacity to destroy all suffering—is *nirvāṇa*, meaning liberation (*mokṣa*); the *antara* is the occasion for that. Alternatively, death itself is *nirvāṇa*, meaning *nirvṛti*, or bliss.
"Nirvāṇa" [is used] in the senses of extinction and liberation, according to the Viśva lexicon;
"antara" [is used] in the senses of opportunity, the internal self, and similarity, according to Medinīkara.
Mālatī:
"I shall honor" means "I shall properly attain.
This is a form of the verb *bhū* (to attain) in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
By the word "now" (*sāṃpratam*), it is shown that [this is the case] both because of the failure to obtain Mādhava and because of the delay in obtaining Nandana.
The implication is that due to her misfortune, she may not even die, just as she has failed to attain Mādhava.
Lavaṅgikā:
Here, "klāmitā" means brought to exhaustion or weariness. It refers to the separation (*vipralambha*) caused by Mādhava, who is favorable [to her];
or alternatively, it refers to the deception (*vipralambha*) by Nandana, who is favorable [to her].
The female doorkeeper:
*peṭaka* means a chest or casket.
Medinīkara states: "The word *peṭaka* refers to a chest for books and the like, as well as to a cluster [of flowers]."
The taking of the cloth, however, is for the purpose of adorning Nandana;
here, "prasādhana" refers to dressing or decoration.
Kāmandakī.
"It is fitting" means that by accomplishing this, I shall adorn Makaranda and marry him to Madayantika; such is the intention. "Māṅgalika" means a cause of auspiciousness.
Portress:

Here is a bodice—a *kūpasaka*—made from a white silk cloth woven with threads. Because of my ill fortune, it has been excessively worn; it is soiled and its fastenings are worn out. This casket for ornaments, this *bhūṣaṇapaṭalaka*, the Minister presents to the Blessed One, the Goddess. (In the *Mālatīmādhava*, it is a necklace.)
This is sandalwood;
this is a wreath of white flowers.
And here is this white silk bodice, and this red-colored silk upper garment.
These are ornaments for all the limbs; this is a pearl necklace;
this is sandalwood paste; and this is a crest of white flowers.
Kāmandakī— (Aside) Madayantikā will indeed look upon the dear Makaranda with delight.
(Aloud) [Taking him by the hand...]
"Let it be so; let the minister be told. — "So be it. So be it."
Thus she exits.
— Lavaṅgikā, you enter the inner chamber with the dear Mālatī.
— And where is the Blessed Lady now?
But where is the lady?
Kāmandakī: As for me, I shall first examine the excellence of these jewels of ornaments according to the treatises in this secluded place.
(She exits.)
Kāmandakī, Mālatī, and Lavaṅgikā—(to themselves): "Alas! I have been reduced to having only Lavaṅgikā as my attendant. (Mālatī: "I have become one whose retinue consists of nothing but Lavaṅgikā.
Lavaṅgikā: "This is the door of the temple of the deity."
Therefore, let us enter.
Here is the door to the temple;
let us go inside.
Thus they enter.
Māka — Friend, let us stand here for a moment, concealed by this pillar.
(They do so. — Friend, here is the cosmetic paste.
These are flower garlands. Friend, this is the cosmetic paste for the limbs;
these are the flower garlands.
Mālatī: What of it?
(tado kiṃ).
Amara states: "Cola" and "kūrpāsaka" are masculine or neuter terms for a bodice.
*Uttarīyarūpam* means a red garment or a cloth dyed with vermilion (*sindūra*). According to Medinīkara, "an *āpīḍa* is a crest-ornament (*śekhara*), not feminine.
The word *bhavati* is used here as a form of address.
Kāmandakī: [She thinks: "Mādhava must not experience his passion for Mālatī in the presence of his elders; therefore she said, 'You enter.
Kāmandakī.
In a secluded, lonely place.
Mālatī:
This is a joyful utterance resulting from her obtaining an opportunity for death as she had long cherished in her heart.
The meaning is that Mālatī does not see [him] because of the absence of external perception.
Makaranda:
"Apavārita" means screened or concealed.
Lavaṅgikā:
Here, "unguent" refers to saffron and similar substances.
Mālatī:

As if not seeing the purpose of that, she says: "What am I to do with this?"—this is the meaning. *Jualam* (pair); *rīam*; *rattaṃsuam*. These [words] are not found anywhere as *sideti*. Let it be so. (To herself: For now. (Aloud: This is the deity. Therefore, dear friend, let us enter. From here, let us watch from behind a pillar. Act Six. Lava: Friend, you have been sent by my mother to worship the deities for the sake of securing auspiciousness at the commencement of this auspicious marriage ceremony.
"Friend, you have been sent by my mother to worship the gods for the sake of ensuring the auspicious success of this commencement of the marriage ceremony.

Mālatī: Why now do you torment me, unfortunate as I am—my mind already scorched by the sorrow resulting from the cruel onset of the wicked play of fate, and already unbearable due to the repeated severing of my vital parts?

Why now do you distress me, unfortunate as I am—my mind already scorched by the sorrow resulting from the cruel onset of the wicked play of fate, and already unbearable due to the repeated severing of my vital parts?
Lavaṅgikā: Is that so? What is it you wish to say?
Mālatī: That which this person, whose fortune is such as to thwart the desires of his heart through its pursuit of the unattainable, is now deliberating upon.
Now, people speak of one whose fortune contradicts the desires of those difficult to attain.
Makaranda: Friend, have you heard?
Mādhava: I have heard it, and my heart is filled with dissatisfaction.

Mālatī—Embracing Lavaṅgikā: "O Lavangika, my true sister and dear friend! Here I am, your beloved companion, now standing on the verge of death. Embracing you with a confidence born from the constant assistance I rendered during the delivery of my child, I entreat you: if I am to be followed by you, then hold me in your heart, O Lavangika, who possesses the full splendor of all good fortune.

In this passage, the mention of "taking the hand" (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) as a general statement carries a double meaning (*śleṣa*) referring to the marriage of Mādhava and Nandana; thus, this is the sentiment of a "bursting jest" (*narmasphoṭa*).
As it is said: "The expression of states of being through double entendre is called *narmasphoṭa*.
Here, in the case of Mālatī, the consequence of her misconduct consists of the abandonment of what is dear and the attainment of what is unpleasant.

"Duḥsaham" (unbearable) is an adverbial modifier. [Makaranda says: "She did not understand my words because they were ambiguous; therefore, let her speak thus. To this, he replies with "Lava, atha kim" and so forth. Mālatī: He is one whose fortune is adverse, being at variance with his persistent desire.
Makaranda, perceiving that Mādhava’s desire was difficult to attain, said: "Friend, have you heard?
Mādhava: [replies].
Fearing that his words might be ambiguous, he says "discontent" (*asantoṣa*).
Mālatī:
Here, by the words beginning with "the ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*), her status as a worthy recipient of confidence is expressed.
"Virūḍha" means grown; "upacita" means increased.
The grammatical connection is: "having embraced her in a manner that was appropriate.
She is one who should be followed and served.

By the phrase "complete auspiciousness," a beauty rivaling the lotus is expressed. As it is said: "O Goddess, when one begins to praise those who possess supreme virtues, there arises a sense of weariness and a lack of correspondence [with reality]. Listen, however, to this: you shall behold the face-lotus of the illustrious Mādhava, which is the sole auspicious object for the acceptance of the blossomed [flower], and which is softened by bliss."

"O dear sister Lavaṅgikā, who stands outside the ultimate truth! This dear friend of yours is now in a state of helplessness, on the verge of death. Having embraced you with a confidence that has grown through constant service since her very birth, she yearns for you. If I am not brought back to you, then, holding me in your heart, you shall behold the lotus-face of Mādhava-Śrī—smooth with joy and the supreme auspiciousness of the pinnacle of all fortune. (She weeps.)

In the *Mālatīmādhava*, Mādhava says: "Friend Makaranda, by good fortune I too have obtained these nectars of speech—which cause the withered flower of life to blossom, which provide complete nourishment, which enchant all the senses, which bring joy, and which are the sole elixir for the heart."

Mālatī: "In such a way that this jewel of a body does not perish while he—who, having heard from me that the person who restored his life has passed away—is consumed by grief; and in such a way that even though I have gone to the other world, that person shall keep me as the sole remaining subject of his remembrance and conversation until the end of time—this is what is proclaimed as 'beauty'. By the phrase "holding me in his heart," it is said that through a lineage of transmission, I too shall eventually behold him.
Regarding the expression *mādhavaśriyaḥ*, since there is no fixed rule for the position of words in Prākṛt, it means *śrīmādhavasya* (of the illustrious Mādhava).
A gaze is said to be "glistening" by virtue of its smoothness with joy.
Regarding the phrase "of the withered," and so forth:
even my words have, by good fortune, been determined to be like nectar.
The meaning of the word "api" (also/even) is that these matters were determined by you previously, whereas they have now been determined by me.
He describes its similarity to nectar: it is the illumination of the flower of life that had withered—that is, become contracted—by the knowledge of the shattering of hope.
For even among nectars, this [the teaching] is the illuminator of the withered flower, owing to its capacity to illuminate everything.
"Satisfying" means producing contentment.
This is likewise true even regarding nectar (*amṛta*).
When there is satisfaction, the external sense organs are gratified.
It is the same with regard to *amṛta*.
The *ānandana*s are the sweets within.
It is called *āyana* because by means of it one is brought (*ānīyate*) [to the goal].
*Rasāyana* is the vehicle (*ayana*) of *rasa*.

The sense is that it is so called either because, by means of words, it generates novelty through the arousal of the mind, or because, like nectar (*amṛta*), it generates novelty by destroying old age and other such conditions in one who has died [to the world].
Alternatively, by the word *amṛta*, water, liberation, and the celestial nectar (*pīyūṣa*) are also expressed.
In this regard, the first phrase [indicates] similarity to water;
the three subsequent phrases have the purpose of establishing similarity to liberation.
For in liberation, regarding the object of perfect satisfaction, there is indeed a state of being free from desire.
There is also no delusion of the senses due to the absence of grasping at objects.
According to the Śruti, "Bliss is the nature of Brahman, and that is established in liberation," there is a state of being composed of bliss in liberation.
Alternatively, by the first two words [of the verse], there is a similarity to water, and by the other two words, there is a similarity to liberation.
The remaining word is used for the sake of comparison with nectar (*pīyūṣa*).
According to the *Dharaṇi* lexicon: "The word *amṛta* [is used] for liberation, the nectar of immortality, water, and clarified butter."

Mālatī: Here she has paused. She requests the exit. Behold the glorious face of Mādhava. Look! Look toward the other world! Even in the other world, act in such a way that you do not slacken the course of worldly life. Act VI.

In this very way, through the favor of my dear friend, Mālatī shall have her purpose fulfilled. Act in such a manner that the body-jewel of that person who gave me life does not perish even as he suffers upon hearing that I am dead; and act so that, even though I have gone to the other world, that person does not slacken his worldly duties even for a moment, keeping me as the sole remnant of his memory and conversation. In this very way, through the favor of my dear friend, Mālatī shall have her purpose fulfilled.

Makaranda: Alas! What a most piteous situation has been presented. Mādhava: Having heard the exceedingly piteous yet heart-stealing lamentation of that fawn-eyed one—her mind distressed by despair—I experience both the calamity of anxiety and despondency, and yet a great festival of joy.

Lavaṅgikā: Oh, may this ill omen of yours now be averted! I shall not hear anything more distressing than this. ayi pratihatamidānīṃ te'maṅgalam | nāto'pyadhikataraṃ śroṣyāmi | ai paḍihadaṃ dāṇiṃ de amaṅgalaṃ ṇe ado vi adhiadaraṃ suṇissaṃ |
The word *mṛtā* means "dead. It is likewise indescribable (*anirvacanīya*). The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "It does not perish, it is not destroyed; you shall act accordingly."
The journey of worldly life refers to the state of a householder or the condition of having a wife.
The restriction "only thus" arises precisely from the destruction of the hope for attaining Mādhava.
Makaranda: "Hanta" expresses compassion; "karuṇam" means piteously.

The distinction between these two is as follows: *karuṇa* (pathetic) arises from indolence and the like and is characterized by a state of indifference; *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) arises from longing and anxiety and is characterized by a state of dependence.
For this very reason, Mādhava expresses the hopelessness indicated by the term "indifference" with the words beginning with "nairāśya."
The mind of that fawn-eyed woman is despondent and agitated due to despair—the destruction of hope—and is cowardly;
her affection manifests as a desire to give up her life upon separation from her beloved.
Her delusion is a state of confusion, characterized by the false conviction of having lost all hope even while still possessing hope.

Having heard the lamentation and wailing of those two—the most piteous and yet charming reflection upon past, present, and future events—I bear the calamity that arises from the despondency born of such anxiety;
or rather, I bear as a great festival that calamity which consists of anxiety and despondency itself.
The word "ca" (and) serves to join these mutually contradictory aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*).
Here, there is a logical sequence by way of cause and effect.
For instance, because his intellect is distressed by despair, there is compassion;
from that, lamentation arises.
Upon hearing that, my mind was filled with despondency;
yet, because my heart had been captivated by her deer-like eyes, hearing her charming lamentations—despite my failure to win her—was like a great festival.
She, moreover, [distressed me] with her loud wailing, her incoherent prattle, and her piteous lamentations.
And through physical exertion and blows, one should manifest the semblance of compassion.
Thus says Bharata.

Lavaṅgikā: Here, the warding off of inauspiciousness is performed by the *vivāhālindara* (marriage-bell). Thus may your dear friend Mālatī have her desire fulfilled. [She acts. Vasanta: O Vasanta, there is nothing further than this. In the *Mālatīmādhava*:
Mālatī: Friend, it is indeed your dear wish that Mālatī’s life be preserved, but not Mālatī herself.
Friend, indeed it is Mālatī’s life that is dear to you, not Mālatī herself.
Lavaṅgikā: Friend, why do you speak thus? Friend, why have you said such a thing?
Mālatī (pointing to herself):
By those arrangements of words which served as the bond of hope, I was made to experience this most loathsome undertaking.
Now, however, my only desire is that I may atone for the offense committed against that noble lord by being his property.

Therefore, in this matter, may my dear friend not stand in my way. By means of words bound by hope and skillfully arranged, I have been made to experience this most loathsome undertaking. But now, this is my very wish: that I shall abandon myself, which has offended that divine being by belonging to another.
"Therefore, in this matter, let my dear friend be no obstacle to me.
(She falls at her feet.
Makaranda: This is indeed the ultimate limit of affection.
Lavaṅgikā summons Mādhava with a sign.
Makaranda: Friend, approach and stand in Lavaṅgikā’s place. Mādhava: I am paralyzed with fear.
Makaranda: This indeed is the very nature of imminent successes. Mādhava stands at ease in the place of Lavaṅgikā.
Mālatī: Friend, show favor out of your affection for Kula.
"Friend, please show favor by complying. "Ha! [expresses] the external;
"because of Mādhava’s presence" [expresses] the internal.

Mālatī, having considered the external object, says: "In this context, Mālatī is the self delimited by that body; life, however, is the conjunction of the body and the self caused by a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Thus, there is a distinction between life and Mālatī.
The sense is that life is dear because it is a cause of happiness, yet since that [happiness] here produces a continuous succession of suffering, it must indeed be renounced.
Mālatī:
Here, by the word "another" (*anya*) in the phrase "another person," Mādhava is meant.
Because it is other than Nandana;
or because, due to its rarity, it is superposed as belonging to another;
or because of the loathsome [aspect], since here one sees the inauspicious sight of the marriage preparations for Nandana.
The negative particle (*nañ*) here has the sense of "not having committed an offense.
For it is a great offense to remain until the conclusion of the marriage ceremony with joy;
since there is an absence of any other enjoyment or the like, it is said that this [state] alone [constitutes the offense].
It is unobstructed and non-opposing;
this consists of the relinquishing of the self.
By means of "designation" (saṃjñā), that is, by convention (saṃketa).
Mādhava:
[He is] dependent on others;
[he is] paralyzed by trepidation.
Makaranda:
Because she has obtained her most cherished desire; "nedīyasām" means those who are near.
*Śvairam* means slowly.
*Mālatī*:
here the meaning is "accept death."

Thus. Having addressed [this] to another person... because of being dependent on others, I am not free. By proclaiming the virtues of the noble one (*mahābhāga*) which are beyond my sight, having abandoned [all else], I shall become tranquil (*nirvṛtā*). Friend, approaching her at will... Act VI.
Mādhava: O simple girl, abandon this rash passion; O lady with thighs like plantain stalks (*rambhoru*), give up your agitation.
Your heart is unable for me to endure the bitter exhaustion of separation.
Mālatī: Friend, this salutation from Mālatī is indeed not to be disregarded by you.
(sahi alaṅgaṇīo jevva de māladīppaṇāmo) Mādhava (with joy):
Or rather, what shall I say to you, who are the cause of such terrible anguish through our separation?
O lady of beautiful hips, do as you wish; grant me your embrace.
Mālatī— (With joy) How am I favored? Rising, she embraces her.
Furthermore, the sight of my dear friend is not obtained because it is obstructed by a flood of tears.
Embrace me with joy!
Friend, the touch of your body today, cool as the filaments of a firm lotus bud, refreshes me in a way quite unlike any other.

[With tears] And furthermore, with palms joined upon my head, inform that person on my behalf: "Let there be no confusion regarding Lavaṅgikā by using the refined Sanskrit language for me, an unfortunate woman, who is like a blooming white lotus. Thus, through the blending of languages, she says: "O simple one," and so forth—abandon your passion and attachment toward this rash act, which disregards your own self.
"O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, abandon this agitation and haste toward death!

The implication is that as long as one lives, there may still be hope. Since my heart is unable to endure the bitter, flavorless sorrow of separation from you, I have given this beloved [son] to you; therefore, abandon your resolve for death. This is Lavāṅgikā’s intention.

Therefore, [the word] *sarale* means "in the ignorant" or "of simple nature. In the sense of Mādhava, *sarale* means "O innocent one," and *ajānati* means "O you who do not know": "Because my heart is unable to endure the fatigue of separation from you, I have come to your side; therefore, abandon that [thought of] death; everything else is the same.
Since there is thus a similarity between the Sanskrit and the Prākṛt, this is called *Prākṛtasamaka*.
"Or what," and so forth.
