Therefore, dear friend, act in such a way that this obsession with the thought of her husband may be entirely uprooted from my heart.
Know this: ignorance is a great evil.
Women of noble character cause pain to the hearts of men through such improper attachments.
Do not say that this was told by Mālatikā.
Pārvatī: O you who are deluded by the incoherent chatter of the world, begone!
I shall not converse with you.
(a~ī asaṃbaddhaloappavādamohide avehi)
I will not speak with you!
[To Madayantikā: O dear friend Mādhava and Mālatī, be gracious, be gracious! Or rather, you do not remain silent when you have been addressed unclearly.
Moreover, we truly know Mālatī as one whose entire world of living beings consists solely of Mādhava;

and by whom has the body of Mādhava—not been perceived? His life is sustained merely by the garland of *bakula* flowers woven with his own hands, which hangs from his neck and is supported by the fragility of his limbs that possess the grace of the interior of a hard *ketakī* bud; and his body, pale like the orb of the morning moon, emaciated yet lovely to behold.

Furthermore, on that day, at the meeting at the entrance of the street bordering the Kusumākarodyāna garden, did you not observe the glances of these two? Their movements were smooth and full of playful grace, with the lotuses of their eyes blossoming wide with curiosity and darting about with agitation; they shone with a charm made radiant by the pupils of their eyes. Moreover, they possessed a sweetness and charm of cleverness fashioned from the instruction of every aspect of the art of love’s dance-master. Furthermore, having heard the news of my brother’s gift, her face instantly turned crimson; for this very reason, there is doubt among others as to whether she is unchaste or not—this is the sense. Lavaṅgikā:
"Depart from here; go far away.
Madayantikā:
"The meaning is that I am despondent because of your ambiguous speech, 'You are not here.'"
The meaning is: "It is not that we do not know;
rather, we certainly do know.
And so, why do you practice concealment?"
The meaning is that it has become hard, matured, and turned pale; or alternatively, "akaṭhorā" means the young *ketakī* flower,
which likewise becomes exceedingly pale.
It has not been eliminated nor has it been known;
rather, the meaning is that it has been known by everyone.
The implication is: "Why then do you deny it?"
*Vibhrama* (graceful movement) is *vilāsa* (coquetry).

As it occurs in a woman: "That particular distinction which arises in her gait, posture, sitting, and so forth, as well as in the movements of her eyes, garments, and other limbs, is known as *vilāsa*. As it occurs in a man: "A slow-moving gaze and a manner of walking like a bull [are examples]."
Playful dalliance (vilāsa) is said to be speech preceded by recollection.

Why was this not observed by you, such that you have been deceived by this [man]? O, neglecting him is a great and terrible error! [She] says, "The noble maiden is being tormented... O heedless one! What shall I say? It must be said. Indeed, it is not unknown to me. In the *Mālatīmādhava*, when the beauty of their bodies was withering from the onset of deep, deceptive agitation, their hearts were not perceived to be loosening their very foundations, as it were. Moreover, this other thing has occurred to my memory.
Friend, be gracious, be gracious!
Or rather, you have not been told anything unclear.
For do we not know for certain that Mālatī has become a world of life dependent solely upon Mādhava?

Or who has not perceived the excellence of Mālatī’s beauty—beauty that possesses the grace of the swelling womb of a *keta-kī* flower, sustained merely by the hanging garland of *bakula* blossoms fashioned by Mādhava’s own hand, her life-breath held fast; and whose body, with its appearance lovely yet wasted and pale like the orb of the morning moon, has not been made manifest?

But on that day, during our meeting in the shade of the middle of the Kusumāyudha garden—those glances of theirs, which were beautiful with the gentle movement of eyes thick with the playful splendor of blue lotuses blooming with curiosity as they shimmered with coquettish charm; and which were sweet, artless, and innocent, fashioned from the instructions of all the arts of love taught by the God of Love himself—were these not witnessed by you?

And did my heart not appear as if its root-bonds were being overturned, its physical splendor withering from the deep, sorrowful groans that overflowed at that very moment upon hearing the news of my brother’s gift?
And furthermore,
this other thing was remembered by me.

Lava: What else could it be now? Madayantikā: Indeed, that very Mādhava—who restored the life of that noble one who granted me my own life—was himself incited by Mālatī, who announced the joyful news of his recovery of consciousness, and by the Lord Mother’s clever speech, to risk a daring act of self-seizure as a reward for her heart and his own life.
And yet, Lavaṅgikā, you yourself said there, "This favor has indeed been accepted by our dear friend.

For when Mālatī—whose heart and life were suddenly entrusted to Mādhava as a gift for his having bestowed her very life, and who was made aware of this through the description of the venerable Vidyādharī’s words—learned of the recovery of that noble-spirited one’s consciousness, she acted with such haste.
And yet, Lavaṅgikā, you yourself said right then and there, "This favor has indeed been accepted by our dear friend."
This is the meaning:
*āvega* is the suffering of non-attainment;
*aṅgāritam* means thoroughly heated.
"Heaving up, he rose up. This is agitation (*āvega*) born from the non-attainment of what is desired.
As it is said: "Agitation occurs for men due to the possibility of not obtaining what is desired. Lavaṅgikā:
"What else now?"— the implication being, "has it been remembered by you?
Madayantikā.

In this context, what is dear is the very attainment of consciousness (*cetanā-prāpti*), which is shown in the verse beginning with "wounded by the beast" (*vyālavraṇita*). [The text continues: "My life... Kedaka... turned back... restored to life merely by the touch of his hand... there, with graceful movements rolling about in its vicinity, with smooth and affectionate glances, charming with the manifestation of the erotic sentiment through the expansion of the pupils, filled with deep and intense emotion, its limbs reddened by that agitation... as if its very root were being uprooted, urged by you, who have yourself grasped it. — Act Seven.

Lava: Friend, who indeed was that illustrious one? I have forgotten. Mādhavī: Friend, remember, remember! On that day, when I had fallen into the jaws of death under the guise of a ferocious and wicked beast, and was left without refuge, I was protected by him—by that giver of life standing nearby with his pillar-like stout arms, my disinterested kinsman—who performed the act of self-sacrifice by offering his own body, the sole essence of all the worlds.

And by him—whose broad, expansive chest was torn open with fierce, firm fangs, who bore for my sake the thunderbolt-like blows from the claw-tips of that most wicked tiger, which resembled a cluster of aged, withered *japā* flowers, and whose mind was solely intent on compassion—that evil beast, that great *rākṣasa*, was slain.

Friend, remember, remember! On that very day, when I had gone to the edge of the Vikaṭaduḥśāvadāva forest and was without refuge, I was protected by my benefactor, who appeared at that moment like a pillar of my father’s arms—an uncaused kinsman who performed the heroic deed of offering his own body, the sole essence of the entire world, for my sake.

For it was by him—with his broad, fleshy, and expansive chest torn open by firm fangs, and with a heart solely intent on compassion—who bore for my sake the thunderbolt-like blows from the tips of the claws of that most cruel and powerful beast, and who slew that great rākṣasa Duḥśāsana.
Lava: Ah, Makaranda! Ah, Makaranda!
Mada—joyfully: Dear friend, what, what do you say? Priyasakhī, what, what do you say?
The meaning is that what has been given is appropriate; it would not be fitting were it not for her affection.
Lavangikā, in the course of stating another matter, says "Ah, friend! in order to conceal the subject at hand.
"Ām" has the sense of recollecting something previously [said].
"Vismṛtam" (forgotten): the intention is that this question is asked for the purpose of recounting that story, even though it was already known.
Madayantikā:
Here, "Smara" (the God of Love) refers to Makaranda;
"vikruṣṭaḥ" means enraged.
"Beast of prey" (śvāpada) means Yama under the guise of a tiger; this is the sense.
Regarding the reading "avalagnasaṃnihitā," *avalagna* refers to the neck (*kaṇṭha*), which is "conceived" or renowned [as such].
Here, a *karmadhāraya* compound is intended.
Vikaṭa means broad;
māṃsala means thick;
uttāna means elevated.
It carries away [the world] like a crown of *uḍra* flowers that has become withered, hard, decayed, and faded.
The suffix *ṇini* is used here according to the rule "when there is a comparison with the agent" (*kartary upamāne*).
Here, "carrying away" (*haraṇa*) means making equal (*samīkaraṇa*).
There is a similarity due to their bodies being smeared with blood.
*Śikhām* means the tip.
*Lavaṅgikā*.
Here, *huṃ* expresses deliberation; according to Amarasimha, "huṃ [is used] in deliberation and astonishment. This refers to Madayantikā.
Here, due to the intensity of his joy, he asks again and again.

Even while drinking the honey of his beloved’s name, O friend... again he, possessed of great majesty, was perceived by a mark upon his chest—a mark that, though causeless, was like a pillar [of support]; a mark that was firmly and broadly bearded; a mark that resounded against his chest; by that treasure-house of compassion, the noble one; even when acting out of pity, he delivered a blow from a cage of thunderbolts that would have submerged the entire body of the sky-dwellers (gods). Mālatī Mādhava: Lava—Indeed, I say it is Makaranda!
"I say it is Māraṇda," she says with a smile, touching her body while resorting to Sanskrit:
"We are indeed as you have said; but what shall I say of this person who has suddenly become distraught in the midst of conversation?
How can a maiden of noble family, so pure and innocent, assume the form of a *kadamba* bud?"
[With bashfulness]—
Friend, why do you mock me?

Indeed, I say that even the mere mention and recollection of the stories of such a person— who acted with selfless resolve and performed a great service by forcibly restoring my life as it was being devoured by Death— serve to cool me.

And so, you too have personally witnessed that noble one, for whose sake the world of living beings—so precious and vast—was cast aside; he who was momentarily distracted from the onset of intense piercing pain by the pressure of perspiration trickling down his body; whose pair of blue-lotus eyes were closing in a faint; and whose physical frame was sustained only by the courage required to brace himself against the sword-blade leaning against the ground.
[He acts out the symptoms of perspiration and so forth. Friend, why do you mock me?

Indeed, they pacify me; for what purpose do they console one such as I, whose resolve is indifferent to self, who has been forcibly seized by the jaws of Death, and who has returned with heavy favor after being nearly devoured?
Lavaṅgikā:
The word "nanu" (indeed) is used here to express her inner intention (*āśaya*).
"Vayamiḥ," and so forth. "Just as you have said, so it is"—
the meaning is that it is accepted that Mālatī is in love with Mādhava.
"What am I saying?"—this is merely a persistent attachment [to one's own words].
But how is it that this young lady of noble family, in the midst of conversation, has suddenly assumed the form of a kadamba bud due to being covered in dense horripilation?
She is distressed and overwhelmed.
Of what nature is he? Pure, meaning stainless;
that is to say, free from the defect of the affliction of desire.
"Infatuated" means ignorant of aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*).
All of this is said with irony (*sotprāsa*).
For this very reason, by virtue of her cleverness, she resorts to the Sanskrit language as a means of artistic expression.
Madayantikā:

[The sense is that] here, when she says "you mock me," the meaning is: "I am not delighted because of my passion for Makaranda; rather, I rejoice in his being taken away by you, so there is no occasion for laughter.
For this very reason, she says "nanu" (surely) as a thief of the heart.

Having thus stated that her own joy is established otherwise [than through passion], she explains that the perspiration and other signs arising from contact with her own body are likewise accounted for in Makaranda’s case—beginning with the words "And so it is.
The phrase "one whose body has been forgotten" is a description of fainting.
"Saṃgalitaḥ" means joined or met together.
*Utpīḍa* means a fullness or swelling.
*Kandodda* refers to the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*).
Regarding the word *moha*: the sense is that the closing of the eyes is due to delusion (*moha*), and not from contact with my limbs.
As it is said: "Delusion arises from calamity, assault, fear, or the recollection of former enmity.
Regarding his fainting from the blow, [the author asks] why he did not fall to the ground; to this, he says: "Upon the ground" (*bhūmi*).
*Viṣṭambha* means contact or connection.
Cast out and abandoned;
most precious and exceedingly difficult to obtain. The world of the living, along with my own affection—and why am I so much more grievous? ... [the memory]. Act Seven.
In times of distress, there is indeed the taking of names and the recollection [of them].

Likewise, you yourself have witnessed Madayantika’s very life—so precious and sustained merely for her sake—in its final state: her body drenched in a flood of sweat trickling from limbs paralyzed by the onset of pain from a deep wound; her pair of eyes rolling in a swoon; her body supported with steady composure by the hilt of a sword plunged into the ground; and her world of living beings momentarily cast aside for her sake alone. (Touching her body.)
My dear friend has resolved [to die] with her body. [She has understood that she must depart] with her body.
Mada—[with shame].
Dear friend, go away!
I have been betrayed by the confidence of my co-resident. Dear friend, depart!
I have been betrayed by the confidence of my co-resident.
Lava: Friend Madayantikā, we too know what ought to be known. Therefore, be gracious.
Because of the designation of cessation:
"Come, let us remain in a happiness similar to the binding of a conversation filled with confidence.
Friend Madayantika, we too know what ought to be produced.
Therefore, be gracious;
desist from this instruction.
Come, let us remain in happiness, engaged in a conversation worthy of the bonds of intimate confidence.
—Friend, Lavaṅgikā speaks well. Friend, she says what is beautiful and not inconsistent with my own heart. —I am now at the service of my two dear friends.
I shall now perform the rite of concealment— since this is so, then tell me, how indeed does your time pass?
If it is so, then tell me, how indeed does your time pass in the world of mortals?

From the recollection of the embrace of a beloved and so forth, there arises perspiration and the like. By the phrase "sweat and the rest," the manifestation of the *kilakiñcita* emotion is indicated, as it has been said: "When women, with limbs engaged in activity due to the internal presence of the Mind-born [God of Love], manifest a display of bashfulness, that they call *kilakiñcita*. Here, the meaning is that through your body, which possesses such sweat and other signs, union with Makaranda is desired.
Madayantika:
Here, the meaning is that it is not from the breaking out of perspiration born of passion and so forth on the part of my co-resident friend, but rather from her confidential conversation with you.
In the reading *abhiṇṇahmi*, the meaning is "I am well-known. Lava:
Here, [the phrase] "we indeed know" means that the conduct of both you and Makaranda has already been known through the mediation of Kāmandakī and others.
The sense is: how can there be a denial of that?
"By means of designation" means through a pretext.
The intention is: "Tell me even the continuity of your affection for Makaranda, which is similar [to what you feel for me]."
Both are adverbs modifying the action.
Buddharakṣitā:
Here, you ought to speak what is auspicious; this is the meaning. Lavaṅgikā:

In this state, separated from Makaranda—how can I endure? Even the mere mention of him [causes me distress]. I am overwhelmed by the deep and heavy wounds of his nails; my strength is gone; my sword has slipped from my grasp; my life is of little value;
and my body is unwell—what is the use of words?
My very body has shown its longing for union with Makaranda.

[Enter Mādhava. Mādhava: Oh, how inconsistent is the character of my dear friend Mālatī! [She] has become so full of confidence toward me that she has composed this beautiful composition. [Friends: Listen, dear friend! From the very beginning, my heart was filled with a longing and intense curiosity for that person, sustained by the conviction born of Buddharakṣitā’s partiality. Then, having been granted a vision through the decree of fate, I have somehow managed to sustain my life, though it is being torn asunder by the heat of an unbearable and cruel love-sickness. Mālatīmādhava: Friends, listen! My heart was already overflowing with curiosity and longing for that person, based on the trust I placed in Buddharakṣitā’s partiality.
Thereafter, having obtained a sight of him by the power of destiny, I have somehow preserved my life, even as it crumbles away, tormented by the irresistible and harsh pain of love.

I am experiencing this upheaval of the world of the living, my attendants distressed by the unbearable suffering of the fierce burning of the fire of passion that has ignited all my limbs with an unprecedented intensity; a state where death—attainable only through the abandonment of hope—is the only relief, yet which is further intensified by the contradictory words of Buddharakṣitā. Listen, dear friend!
By virtue of my confidence in Buddharakṣitā’s partiality, from the very beginning my heart was filled with a longing and desire for that person which overflowed its bounds.

Thus, having become one whose sight is directed toward the fulfillment of destiny, I am tormented by the unbearable pain of Love that is difficult to resist; my life-breath falters as my heart is shattered; my attendants are distressed by the unbearable and improper heat of a forest fire of love that has suddenly flared up across all my limbs; and my mind is rendered agitated by the course of events intensified by the words of Buddharakṣitā—which, though contrary to the extinction of suffering found easily only in the abandonment of hope, have increased my anguish. Furthermore, deluded by the madness of desire, I behold that person within the intervals of my fancies and dreams.
She too, O dear friend, has the sense of being one whose graceful gait is expanding as she stumbles and reels from the astonishment experienced for a moment.
Mādhayantī: Listen to this; hear it.

The singular number here is used with reference to the courtesans (*lavadbhikā*), because Buddharakṣitā is already aware of the events. However, the telling of the story is for the purpose of increasing passion, as it is said: "A journey, a festival, or a celebration; a dream, a painting, or a conversation about sexual pleasure."

"For it is at the first sight that expedients arise for young people, from which passion increases. The phrase "partiality" (pakṣapāta) implies the sense of "trust" (viśvāsa), meaning that partiality toward Buddharakṣitā cannot exist without an abundance of virtues. "Filled" (bhṛta) means overflowing or becoming excessive.
The analysis of the compound is: curiosity (kautūhala), longing (utkaṇṭhā), and desire (manoratha).
Then there is the *bahuvrīhi* compound:
that state of longing (*manoratha*) in which curiosity and yearning have become excessive; or rather, that state in which all burning has ceased, which is a stage of the disease.

As it is said: "The dramatic representation of the disease is through such things as mental delusion, a burning sensation throughout the limbs, and likewise [distress] of the head and face. Death itself is *nirvāṇa*, because it is liberation (*mokṣa*) due to its quality of removing all suffering.
"By my effort, you shall have union with your beloved"—this is the speech of Buddharakṣitā.
"Disturbed" means having a wavering mind.

"Revolution" (*parivarta*) refers to the transformation or alteration of the world of living beings, which is to say, fainting; or alternatively, it refers here to re-entering the world of living beings after a state of fainting.
The meaning is: within another mental construction (*saṃkalpa*), within the knowledge born from the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and within dream-knowledge (*svapna-jñāna*).
"Nirvyūḍha" means accumulated (*upacita*). [In the commentary:
"Filled and overflowing" (*bhṛtodvṛtta*) refers to a mind longing for that person; love has reached its highest stage toward that individual.
Moreover, toward that person— dense and charming, long-employed by necessity, burning with the intense torment of cruel and unbearable suffering, and with the hope for life expanded far and wide—
he gazes at me for a long time, as if intoxicated by the potent liquor of passion that has grown wild like the frantic dance of a white lotus.

Moreover, my dear Madayantikā, she addresses me by name, saying "Madayantikā," while filling the cavities of my ears with a deep, resonant, and faltering voice like the warbling cry of a swan whose throat is reddened by swallowing the filaments of lotuses.
And yet, by the indignity of her clutching at the hem of her upper garment as it slips from her throbbing breasts, she terrifies me, my heart heaving and thumping in agitation.
Furthermore, in the intervals between my thoughts and dreams, deluded by the intoxication of my desires, I behold that person.

Even she, O dear friend, for a moment—her eyes wide with a sudden, overflowing wonder, like a grove of white lotuses blooming intensely within a vast expanse of water—gazes at me for a long time as if intoxicated by the wine of passion.

Moreover, she addresses me as "dear Madayantika," her throat deepened and resonant with a laugh like the cry of a swan whose throat has been parched by the bitterness of swallowing the filaments of a lotus.
Now she terrifies me, her heart fluttering with agitation as she struggles to catch hold of the hem of her upper garment that slips from her swelling breasts.

Suddenly casting off her cloth, she has at that moment blocked the emergence of her breasts with her arms, which have become like the stiff stalks of lotuses; her forward movement is checked by her thick thighs bound together by a loosening and broken girdle-belt; and though she speaks in opposition, I turn back her momentary frown with great effort and earnestness.
*Prarūḍamaireya* refers to clear liquor (*prasannamadya*). Its *mada* is intoxication.
According to Amara, "maireya," *āsava*, and *sīdhu* are synonyms for liquor.
"Whirling" (*ghūrṇitam*) is an adverbial modifier of the action.
"He meditates" (*nirdhyāyati*) means he reflects.
"Astringent" (*kaṣāyaḥ*) means fragrant.
*Kalahaṃsa* refers to the royal swan (*rājahaṃsa*).
*Ghoṣa* means sound.
*Gharghara* means indistinct.
"Skhalita" means fallen;
both of these arise either from the influence of trepidation or from a change in voice produced by joy.
As it is said: "A change in voice may occur due to fear, anger, intoxication, joy, and so forth. The phrase "filling the cavity of the ears" is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṇa*).
The act of pleasing a woman by grasping the hem of her garment is as follows:
"By seizing [her] in private by the hand, by the garment, or by the head..."
One should effect the appeasement of a woman and the clearing of her offense in the presence [of witnesses].
Out of contempt, with the thought of retaliation; out of fear due to previous experiences;
and here, trembling like a wave, wondering "what might happen?"—thus [he acts].
Her mind was as if hot,
throbbing with agitation due to distress; or rather, it was surging with rising waves and trembling.
A "wave" (*kallola*) is the progressive intensification of trembling;
it "terrifies," meaning it causes her to become startled.
And she, having quickly cast off her garment, was "set forth," meaning prepared to depart.
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
By virtue of being bristling with horripilation (*pulakit*), there is a state of standing like a staff (*daṇḍāyamānatā*). "Apavārita" means covered or concealed (*apihita*).
"Udghama" means expansion.
Having broken the embrace and withdrawn, the hero experiences such things as gazing upon the heroine's breasts;
the sense is that at that moment, the heroine is no longer able to conceal herself.
To the question, "If that is so, why does she not flee? he replies:
"Because of the mass of horripilation arising from the loosening embrace.
She is "distraught" because of the shifting of her position.
"Saṃdāna" means a bond;
the meaning is "by those two which have brought about that [bond].
"Pratīpam" means adverse or contrary.

Furthermore, what consideration can there be for intention in the absence of movement? Thus: for a moment, [he gazes at] her whose stalk-like arms are raised and extended to their full length; who possesses a pride of intoxication manifested through the grand display of frantic dancing (*tāṇḍava*); whose nature is reeling with madness; and who is exhausted from rolling about. [He is] poor in the power of discernment. Then, as if manifesting his own power, he—[Makaranda]—having crossed over the edge of the upper garment (*uttarīya*), mocks Mālatī, whose heart has been made harsh by the pain of the eclipse of her love’s anger, and whose entire inner essence is revealed by her eyes that are moist and repeatedly cast about. In the *Mālatīmādhava*, [Makaranda] mocks her whose heart has been made harsh by the sorrow of the eclipse of her love’s anger, and whose entire inner essence is revealed by her eyes that are moist and repeatedly cast about.

Having restrained me with the embrace of his double-stemmed arms, and having rendered me helpless by the harsh pressure of his chest—its surface adorned with the fierce patterns of the claws of a tiger that had grown upon it—he, whose lotus-face is cleverly blooming as he holds my head with his hand placed upon the trunk of a female elephant shaken by agitation, and whose body’s beauty is intensely thrilled by the charming touch arising from his quivering, swollen lower lip pressed long against the root of my left cheek, now makes a request of me, who should not be requested, for some undertaking worthy of his audacious insolence; while my eyes, wandering in a daze due to the uneven confusion of rising fear and joy, move slowly and unsteadily.

Having suddenly released the extension of her arms, and having blocked the upward movement of my breasts with the binding of her arms—which at that moment were as rigid as the stalks of hard lotuses—she prevented my further departure by restraining my stout thighs with the fastening of her slipping and loosened girdle; yet even though she speaks in opposition, she mocks me, whose heart has been made harsh by the pain of a momentary anger resolved upon in excessive haste, and who has had the entire essence of my heart revealed through my eyes that are wide open and repeatedly cast down in affection.

O dear friend, having made my broad chest—its surface covered by rows of broad leaves that are thick with newly sprouted, lush, and hard hair—unbearable for the placement of her breasts, which were pressed down by her arms as long as staffs; and having placed my hand upon her loosened braid (which had slipped from its knot), I held her face close, its lotus-like mouth unrestrained and skilled in expressing the playful gestures of a lover’s face. Because she was obstructed by her left arm, she uttered prohibitions such as "Hūṃ! Hūṃ!"—this is what is meant by "pratikūla" (contrary).
*Uparāga* means connection or contact.

In the case of a repeated prohibition—where there is a statement of negation again and again—it is "perversion" (*paryasta*), meaning the opposite of negation, because it possesses qualities such as affection. Alternatively, "perversion" means delusion.
The essence of the mind is the state of being intent upon the desire for enjoyment.

"Upahāsaḥ" means "parihāsaḥ" (jesting). Its nature consists in a desire for union in the heart, while in speech there is merely a refusal; such is the meaning. In the reading "snigdhapunaruktam," the sense is that the eyes are cast or directed repeatedly with affectionate glances.
*Āveṣṭana* means *āveṣṭa*; by this, a firm embrace is expressed.
*Kararuha* means a fingernail.
*Orampha* means an assault.
The meaning is that his fingernails are as hard as the claws of a mature tiger;
"niṣṭhura" means dense or firm;
"niveśa" means the act of placing or applying.
"Niḥsahām" means incapable of speech and the like.
Here, there is a metaphor (*rūpaka*) in which the act of treading with fingernails is itself the "row of petals. He describes the kissing: "With impetuosity," and so forth.
*Ovaggidaṃ* means gathered into a heap or suspended;
it refers to the facial features such as the forehead and so forth.
*Vikāsitaṃ* means employed for kissing and other such acts.
The cleverness of the face arises from skill in kissing.

These *ketaka* flowers, enjoying the fragrance of the city’s bold women as their faces are repeatedly licked by the dangling creepers of their tossing tresses—furthermore, these monsoon winds, charming with the humming of swarms of bees rolling in the pollen within the cups of blossoming *kadamba* buds, draw away those separated from their lovers.

[The text] is thus supplemented in some places: "O Lord, O God! It is even so; fashion for me just this much. Or rather: "But you, [Makaranda], bowing with joined palms, pays homage in the *Mālatīmādhava*.
Saudāminī: "The moment for the delivery of the token of recognition is indeed well-prepared.
She unties the Bakula garland from her hand.
Mādhava—(With feigned astonishment and joy):
How is it that this is the Bakula flower garland, fashioned by me, which serves as the courtyard for the temple of Anaṅga and possesses a form so charming due to the swelling of my beloved’s breasts?
(He speaks with joy.)
Of what doubt is there?

For indeed, this very section of Lavaṅgikā’s hair—though unevenly braided and fashioned with poorly placed flowers—brought her satisfaction; it served to conceal the unrestrained curiosity born from the effortless grace of beholding her face, which is as beautiful as the lovely moon.
By the word "saha" (together), it is said: "If even my mind were to go toward that collection [of atoms] in the form of atoms, then you would not even have the effort [to prevent it].
Or else: "Give—that is, bestow—upon me whatever object is like cold [refreshing] that always resides upon the limbs of my beloved.
In the reading "īraya," the meaning is "impel" (or "send forth").
The sense is: "May that very thing lead to the pacification of my distress.
He states the reason for this: "Because you are my *gati*, my refuge.
The sense is that it is entirely appropriate for a refuge to sustain those who depend upon it.
Even in the reading "api vā," the word "api" expresses possibility.
Saudāminī:
Composed and attentive;
because of the context concerning the prayer to Vāyu.

Mādhava: [He expresses joy upon seeing the garland clinging to his beloved’s body. As it is said: "Whether an object is attainable or unattainable, once that desired thing is obtained, or even upon the reunion with a beloved..."
Upon the attainment of the heart's desire, joy arises in men.
"Unnāha" means height, elevation, or being carried above.
"Durlalitā" means one who is exceedingly dear.
It is either the temple of the bodiless god (Kāma) or the temple belonging to the bodiless god.
"O innocent one," and so forth:
that very portion of this garland which even brought satisfaction to Lavaṅgikā is this one.
The meaning is "even from the *mālatī* flower.
It refers to that in which there is an unevenly woven arrangement (*granthanā*),
or one that is woven in an uneven manner.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because Mālatī’s face is charming, lovely, and as pleasing as the moon."

Alternatively, when that face—which, due to emaciation from separation, is as curved as the young moon—is beheld, a certain curiosity arises that extends everywhere through the playful gestures (*hela*) of love; to conceal this, [the face] was fashioned with flowers poorly placed, arranged otherwise than their previous arrangement.
This, however, is evident already in the first act.
Now, one might object: "Playfulness (*hela*) pertains to women."

As Bharata says: "In youth, the transformations of the women of the gods arise from the casting of glances; among them, three are born of the body (*aṅgaja*), and likewise ten are natural (*svābhāvika*). Regarding those born of the body, the definition of *hāva* and *helā* is as follows: "The movements of the eyes and eyebrows that indicate the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), along with the postures of the neck, are *bhāvas*; from these, the *hāvas* arise."

"That very *hāva* which arises from the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) is designated by the wise as *helā*, consisting essentially of graceful gestures. Therefore, it is incorrect to say "the *helā* toward Mādhava.
Not so.

Because the term "of women" (*strīṇām*) is used figuratively (*upalakṣaṇatvāt*), this applies to men as well, due to the similarity of the stages of passion (*kāmāvasthā*) and because of the mention of *helā*. As it is said: "*Helā* is the desired object; it is the occasion for the offering of knowledge. He offers [it] with a meaningful look, with joy, and with wonder. Having gazed upon the breasts of his beloved, and having properly arranged them like a cluster of flowers at his feet, one part is spread out; that division... the ninth act.
Rising up with joyful madness.

Dear Mālatī, here you are being watched. (As if with anger: O you who do not understand my state! My life-breaths seem to depart, O fair-limbed one; my heart seems to shatter; my limbs seem to burn; and darkness seems to spread on all sides.
This is an occasion for haste, truly not a matter for jest; therefore, bestow joy upon my eyes, and let there be no lack of compassion toward me.
Looking all around with despondency:
"Where is Mālatī here?
(Pointing toward the Bakula garland:)
O Bakula garland, you who fulfill the desires of my beloved, you have been a benefactor;
therefore, welcome to you!
Friend, when the frenzied impulses of Love—burdensome with the calamities of bodily torment—became irresistible and unimpeded, [it was you].
At that time, for the lotus-eyed one, union with you alone was the effective means of saving her life, being almost equivalent to an embrace from me.

Gesticulation (*hāva*), emotion (*bhāva*), artifice (*vyāja*), confidential conversation (*viśrambhabhāṣaṇa*), endearment (*cāṭu*), the expression of love (*premābhisaṃdhāna*), timidity (*cakita*), and playful grace (*vilāsita*).
In that context, "helā" refers to the exhilaration of the mind (*cittollāsa*) which is the cause for engaging impulsively out of passion.
Alternatively, *avaloka* means "that which is looked upon"; the suffix *-ghañ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The meaning is: for the purpose of concealing that unrestrained curiosity of Mādhava which was visible upon beholding the playful gestures on the face of Indu-sundara-Mālatī.
Joy arises from beholding the beloved as depicted in a mental construction;
yet, because that vision is not attained, he says again, "Is it not so? Here too, she is reproached due to the failure to obtain her.

"O! [She says. Fearing that her disappearance might be due to derision, he states that such an occasion does not exist, beginning with "The vital breaths," and so forth: the vital breaths seem to depart from all sides because of the state of emptiness.
O fair-limbed one, my mind seems to crumble from delusion;
my limbs burn with excessive heat.
By this, disease is described.
Darkness seems to spread from all sides; by this, there is a state of insensibility due to the non-perception by all the sense organs.
He says that immediately after this numbness, when there is apprehension of death, consolation alone is appropriate—starting with the word "tvara" (hasten).
The particle "khalu" indicates certainty.
Since this is so, therefore, grant the pleasure of [your] sight.
The meaning is: "Show yourself.
You shall not be merciless toward me;
or rather, you must not be, nor do you become, pitiless.
The particle *māṅ* indicates the *luṅ* (aorist) tense used for general time (*kālasāmānye*).
The meaning is: "Let that former compassion be carried out even now.
The word *iva* is used in the sense of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
"From Niriti," and so forth.

When Mālatī’s—Padmākṣī’s—intense, unbearable agitation caused by the madness of desire arose, becoming exceedingly difficult to endure and bringing great pain from the burning of her limbs, and when the causes of that suffering came together and converged at that moment, at that time, for her, nothing other than your embrace was a swift protector of her life. Therefore, it is equal to my own embrace.
*Unmātha* means *unmathana*, that is to say, agitation (*udvega*).
In the reading *praguṇam*, the meaning is "possessing excellent qualities" (*prakṛṣṭaguṇa*);
or it may function as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
The absence of obstacles arises from the failure to obtain union with the beloved, which causes agitation due to the suffering of desire.
She is called "dear friend" because of her affection for Mālatī;
she is "unbearable" because she causes a lack of fortitude.
*Uddāha* means "intense burning.

Regarding the reading *vyasanasthāne vyathana*, it means "O fierce one, you are seen as a source of distress"; indeed, this is the state of love (*madanāvasthā*). Looking toward the directions, [she says] to the garland: "O you who are supremely helpful, [you are] the remedy for the overwhelming delusion... capable of protection... quickly becoming effective... In the *Mālatīmādhava*, having gazed [at her] with compassion: "At that time and at that time, [the glances] were filled with the essence of deep passion, igniting the fever of love mixed with joy..."
O charming Hara, I painfully remember those movements of yours as you moved back and forth around my neck, creating waves of affection.
Placing it against his heart, he faints.
Mādhava—approaching and fanning him:
Friend, take heart, take heart!
[From the *Samāśvāsa*: Makaranda, do you not see how Mādhava has suddenly obtained from some source this *bakula* garland that bears the scent of Mālatī’s affection?
Therefore, what do you think—whence could this have come?
Therefore, friend, this noble lady is the bearer of the token from the Lord of Yogis, the *Mālatīmādhava*.
Mādhava, looking at her with compassion and joining his palms in reverence, says: "Noble lady, be gracious; tell me, does my beloved still live?"
Saudāminī: My child, take heart, take heart!
That auspicious lady lives. Mādhava and Makaranda: (Recovering their breath)
"Noble lady, if that is so, then tell me: what is this account? Saudāminī: "It is said that Aghoraghaṇṭa, while offering Mālatī at the temple of Karālā with sword in hand, was slain by Mādhava.
Pīḍā: [Laments.]
The underlying sentiment is: "Now, how will her life continue without this garland?"
Having gazed upon and scrutinized [her],
[he says] "O Ānanda," and so forth:
I remember your comings and goings at the throats of both myself and Mālatī.
It is a hardship because remembrance causes such extreme suffering.
"At that time, at that time" means at each respective moment.

In this regard, there is one instance where [the necklace] had gone to Mālatī’s neck prior to the secret marriage, and was then returned when it came to Mādhava’s neck through Lavangikā’s mistaken perception.

In the secret marriage, [the necklace] went from Mālatī to Mādhava’s neck, and then returned after being placed upon her own neck upon seeing his face; this is the second instance of going and returning.
Again, there it went from Mādhava to Mālatī out of affection, and now it has returned after Saudāminī brought it from Mālatī and gave it back; thus there are three instances of going and returning.
For this very reason, the plural number is used.
Of what nature are they?
At that stage, they manifest the heat of desire mingled with bliss due to the occasional attainment of joy;
they are characterized by the union with the essence of firm passion.

Those things in which there is the source (*ākara*) of affection are "affection-generators" (*snehakarāṇi*). They generate—that is, they manifest—affection (*sneha*), meaning love. The suffix *ṭa* is applied according to the rule *kṛño hetutācchīlyānu-lomyeṣu* (Pāṇini 3.2.20).
The word "and" (ca) in the phrase "at that time" (tadā ca) includes other points in time as well.

Makaranda: Noble lady, worthy one! (Sighing) Her gladdening words and her affectionate gestures—[at this, his heart] faints and he falls. Friend, the gain of the very hand of affection! (Bowing with joined palms) Does she still live? Previously, at the temple of Karālā, the beloved friend Aghoraghaṇṭa was stationed with sword in hand. Act Nine.
Mādhava (with agitation):
Noble lady, desist, desist!
The circumstances have been understood.
