Makaranda: Noble lady, is it even so? Saudāminī: It is exactly as my child has understood.
Makaranda: Alas! Oh, how painful! Alas! Alas!

If the moonlight of the autumn moon has united with the bed of night-lotuses for the sake of their mutual beauty, let that be a virtuous deed; but what kind of fate is this, which has now separated them by spreading a mass of unseasonable clouds?

Mādhava:— Alas, dear Mālatī! How painful; you have fallen into a most loathsome state. O lotus-faced one, how indeed did you come to be seized by Kapālakuṇḍalā? You were like a digit of the moon overtaken by a streak of smoke from a portentous calamity.
O Blessed Kapālakuṇḍalā, indeed only a created phantom (nirmāṇa) is to be cherished by them; do not become Pūtanā, but be Śivā! Mādhava:
[The meaning is: "Your desire is fulfilled, for you have accomplished your vow through my destruction."
*Kumudaty-ādi*:
If the autumnal moonlight has united with the cluster of night-lotuses for the sake of the quality of beauty, let that be a virtuous act— a beautiful accomplishment—
since both are lovely.
But what kind of thing is this, or rather, what base sort of thing, that it has yoked and then separated the pair [of Mādhava and Mālatī], like a streak of untimely clouds?
The meaning is that she has caused their separation.
By means of suggestion (*dhvani*), it is stated here that the lily pond is Mādhava, the moonlight is Mālatī, and the mass of clouds is Kapālakuṇḍalā.
"Extremely loathsome" (*atibībhatsam*):
the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) arises from seeing Kāpālika Kuṇḍalā, who is a cause for agitation.
As it is said: "The loathsome rasa arises through many things that cause agitation."
"How," and so forth.
"How were you then, O lotus-faced one, when swallowed by him?
The general inquiry "how" is used to indicate such questions as: "How were you out of fear? What did you say? Who became your protector? and so on.
Like a digit of the moon eclipsed by Ketu;
by this simile, languor (*glāni*) arising from the *bībhatsa* (disgustful) and *viṣāda* (despairing) sentiments is also expressed. As it is said: "Epilepsy, insanity, despair, and intoxication..."
Death, disease, and fear—these states arise from the loathsome.

"You have caused her death while knowing your own duty that 'one must never kill a woman or a child,'" he says sarcastically: "O Blessed One! [He continues with] "Her creation," and so forth. That creation—her form as Mālatī and the like—is something that ought to be protected with great care; it has been offered up. O, by what merit? Let it be for the sake of good deeds. How could she possibly be spread out [as a sacrifice]? She is but a line [of beauty]. At that time, your very nature was that of a *pūtana* demoness. In the *Mālatīmādhava*, it is established that the natural position of a fragrant flower is upon the head, not blows from pestles.
Saudāminī: My child, enough with this agitation. That woman would have committed the sin, being utterly merciless, had I not stood as her adversary there.
Both bowing:
"Our noble lord has been exceedingly gracious.
Therefore, tell us, who indeed is such a kinsman as this to us?"
Saudāminī: You shall indeed come to know this.
(Rising) This [power] of mine is now born from the application of the practice of serving my guru, asceticism, ritual manuals, mantras, and yoga.
I bestow this power of attraction for your welfare.
Thus she exits, having regained her composure.
Māka — Wonderful, wonderful!
Like a terrifying confluence of darkness and lightning, it arose for a moment, obstructing the function of my vision, and then subsided.
He becomes Śiva because of his very loveliness. Do not approach— that is, do not go to— the state of being Pūtanā or a Rākṣasī by means of that destruction.

Alternatively, "the state of being a *pūtana* (pūtanatvam)" refers to the thought, "Since there is meat, it must be eaten by me"; thus, it signifies the nature of a *pūtana*. In the reading "pūtanatvam," the meaning is the state of being a *rākṣasa*.
A *pūtana* is a specific type of female demon (*rākṣasī*), and the term *pūtana* also refers to the *harītakī* fruit.
"Thus, *viśvastātiḥ* means 'be one who brings about welfare.

In the reading *śiva ity abodhīḥ*, it means 'you understood that its creation was for the sake of auspiciousness (*kalyāṇanimitta*) in Śiva. In the reading *śivatām upaiti*, it refers to its creation [as attaining the state of Śiva]."
The agent goes to the state of Śiva, which is auspiciousness;
therefore, this constitutes his protection.
He says that the honoring of auspicious objects occurs by their very nature: the placing of a charming, famous, and fragrant flower upon the head is established by its own nature;
likewise, the crushing [or treading] under the feet is not established by its own nature—this is the meaning.
"akariṣyat" means:
that Kapālakuṇḍalā would indeed have committed that evil act,
namely her murder, because she is utterly devoid of compassion.
If I had not been an adversary to her there at that place or during her killing— this is the *laṅ* (imperfect) used in the sense of a conditional past (*kriyātipatti*).
This is because she was directly perceived by the intellect.
Both:
A most gracious favor has been bestowed.
Saudāminī:
"You two shall know"— this is the implied meaning.
"Heavy," and so forth.
The conduct of the guru, service to the guru, and the weighty conduct are distinguished practices.
Austerity refers to the *cāndrāyaṇa* and other such observances. Tantra refers to the drawing of mandalas and related rituals.
The *mantra* is that of goddesses such as Tārā, or the mantra of this tantra or its verbal expression;
*yoga* is meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Through application to and practice of these, I shall expand for your welfare this accomplishment (*siddhi*) of attraction which has arisen.
Regarding the term *vyatikara* (disturbance/conflict):

because he is ignorant even of Mālatī’s news, this [conflict] is born of the darkness of *tamas*, and for that reason it is terrifying. From the knowledge of her being alive, this [conflict] becomes like lightning; there are the beatings with clubs (*laibana-kuṭṭanāni*). It is difficult [to endure], since she is indeed pitiless. [He is] of such a kind toward Mādhava, and toward us without cause. It will be known through the application of his conduct; through the attainment of success, the *mākarṣiṇī* spell... Thus ends the ninth act.

Seeing [this], he thought with fear, "How is it that my friend is not here? What could this be? Having reflected, he realized: "What else could it be? For she is the Mistress of Yoga, who prevails by her own majesty."
With deliberation: "What kind of matter is this? At present, I am utterly bewildered.
Moreover:"
Our mind— filled with great astonishment, having forgotten all former events, and shattered by the fever of a newly arisen fear—
attains a state variegated by joy and sorrow, as its delusion is broken and then reassembled in a single moment.
"Therefore, having entered this dense forest with my own group, I shall search for the Blessed Lady and relate this account of her.
Thus, all exit.
The ninth act, titled "The Search for Mālatī," is concluded.
"Connected with splendor" (dyutsambandhī);
"mixture" (vyatikara) means contact.
For this very reason, the function of his eyes was obstructed by a flood of tears of joy.
Of what nature is it?
Having arisen for a moment, it is stilled;
therefore, it is like a flash of lightning, characterized by discursive thought.
"How is it that even my friend Mādhava is not here in this place?
What has become of him, or by whom has he been taken away?"—this is the sense of his reflection.
He states the conclusion: "What else could it be?"
The meaning is that she has been led away by this mistress of yogis, who prevails through the power of her own asceticism.
He says "What is this? while doubting;
the meaning is that there is a purpose (*artha*) in bringing Saudāminī, whereas there is a disadvantage (*anartha*) in bringing Kapālakuṇḍalā.
[Regarding the verse beginning with] *astoka* and so forth:
Our mind is the agent;
it undergoes a state of variegation, that is, a mixture, through joy and sorrow.
Of what kind? It is of little wonder,
because various aesthetic sentiments (rasas) arise simultaneously.
Therein, the former event consisting of the abduction of Mālatī has been forgotten; hence there is joy.
Yet, a new fear has arisen, caused by the suspicion of harm to Mādhava; by that fever it is worn out, and hence there is sorrow.
Or rather:
it is that in which delusion— shattered by the fever of a fresh apprehension arising from not seeing Mādhava, and intensified by grief—
is both broken and reassembled in a single moment.
The sense is that [the plan] was broken by the hope of obtaining Mālatī and joined again by the suspicion of Mādhava’s malice;
for this very reason, it is most extraordinary.
The word *stoka* is a synonym for "little."
By our group, [namely] Madayantikā and Lavaṅgikā;
in a certain manuscript the reading "vipranaṣṭām" (lost) is seen, which means "not being seen."
To the venerable Kāmandakī.
Since this also indicates the entry into the subsequent act, it is an "act-transition" (aṅkāvatāra).
The ninth faultless chapter has concluded in this new commentary composed by Jagaddhara, whom the highly learned Ratnadhara and Damayantī, whose learning was radiant, brought forth.

Thus ends the ninth act. [End of Act IX]. What else? I am deluded by this calamity that has befallen me of its own accord. O awakening, O joy, enough! Having followed him here at the conclusion of the night, the scene involving the sight of Saudāminī has ended; he has departed. In the *Mālatīmādhava*, the tenth act begins. Then enter Kāmandakī, Lavaṅgikā, and Madayantikā.
Kāmandakī (with compassion and tears):
Alas, child Mālatī, you who adorn my heart, where are you? Give me an answer!
From the moment of your birth, those various deeds of yours were delightful at every passing moment; now, alas, they are gone.
The charming and sweet words of endearment, once remembered, burn the body and tear the heart asunder.
Moreover, my son, I remember your lotus-like infant face— with its incessant crying and smiling, its few radiant and tender bud-like teeth, and your faltering, incoherent, and charming prattle.
The others: Sāla!

O dear friend, you whose moon-like face is so serene and beautiful, where are you? Or rather, who can endure the ill-conduct of fate toward your body, which is as delicate as a *śirīṣa* flower, when we—your own circle—are present? By indicating this immediately, he describes her entrance with the words "Then... (*tataḥ*).
Having heard of Mālatī’s separation, Kāmandakī laments: "Alas," and so forth;
"From birth," and so forth.

From the moment of my birth, those various previously experienced gestures of yours—such as modesty and the like—which have become more charming with every passing moment, now that they are remembered, burn my heart and rend it asunder.
By this, external and mental affliction is described.
Likewise, flattering words and verbal skills are known to cause burning sensations and the like.
The charm of discipline and other virtues lies in their being free from hatred.
What kind of flatteries (*cāṭūni*) are they?
They are beautiful (*cārūṇi*), radiant, sweet, and free from vulgarity. As it is said: "In all circumstances and specific states, whether intense or graceful..."
The absence of harshness in actions is designated as sweetness (mādhurya).
"Indeterminate," and so forth:
I remember this lotus of yours, O young girl.
Of what sort is it?
Where there is unstable weeping and laughter,
and where the tips of the slightly tender buds of the teeth shine,
yet falter due to the absence of proper placement and effort.
It is "incoherent" (*asamañjasam*) due to the loss of reality, or it is "incoherent" due to the transgression of number or ignorance. It is "deluded" (*mugdham*) because of the absence of meaning.
"Jalpita" refers to that wherein there is dull speech.
In all cases, childhood alone is the cause.
In the word *kamalaka*, the suffix *kan* is used in the sense of "small.
It is called *samañjasam* because it exists properly, directly, and in accordance with reality (*tattvena*).
According to the Viśvakośa, "añjasā" means both "truth" and "quickly.
"Mañju jalpitam" means speech that is charming or beautiful.
The others:

Here, for her who is alone and whose nature consists of a single measure (ekamātra), those words beginning with "ādāvupasthita" and "athā madalaṃkārakā," O lovely-eyed one, which were spoken even in the sky—those very words are beautiful and charming. [Madayantikā: Lavangikā, that indeed! Act Nine.
Moreover:

Because she had lost all hope regarding me before the marriage rites, she expressed her affection through tears so full of piteous longing— as if distressed by the agony of a vital wound being torn asunder— that even I became one whose mind was rippled with pain.
With agitation:
Alas! Indeed, O friends!
My heart breaks with intense anguish, yet it does not split in two; my distressed body trembles, yet it does not abandon consciousness.
The internal burning inflames the body but does not reduce it to ashes; the stroke of fate cuts into the vital organs but does not sever life itself.
"Friend, the cruel sun burns like an unrestrained fate,
and such is the condition of your body. Therefore, let us sit for a moment on the bank of this lotus pond."
For here, because it is included within the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), there is no agitation for the wise;
as stated by Daṇḍin: "Where there is no agitation for the wise [it is *dhvani*]."
"Mayi," and so forth.
"Friend, you remember that she [the beloved] expanded her display of affection through such weeping that even I, whose mind was already restless with pain, became truly so"—
here, the word "iti" (thus) is to be supplied.
Otherwise, the action would not be possible.

Since weeping is produced by compassion, he states the cause of that compassion: "Before the marriage ceremony, my senses (the organs) were observed to be dejected due to despair regarding me, and turned away from their respective objects.
By this, delusion (*moha*) is expressed.
The third case ending is used in the sense of a characteristic.
Of what kind? As if characterized by the pain of the cutting of vital organs and so forth.
By this, her state of trust is expressed,
as the cutting of her vital organs is inferred from her sighing.
Thus, the pathetic sentiment (karuṇa-rasa) is expressed through sighing, weeping, and fainting.
Or rather, he performed the other [rite] in the same manner, as if with impaired organs that were, as it were, silenced.
"O, how wonderful indeed!"—thus [expresses] astonishment.
"It splits," and so forth: my heart splits, that is, it breaks asunder, because it is accompanied by pain.
It does not split in two; that which is split in two does not exist.
The meaning is that when it bursts open, the pain is pacified.
The word *śabda* itself [is used] either for the sake of meaning or for the sake of emphasis;
[it is said] "it is not divided again," which implies that it is not divided. The form *bhidyate* is the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending used in the sense of the reflexive passive (*karmakartari*).
And yet it cracks, yet it does not break—this is an apparent contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*).
The same applies to what follows:
the body is overwhelmed and falls into delusion, yet consciousness does not abandon its presence.

Furthermore, due to the association with consciousness, when delusion is stable, the thought arises: "May I achieve my purpose through suffering and ignorance. Thus, the two types of internal calamities have been described here.
Internal burning inflames the body but does not reduce it to ashes;
the meaning is that it does not completely turn it into the form of ash.
*Sāti* means "completely."
The intention is that, such being the case, there would be nothing but suffering and ignorance;
by this, the calamity pertaining to living beings (ādhibhautikī) is described.
Thus, in this context, delusion and so forth are mentioned in the state of illness.

As it is said: "The dramatic representation of illness should be performed through mental confusion, a burning sensation throughout all the limbs, physical agitation, and likewise through pains in the head."
Thus, here the self as delimited by the body is expressed by the term "body.
Otherwise, it should be understood that since delusion is a property of the self, it would be impossible for it to exist in the body.
According to Amarasimha: "In the feminine, *mūrti*, *tanuḥ*, and *tanūḥ* [mean body]."
In order to remove his dullness and to turn Mādhava’s mind elsewhere, he says, "Friend," etc.,
meaning in an unrestrained and unimpeded manner.
[He is] broken by the compassion arising from his state of distress. Friend Mādhava, this forest fire is unrestrained. [End of page]. Here it is: In the *Mālatīmādhava*, [the verse reads:

The breeze—its kinship with fragrance intensified by its contact with the flowing nectar of the blossoming young lotus-pools, chilled by the frost-like spray of the waves rolling before it—will delight you.
They walk about and sit down.
Mādhava—
(to himself) Let it be.
Thus, for now, I shall interrupt you.
[Aloud] Friend Mādhava, here— where the large-stalked white lotuses quiver, shaken by the wings of swans warbling with intoxication;
Let the intermediate spaces between the falling and rising of teardrops be seen, possessing an uninterrupted splendor.
Mādhava rises with agitation. How is it that, having risen, he has turned away elsewhere, devoid of resolve?
(Sighing, he rises and speaks to Makaranda.)
"Friend, be gracious!
Look, look! Lomaśa said: "The wind—'unnāla' and so forth—will gladden you, will make you joyful here."

He describes its suitability: "Mixed with the fragrance that is nourished by the trickling of the nectar from those young clusters of lotuses whose stalks have emerged due to the scarcity of water at the end of summer;
and [a breeze] cool, sluggish, and gentle with the spray of tossing waves—or rather, cool and chilled by the frost-like spray itself."
"Ākara is said to mean a collection, a source of origin, and something excellent," according to Medinīkara.
[The word is] *mākaranda*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied [to form a derivative] in the sense of "this belongs to that."
Distraction (*ākṣepa*) is the state of having the mind elsewhere.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In this," etc.:
here, let the regions of the earth be observed in this lake.
Fearing that they might not see him because their eyes were filled with tears, he said: "Between the falling of one tear and the rising of another.
Of what sort were they?
They were like lotuses with long stalks swaying as they were shaken by the wings of a particular kind of *haṃsa* bird, whose sweet, indistinct cries were uttered out of joy.
And they are joined with blue lotuses.
There is no tautology here, because previously the "distinguished lotus" was mentioned, whereas here only the "blue lotus" is specified;
or else, previously the "white lotus" was mentioned.
In this case, however, there is no fault in saying "that is blue.
By the mention of the white and dark lotuses being mingled together, their extreme loveliness is expressed.
Regarding the reading *avirahitaśriyaḥ*, *śrī* means either beauty or Lakṣmī.
Because of their constant dwelling in that lake, they are thus endowed with beauty; this is the meaning. "Those [swans] with dark [marks] are *mallikākṣas*," according to Amara.
From the *Medinīkośa*, which states "mallikaḥ haṃsabhid api," it is understood that he whose name is Mallika [is meant].
Furthermore, it should be noted that the alliteration (*anuprāsa*) in the word "nāgarāge" is possible even through identical phonetic resonance (*samānaśruti*).
The sense is that it is "with agitation" because of the unbearable nature of the cold wind and other such factors.
Avoiding the giving of counter-arguments and so forth, as well as looking at the scriptures,
silence and mental inactivity indeed occur in the state of being dull-witted.
Thus, with wonder, he says regarding Mādhava, "How [is this]?"—a sign of insensibility.
Having observed it, he says, "This is not insensibility, but rather remembrance," namely, "The void.
The void is that which is without a perceptible object; the remembrance arises from departing from that state.

Or rather, with its surging movement, turning back as it gathers life-force—thus "pari" [is used]. O Earth, possessing blue lotuses, known as the land of Malla, accompanied by longing! The water, which has taken up residence along the banks of the rivers and groves of *vānīra* reeds, now blooms at their edges with the buds of *yūthikā* flowers. As the clouds spread out like canopies over the mountain peaks, which laugh with blossoming *kuṭaja* trees, they provide a stage for the dancing of peacocks upon the ridges. Ninth Act.
Moreover:
the quarters of the sky, possessing the dense beauty of kadamba trees whose clusters of blossoms are loosened by yawning, become dark with banks of clouds over the expanse of the mountains;
the riverbanks bear lovely ketaka flowers with emerging sprouts; and the forest ranges smile with the fragrant silindhra and lodhra blossoms.
It is empty of anything else because of the non-perception of any object other than Mālatī;
for this very reason, due to intense longing, there is a recollection of other activities as previously described.
Regarding the reading "empty of non-apprehension" (apratipatti-śūnyam), the meaning is that there is a departure from consciousness through inattention, or in whatever manner [the mind] may arise.
"Vānīra," and so forth: O friend, behold the water of the rivers belonging to the grove;
it is infused with fragrance by the flowers of the cane trees (*vetasa*).
And in the vicinity of those very [trees], it has blossomed with the clusters and buds of *yūthikā* flowers;
or rather, with the clusters of both *yūthikā* and *sumanas* flowers.
*Yūthikā* is commonly known as *jūhī*.
The *jāti* flowers are *sumanas*.
As Amara states: "The *mālatī* and *jāti* are *sumanas*.
Likewise, having taken hold of the ridges—the various parts—of the mountain, the clouds here form a canopy over the peaks.
The practice of spreading a canopy is performed for the purpose of enacting the peacock dance; this is an instance of the locative case used in the sense of "purpose" (nimitta-saptamī).
In what kind [of clouds]?
Those possessing smiles in the form of blooming *kuṭaja* flowers.
Thus, the meaning here is: "Behold that canopy formed by the clouds for the sake of the peacock's dance, and that smile consisting of *kuṭaja* flowers."

Thus, the *kuṭaja* trees are the spectators and the peacocks are the dancers; the cloud is the canopy—this constitutes the equipment for the dance. Furthermore, by the word "peacock" (*śikhaṇḍin*), the jester (*vidūṣaka*) is indicated through his head being endowed with five crests (*pañcacūḍā*). And by the word "slope" (*prāgbhāra*), the spectator who is a fool is indicated: one whose burden (*bhāra*) is difficult to bear is a "forward-burdened" (*prāk*) person, meaning one possessing excessive knowledge (*prakṛṣṭajñāna*). Sound (*dhvani*), however, refers to the jester by means of the term "peacock," due to the presence of the five-crested head. And by the term "slope" (*prāgbhāra*), the foolish spectator is indicated, as it means one for whom there is a "forward" (*prāk*) and "excessive" (*pra*) burden (*bhāra*) of [misguided] cognition.
And his laughter is indeed appropriate;
or rather, by the word *śikhaṇḍin*, the boy is referred to as one possessing three tufts (*tri-śikhaṇḍa*);
and a fool laughs at such a dance.
"Even for children, the ornament of the three crests must be worn."
Thus is the proof for the peacock-hood of the young ones.
Regarding the term "vānīravañjulāḥ," Amara states:
"Kṣāraka" is neuter and means "jālaka"; "kalikā" is feminine and "koraka" is masculine, both meaning a flower bud.
And thus:
in the sense of "he performs a canopy," from the root *tan* with the suffix *kyan*, followed by *āya* and *kyaṅ*, the form is *vitānāmyate*.
"Jṛmbha," and so forth.

O friend, behold that wherein the lands at the edges of the mountains have become *jarjara*—torn asunder—by the *ḍimba*, the swelling mass, through the process of *jṛmbhā* or expansion; and because they are pervaded by this *ḍambareṇa* or onset, the majestic *nīpa* trees therein become such as they are.
Thus, in every direction, the quarters of the sky become dark with masses of clouds.
Alternatively, they are darkened by *kādambinīs*, which are the flocks of female *kādamba* swans;
and the riverbanks (*kacchāḥ*) become beautiful with lovely *ketaka* trees that possess emerging, blossoming *kandalas*—that is, new sprouts.
Or rather, it means that the lovely *ketaka* tree has an emerging *kandala*, where *kandala* refers to its bulbous root (*kanda*).
*In the Nīvāra-niha-bhāga [section] of the *Jharjhara*: In the *Mālatīmādhava*, Mādhava says: "Friend, I see it.
However, the mountain terrains of the forest are now difficult to behold because of their beauty.
So, what is this?"
[With tears] Or rather, what else?
The rows of clouds, glossy as fragments of sapphire, are tossed by the eastern gale that blows scented with the blossoms of the *arjuna* and *sarja* trees.
Now these days have arrived, fragrant with the earth sprinkled by showers of rain, bearing the splendor of the transition between the departure and arrival of the waters of summer.
"O dear Mālatī!"—thus says Amara.

Or rather, the meaning is that she bears a forest (vana) consisting of rising *kandalas* and *mallikā* trees, as well as lovely *ketakas*. She is as if smiling with the *śilīndhra* and *lodhra* flowers, which possess the fragrance of a garland of forests (*vanamālā*) whose scent is becoming manifest.
Or it is pleasing to the mind.
According to the *Viśva* lexicon, "śilīndhra" means the flower of the *kandalī*.
Śilīndhra is known as "sūla."
"In this context, *vana* means a lotus, water, or a forest;
*jṛmbhā* means both yawning and blooming," according to the Viśva lexicon.
"The word *ḍimba* refers to a mass and also to a ball," according to the Dharaṇi lexicon.
"Ḍambara is a masculine noun meaning 'commencement' (samārambha)," according to the Viśva lexicon.
"Kādambinī is said to mean 'a row of clouds' as well as 'the female of the kādamba bird,'" according to Śāśvata.
"Kandala refers to a quarrel, a bulbous root, a wrestler, and a cluster of sprouts."
"Thus says Medinīkāra:
'The word *kaccha* is masculine when it refers to such [a place]; it is neuter when meaning water, a lotus, a forest, or a dwelling.
Thus says Medinīkāra.
"Utphulleti," etc. The meaning is:
"Now those very days have arrived which were held fast by me through my imagination.
Here, by the use of the two pronouns "ta ete" (those these), the fact that these days are the cause of extreme longing is suggested (*dhvani*).
Of what sort are they?

They are those in which dark clouds—resembling fragments of sapphire, dislodged from their positions and scattered by the swaying and tossing of the eastern gale (the fierce wind or monsoon breeze), which carries with it the fragrance of blossoming *arjuna* and *śāla* trees. Here, although only the *arjuna* is mentioned, the inclusion of the second tree, the *sarja*, is intended as an illustration for the *kadamba* and others as well.
Likewise, they possess the fragrance of sprinkling the earth scorched by the summer heat;
they possess a slight rain because of its emergence from that [sprinkling].
They are those whose nature it is to bear the beauty—the splendor—arising from the conjunction (*vyatikara*) of the departure of the summer heat (*gharma*) and the arrival (*āgama*) of water.
Alternatively, "vigamāgama" refers to the departure and arrival of the "gharmāmbhas," which is the water of perspiration; their "vyatikara" is their conjunction.
This means the onset of the rainy season.
"Tadvāhin" means possessing the excellence (śrī) of that [onset].
"Paurastya" is derived from "puras" with the suffix *astyak*. According to Modinīkara, "jhañjhā" refers to a particular kind of sound;
wind accompanied by that is "jhañjhānila."
Alternatively, the *Ratnakośa* states: "The *jhañjhānila* (gale) is that which belongs to the rainy season (*prāvuṣeṇya*).

Here, although one should have used the word *vāsyamāna* (being scented), the employment of the word *vāsita* (scented) at the end of the compound indicates the transfer of the fragrance of all the flowers to the wind; thus, the excellence of the gale is hinted at.
Mādhava is in the state of madness.
And madness [arises] from separation from what is beloved;
as it is said: "Madness [results] from separation from a loved person and from the loss of wealth."

Distant is the riverbank; the wind is agitated; the jewel of Indra’s sovereignty is a woman. Thus, because the action is complete, there is a suffix denoting the past perfective state (*pariniṣṭhā-pratyaya*). For this very reason, [it is said] "from Malaya"—the ninth act. With clouds rising thickly, dark as young *tamāla* trees, and with fresh droplets of water shaken by the cool breeze;
How shall we now behold the quarters of the sky made resonant by the warbling of peacocks intoxicated with passion, which bear the marks of Hari’s arrows?
[He gesticulates the end of his grief.
Makaranda: A most terrible turn of events has now befallen my friend.
[With tears.]
I, however, acting like a thunderbolt, began a diversion. (Sighing) And thus, our hope regarding Mādhava has almost entirely come to an end.
Looking around apprehensively: What? He has actually fainted!
[Looking into the air:]
Mālatī, Mālatī! What more can be said? You are utterly merciless. Out of greed, you have committed this act of violence against one whose kinsmen you have cast aside.
Therefore, O friend, what is this cruel course of action toward my innocent beloved?
Why does he still not breathe?
Alas, I have been deceived by fate!
Mother, Mother! My heart is splitting, the bonds of my body are crumbling; I perceive the world as a void, and I burn within with an unceasing flame.
Sinking into blinding darkness, my distressed inner self is drowning; how can I, unfortunate as I am, act when delusion obstructs me on every side?
"O young woman," and so forth.
How may I now behold the quarters of the sky?
They are those in which there arise abundant clouds as dark as young *tamāla* trees, or else blue like them.
They possessed fresh droplets of water tossed by cool breezes;
they were equipped with the weapon of Hari, namely Indra’s bow;
and they resounded with the clamor of peacocks warbling in rut.
According to the Viśvakośa: "Kalaham means both strife and clamor.
In the reading *saritaḥ* (rivers), they possess the nature of clouds by virtue of their reflections.
They are possessed of birds named after Hari’s weapon, the discus (*cakra*).
One who is afflicted by suffering perceives the seasons as consisting of suffering alone.
As it is said: "Afflicted by suffering, one sees all the seasons as being entirely dependent upon suffering."

Thus, by this continuous exposition, the rainy season has been described. As it is said: "One should indicate the monsoon season by means of the kadamba, nīpa, and kuṭaja trees, by the grassy meadows, by the indragopa insects, and by the clouds and winds that are pleasant to the touch."
"From grief," he says;
the sense is that he falls down in a swoon. Makaranda.
Amusement is the composure of the mind;
one who is stupefied is devoid of consciousness;
compassion is pity, whereas you are its opposite.
"Apetya," and so forth:
O friend, you have committed this rash act out of greed for a mere trifle. Therefore, O beloved, what is this merciless conduct toward me, who am pleased and innocent?
"What is this sequence of yours? is the meaning; the implication is: "How can you be so merciless as to abandon such a husband?"
The *ucchvāsa* (aspiration) is the recovery of consciousness.
"O Mother! and so forth;
"O Mother! O Mother! expresses agitation (*āvega*).

"My heart is split in two"—this is the pain. "Yehama" (alas)—sighing thus, he says: "This grief, which is exceedingly intense, prevails at this moment. With that which is like a thunderbolt—meaning, acting like a thunderbolt—he has begun to divert himself; yet again, through ignorance, as it were, with that which is like a thunderbolt, he has commenced this diversion. Generally speaking... [Mādhava’s reply: Friend, do not trouble even me with such timidity. [In the *Mālatīmādhava*, uninterrupted and unimpaired: Alas! Oh, what misery! What misery!

That very moon who is the festival of moonlight for the hearts of kinsmen, the charming moon for the eyes of Mālatī, that Makaranda— the delight of his kin and the ornament of the world of living beings— is today perishing.

Alas, friend Mādhava! You who were sandalwood paste upon my limbs, the autumnal moon upon my eyes, and indeed joy itself within my heart— you, so exceedingly lovely, have been snatched away by Time all of a sudden, like my very life, and I am destroyed.
O merciless one, bestow upon me a glance radiant with a smile; O most cruel one, grant me your speech!
Why do you not acknowledge your beloved Makaranda, whose heart is devoted to you as his companion?
Mādhava regains consciousness; his limbs become limp, indicating a state of physical malaise. "I consider the entire world empty" refers to external perception, which is despondency.
"I burn within as if with unceasing flames" refers to the burning sensation produced by anxiety.
*Glāni* (dejection) is when the inner self, being without support and sinking, undergoes despondency as if plunging into dense darkness.
*Moha* (delusion) is that which covers or obscures from all sides and everywhere.
*Dainya* (wretchedness) is the thought, "I am unfortunate; what shall I do?"
How is the word *katham* used? It is used in the sense of "what" (*kim*).
Because it is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), it possesses multiple meanings.
In the word *viṣvak*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs because it belongs to the *suṣamādi* group.
He speaks of lamentation: "Alas!

and so forth. The meaning is that this very person—the festival for the minds of his circle of kinsmen, the young moon to Mālatī’s eyes, the producer of joy for Makaranda, and the ornament of all people—is today meeting his end.
"A great festival" (mahā-uddhava-utsavaḥ), according to Amara.
"Upon my limbs," and so forth: you who were the sandalwood essence upon my body because of its pleasant touch.
In his eyes, he was the autumn moon because of his capacity to produce bliss;
in his heart, he was bliss itself, appearing as if it were raining down directly.
I am destroyed by Time, by Fate, or by Yama, who has suddenly uprooted you—who had passed away—just as one might uproot my own life;
the sense is that just as I was "killed" when my life was extracted, so too am I killed by the extraction of you.
Possessed by madness, he laments: "O merciless one," and so forth.
"O heartless one, give me a glance charming with laughter"—that is to say, look at me with a smile.
Or rather, [the meaning is] "radiant" through the blossoming of a smile—that is, fully opened. O you who are exceedingly cruel in speech and in taking [what is not given], give me my word!
O dear Makaranda, whose heart is devoted as a friend, why do you not heed me?
Why do you not accept this?
Here, because of the presence of agitation (*āvega*) and other such transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*), there is the rasa of compassion (*karuṇa*).
As it has been said: "By the loss of what is desired, the departure of wealth, the misfortune of a kinsman, and by beatings..."

The sentiment of compassion (*karuṇa-rasa*) arises from curses, afflictions, and injuries. It is to be represented by the wise through tears, sighs, paleness, drooping limbs, loss of memory, lamentations, grief, and so forth. [Thus ends the ninth act of the *Mālatīmādhava*. Then, touching his heart and body, [the King says: "O innocent one... [End of Act Nine.]
[With a sigh of relief:
This [cloud], with its thick and beautiful luster like a freshly washed royal turban, revives my dear friend with a shower of water droplets from fresh clouds.
By good fortune, he has at last drawn breath!
Mādhava: So, whom shall I employ here in this forest to bring news of my beloved?
(Looking) Excellent! Excellent!
To the north of the flowing river, whose slender ripples are checked by groves of jambu trees dark with the ripening of their fruit-laden weight,
a fresh cloud— deep blue as a mature tamāla blossom— breaking apart as it rises above, takes refuge upon the mountain peak.
Rising with great impetuosity and joining his palms in reverence, he asks:

"O gentle one, does your dear companion, the lightning, embrace you, made beautiful by her manifest affection? Or do the cātaka birds, lovely through their burgeoning love, attend upon you? Or does the eastern breeze bring you joy, bearing the auspicious marks of Indra’s bow and spreading its beauty through its skillful fanning?"
Makaranda:
By the mention of the "recently washed" state of the royal turban (*rājapaṭṭa*), its blueness and glossiness are expressed.
*Rājapaṭṭa* is known as *khaḍī*.
He whose complexion and luster are beautiful, radiant, full, and dense—
[that is] Mādhava. A messenger is one who conveys news.

When the time has become excessively advanced, one should dispatch a messenger; as it is said: "One who is afflicted by irresistible passion and has arisen from many circumstances should send forth his own messenger in order to reveal his condition."
"Phaletyādi" and so forth.
A fresh cloud takes refuge on the mountain peak,
near the northern bank of a river whose waves are small due to stumbling against the groves of rose-apple trees (*jambū*) darkened by the ripening of their fruit-laden branches.
The second [verse] is as follows: Of what sort? "Cracking open above," meaning abandoning its upper position;
"blue like a blooming mālatī flower," that is, blue like that.
Regarding the reading *upacitaghanamālā*, the meaning is "those who possess accumulated and dense garlands.
"Dense" (*ghana*) refers to extreme blackness due to its freshness.
Alternatively, it means "resting in various ways upon the flowing river," breaking apart as it flows above.

"Uttareṇa" means "in the northern region. The word "uttareṇa" is an indeclinable (nipāta) that functions like a case ending; it is used in the same manner as the expression "kiñcid eva uttareṇa" (just a little to the north).

The verb *ghaṭ* (to flow) is transitive because its meaning involves an objective substratum (*āśraya*). According to Amara, "sravantī," "nimnagā," and "apagā" all mean a river. By the phrase "with palms joined" (*kṛtāñjali*), humility is expressed;
for a message must be delivered preceded by such modesty.
As it is said: "One should deliver a message concerning love to the messenger;
indeed, one should convey 'her condition is such' with humility through a narrative."
"Kaccit," and so forth.
He utters a question regarding his beloved, appropriate for a request: "O gentle one, O handsome one, does your dear, beloved companion—the lightning that follows you constantly—embrace you?
Tell me," is the meaning.
*“Kaṃcit” [is used] in the sense of making a request, according to Amara.
Because of the state of separation, there arises a longing for the beloved; hence, first comes the inquiry regarding union with the beloved.

*Cārucandrajala-daḥ*—how is this? What is it like here? *Pariṇāhaskhalita-*; those of slender bodies, those with thick and abundant garlands, those who move about with respect, those with beautiful faces, those who are talkative, and those who are happy—this is the presence of *lakṣmī*. [Thus ends the passage] from the *Mālatīmādhava*, having heard [this].
Ah! The blue-necked peacock, his longing delighted by the mountain caves filled with echoing sounds, greets me with a deep "hum" following his single cry;
I shall therefore address him.
O Blessed Cloud!
If, by chance, while wandering through the world, you should behold my beloved, first comfort her, and then describe Madhava’s condition;
for the thread of hope, if not spoken of, cannot be utterly severed, and it alone somehow effects the preservation of the long-eyed one’s life.
"Saumya" [is used] for "jayoḥ," according to Śāśvata.
It is implied that you too know that there is happiness in the embrace of a beloved and sorrow in separation from her;
or else, the meaning is: "Is this indeed agreeable to me?"
The fortunate and fair-faced cātaka birds serve you because they have conceived affection for you;
or [the word "vā" indicates] a conjunction. By this, the fulfillment of the needs of supplicants is expressed.
The forewind also comforts you with gentle breezes; there is an implied suggestion that even another companion performs a massage for you by grasping your feet and fists.
By this, the excellence of your companionship is expressed.
Bearing beauty and splendor on all sides, the rainbow acts as the agent that spreads your mark— that is, your emblem.

Regarding the phrase "otherwise":
the matter that occurred through stealth refers to the act of marriage.

Having seen us gathered from afar, the noble Saudāminī, Avalokitā, and Kalahaṃsā have begun right there, overflowing with joy; and the swan, seeing us arrived from afar, is dancing right there, overflowing with joy—he comes this very way. "Everything is completely fulfilled, everything is perfectly accomplished"—in place of the words "who indeed could be [otherwise]," [it should be] "even the past task has been completed here. Therefore, he dances in a festival of every kind of accomplishment.
His task too is now complete;

therefore, he dances in this great festival of every kind. (I.Pā. Thus, it is a great abundance, a great wonder, a source of delight, an exquisite beauty, a perfect form—how can that be? The matter has proceeded otherwise; the turn of words [ends]. Tenth Act.
Lava—(Aside) Venerable lady, what should be done?
"Revered one, what should be undertaken?
Kāmandakī—
(to herself) "Now, indeed, because of the alliance with Madayantikā and the securing of Nandana, our apprehensions have been dispelled."

[Aloud] Dear children, the facts of the matter are certainly not otherwise; for during our time as disciples, this vow was made before our very eyes by Saudāminī: "We must certainly establish a matrimonial alliance between these two.
Thus, the provocation of the primary ministers has been avoided.
Mālatī: Oh, what a concealment! Oh, what a concealment!
Mādhava and Makaranda: How marvelous!
Victorious are the auspicious policies of the great, which conceal their own praise!

Kāmandakī: My child, that very blessing which was previously desired by your long-lived self through your heart's wishes has now borne fruit through your merits and my own efforts; even the hardship endured by my two disciples has been rewarded.
A meeting has been arranged for your beloved with his wife, and both princes are well-pleased. Tell me, what further favor can be requested?
"Minyā's speech is otherwise," meaning that it is beyond the reach of ministers. Lavaṅgikā.
The intention here is to ask: what is the nature of Saudāminī’s speech? Kāmandakī [says]:
"O listener" (*śrāvaka*)—this refers to the state of being a reciter (*pāṭhaka*).
Prakṛti: [He is] instructed.
Mālatī:
Oh, what a concealment!
In this context, the words "of my father, the minister" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. Mādhava and Makaranda [say]:
"The thought is that I have become fortunate."

"Yad ityādi": O long-lived ones, that auspicious mutual acquisition which was previously chosen and desired by you both through mere mental aspirations has now borne fruit through your merits and my own undertakings, employing the stratagems of a messenger whose mission is already accomplished.
The suffering of my two disciples, Avalokitā and Saudāminī, has also borne fruit; this is understood through a change of gender (liṅgavipariṇāma) due to its appropriateness.
If the reading is "kleśena" (by means of suffering), the meaning is that it has borne fruit by those two alone.
Likewise, the union of your friend Makaranda with Madayantikā has been accomplished—meaning it has been performed without hesitation.
The two princes have been made exceedingly dear [to her];
for this very reason, there is fearlessness.
What is the point here? [She speaks] aside, because of the connection with the word "Nandana. The actual matter has proceeded one way, yet her speech is otherwise.

Frustrated in their presence, he approached the battlefield. Truly, the auspicious, reliable, and effective strategies of the great prevail; truly, the auspicious policies of the great, which are consistent and unerring, prevail. The auspicious women of the great are not confounded nor do they act perversely; indeed, for the great alone, they are praised as being free from blemish. My dear Mādhava, [this is] by our... through sufferings, and even in suffering. And through completion, and fullness, and expansion—what [more]? In the *Mālatīmādhava*, Mādhava—bowing with joy:
"Venerable Lady, there is something even more pleasing than this."
Nevertheless, by the grace of the feet of the Blessed Lady, may this come to pass:
may the virtuous be ever contented, their rise of sin destroyed; may kings, established in righteousness, protect the earth at all times;
may the clouds rain continuously in due season upon the earth through merit; and may the subjects rejoice in the delight of assemblies with their kinsmen, relatives, and friends.
Thus all exit.
Thus ends the tenth act of the *Mālatīmādhava*.
Thus the drama named *Mālatīmādhava* is completed.
Furthermore, let that which is more excellent than the highest, which is dear and ought to be performed, also be told.
The meaning is: "I shall do that."
"May they be peaceful," and so forth.
May virtuous people be constantly righteous.
Herein lies the reason.
"May the excess of evil be destroyed.
Thus, the meaning is: "May the merit of the virtuous flourish and may evil perish.
May kings, ever established in the duties of sovereignty such as protection and so forth, protect the earth.
By the term *vasudhā* ("the earth"), which means "she who bestows wealth" (*dhanaṃ dadhāti*), the possession of abundant riches by the earth is expressed.

May the clouds be disposed toward raining in such a way that they are well-distributed and pervasive at the proper time—such as the beginning of the rainy season—and not contrary to the growth of crops.
The word "proper time" (*kāle*) is used because the destruction of crops occurs through unseasonal rain.
He states the reason for this: "by the merit of the people, of the worlds.
May the subjects rejoice!
They are those by whom there is great joy in the assemblies of kinsmen, relations, friends, and companions, which is firmly bound—that is, made continuous.
Thus, by this, the eulogy has been stated;
the conclusion of the poem has also been made by this very means. As it is said: "The statement of the granting of a boon is the conclusion of the poem."
Thus it is said.

The rare teaching was obtained from Kaivartika, who was like a leader of the host of gods; and even while both auspicious umbrellas, adorned with the lineage of his learning, were being held [over him], there arose this Caṇḍeśvara, the ornament of the twice-born—a scholar whose heart was mastered by the singular secret of Mīmāṃsā, and a giver of pure intent.
In that stainless lineage, Deveśa gave birth to this very Mīmāṃsaka Satkavi; he, too, was born as the highly learned Rāmeśvara, a master of Jaimini’s doctrine.
He, in turn, begot a son of pure intent, the excellent poet Dhīra-Gadādhara, who surpassed his opponents through Mīmāṃsā and was adorned by it.
He bows and delivers the Bharata-vākya:
"May there be auspiciousness and prosperity for all the worlds; may the hosts of beings be devoted to the welfare of others;
may faults come to rest everywhere, and may the world be happy."
Firm in their conduct, they are bound by the enjoyment of their social circles. Beyond this, there is nothing more than the fulfillment of desire—let it be so.
Thus ends the tenth act of this work composed by the illustrious Bhavabhūti.
This [work] produced Vidyādhara as its excellent son—a steadfast diamond among men, victorious, and one who has mastered the sciences taught by his preceptors.
He has brought forth this stainless and virtuous son, Ratnapūrvadhara, and this Jagaddhara.

May this *Ṭīkā* (commentary) on the poem of that world-renowned poet flourish—he by whom was studied the crushing refutation of the hard-to-defeat Gautama and Vaiśeṣika systems; by whom was heard the entire collection of poetic works along with their commentaries and the doctrine of Pāṇini; and by whom were mastered prosody, poetics, and the auspicious Bharata [Nāṭyaśāstra], as well as the Veda.
The tenth faultless chapter has reached its conclusion in this commentary composed by Jagaddhara, whom the most auspicious Ratnadhara and the most beautiful Damayantī brought forth.

Thus ends the tenth act in the commentary on the *Mālatīmādhava*, composed by Śrī Jagaddhara, son of the venerable Ratnadhara Paṇḍita— the illustrious Mahopādhyāya, Paṇḍitarāja, Mahākavirāja, and Dharmādhikārin—
who has made the words of Bhavabhūti, whose seal is the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha, his own abode.
